World.title: The final innings
World.content:
People observe a minute’s silence for West Indian cricket legend Sir Garfield Sobers ahead of the third one-day international cricket match between England and India at Lord’s Cricket Ground in London on July 19, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

BRIDGETOWN, Barbados (CMC) — Garfield St Auburn Sobers played his final innings at the Kensington Oval here on Wednesday under bright sunshine for nearly three hours, still able to mesmerise local, regional and international spectators, most of whom, including Britain’s King Phillip, acknowledging that there have been few, “whose name alone brings a smile to people’s faces across Barbados, the Caribbean and the entire Commonwealth”.

Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, in her “grateful from the nation” tribute at the State Service of Thanksgiving, said the visit to the Kensington Oval, “this most iconic of cricket grounds where Sir Garry’s casket was draped with the national flag of Barbados”, was to pay tribute, “but also to send a message to the future”.

She said the 89-year-old Sir Garry did not come to be the best or the first or the last, but “came to do his best and to be his best, not for the world, but for goals that he set himself, conscious that if he did that, along with whatever else everyone else did, that glory could come, victory could be assured”.

Sobers was buried one day after he would have celebrated his 90th birthday, and Mottley said that the gods would have conspired to ensure that the West Indies cricket team had defeated the visiting Pakistan test team by 90 runs on Tuesday in Trinidad and Tobago, thereby allowing the seven members of the regional team to attend the ceremony.

“I say today as we say farewell to you, Sir Garry, this is your final walk from Kensington Oval. This will be our country’s last opportunity to give you that which you became so accustomed to, a standing ovation,” Mottley said in blazing sunlight over the picturesque ground on the outskirts of the capital, Bridgetown.

“I ask each and every one of us in this Oval today …to let us stand and give Sir Garry, our Sir Garry, our hero, our beloved man. A man who guided me in my own personal journey with the confidence that I think that each and every one of us as children need to take on this world.

“We thank you for teaching us that greatness could wear humility, that excellence could still belong to ordinary people, that the dreams of a little boy from the Bayland could become the inheritance of an entire nation,” Mottley said of the man, who until July 17, was one of two Barbados living national heroes, the other being the internationally acclaimed singer, Robyn Rihanna Fenty, who was also present at the funeral.

Former West Indies captain, Brian Lara, who in April 1994 broke Sir Garry’s long-standing world record of 365 runs which he made against Pakistan in 1958, in an emotional address, described the gifted batsman as “my mentor, my dad, and my friend”.

Lara added: “First time I met you, you were Sir Sobers. Over the last few days I struggled with what I would say today, but now I am here, I realise something, this is not a sad moment, this is a moment for us to celebrate and I hope you feel the same.”

Lara said he hopes that 10 years from now when there will be a celebration of Sobers’s 100th birthday “we might also be celebrating the rebirth of West Indies cricket”.

Another former West Indies captain Sir Clive Lloyd, who at one time played alongside Sobers, said, “Today I believe we can honour Sir Garfied in ways that extend beyond statues and ceremonies, worthy those are.

“His extraordinary achievement as a fast bowler, as a left-arm spinner, in three distinct styles, as perhaps the greatest close catcher of the game ever seen, and as an incomparable batsman, should become the foundation of institutions dedicated to nurturing future generations.

“Today, we should study not only what Sir Garfield accomplished, but how he accomplished it. What inner drive compelled him to reach such heights? What vision inspired him each time he walked to the crease or began his run to the wicket? What dreams guided him as captain of the West Indies team?”

The Guyanese-born Lloyd said that these are questions worth asking because the answers can inspire generations yet unborn.

Sobers represented West Indies between 1954 and 1974 and played 93 Test matches, scoring 8,032 runs at a spectacular average of 57.78. Sobers also claimed 235 wickets at an average of 34.03 and an economy rate of 2.22. By an act of Parliament in 1998, Sobers was named as one of the 11 National Heroes of Barbados.

Two of Sobers’s children, Mathew and Daniel, recalled the influence their father had on their lives.

“Whether it was cricket, table tennis, golf, or just shooting hoops with the kids, he was blessed with rare talents few people had. But as I grew older, I realised his greatest gifts had very little to do with sport, but everything to do with the way he lived,” Mathew Sobers said.

“The world knew him as the Right, Excellent Sir Garfield St Aurbun Sobers. Many believed he was the greatest cricketer who ever lived,” he said noting, “but remarkable as those achievements were, they tell only part of the story.

“Dad was born into a Barbados still emerging from the long shadow of plantocracy and colonial rule. At a time when opportunity was limited for so many, he became living proof that excellence could come from these shores.

For his part, Daniel Sobers, who together with Matthew flew into Barbados from the United States, and with his younger sister Genevieve cutting short a visit to Australia with her mum, described his father as “the greatest”.

He said while he welcomes the avalanche of thoughts, prayers, and kind words about his father, he would like to thank all those who had been taking care of his father “during the more than 18 months of his steady decline”.

“Growing up, I never really understood the gravity of the mastery of my dad’s achievements. I was born into his life and just took them for granted. For me, it was a thing of normalcy.

“Doesn’t every dad at the age of 21 score 365 not out and hit six sixes in an over whenever he feels like it? What I also remember is that he was always busy and travelled a lot, and that I missed him when he was gone,” Daniel Sobers added.

Following the funeral, Sir Garfield Sobers, considered to have been the greatest all-rounder in cricket’s history, was given a 19-gun salute as his body was buried at the Coral Ridge Memorial Gardens on The Ridge, Christ Church Parish.

World.title: Dream Wknd, partners ready to welcome thousands to MoBay
World.content:
Mobay Mayor Richard Vernon addresses the recent launch of Dream Wknd 2026 held at Pier 1.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Dream Entertainment Limited, St James Municipal Corporation, and Jamaica Constabulary Force say all systems are in place for Dream Wknd’s inaugural staging in Montego Bay.

With months of planning and cross-agency collaboration will culminate in what is expected to be one of Jamaica’s largest entertainment events of the summer.

More than 30,000 patrons are expected to descend on the tourism capital over the coming days for the festival’s first staging outside its long-time home of Negril, bringing a significant boost to the local economy while showcasing Montego Bay’s growing capacity to host major international events.

Chairman of Dream Entertainment Kamal Bankay said organisers have spent months working alongside government agencies, venue operators, and service providers to ensure every aspect of the festival is ready ahead of Thursday’s opening.

“We have been working very closely with the venues and the planning authorities in St James,” Bankay said. “That includes the municipal corporation, the Jamaica Constabulary Force, the Ministry of Health, the Jamaica Fire Brigade, and the other agencies responsible for issuing the relevant approvals.”

He said the work has extended beyond regulatory requirements to include detailed coordination with venue operators and event partners responsible for delivering the festival experience.

“Based on where we are now, all of those preparations have been completed and the necessary systems are in place, so we’re ready to welcome patrons when the events begin on Thursday,” he said.

Bankay added that while Dream Wknd will deliver its signature entertainment experience, the festival also provides visitors with an opportunity to experience Montego Bay beyond the event venues.

“When you come to Montego Bay, just know that it’s a great city in its own right, and Dream Wknd is really there to elevate what’s already on offer,” he said. “Visitors can enjoy the city’s hotels, restaurants, beaches, and attractions throughout the weekend.”

Mayor Richard Vernon described Dream Wknd’s arrival in Montego Bay as a significant milestone for the city, saying it reinforces its standing as one of the Caribbean’s leading tourism and entertainment destinations.

“Dream Wknd’s expansion to Montego Bay is a landmark moment for Jamaica’s tourism capital,” Vernon said. “It affirms our city’s reputation as a premier entertainment destination in the Caribbean and demonstrates confidence in our ability to continue hosting world-class events, even during our most challenging times.”

Vernon said his team has worked closely with partners to ensure the city is prepared to welcome the influx of visitors. Traffic management plans have been finalised, public health protocols activated, and emergency contingencies established to support the festival weekend.

“Our hospitality sector has mobilised to meet demand, while local businesses are prepared… This readiness ensures that Dream Wknd will be a successful event and drive sustained economic activity across Montego Bay,” said Vernon.

Senior Superintendent Eron Samuels, commander of the St James Police Division, said the police have developed a comprehensive security plan in partnership with other stakeholders.

“Our objective is to create a safe environment where patrons can enjoy the festivities while residents and visitors continue to feel secure,” Samuels said.

He encouraged patrons to celebrate responsibly by planning their transportation in advance, avoiding drinking and driving, securing their personal belongings, remaining aware of their surroundings and following the instructions of police officers, event security personnel and emergency responders.

“Our message is simple: Enjoy the event, make lasting memories, but make safety your priority,” he said.

In addition to extensive logistical preparations, organisers say patrons can also expect an elevated festival experience through the involvement of Dream WKND’s major brand partners, each bringing unique activations designed to complement the music and entertainment.

Red Stripe and its portfolio of brands will deliver vibrant social spaces across four signature events: Guinness at Dream Live, Casamigos at Daydreams, Red Stripe at YUSH, and Smirnoff at Igloo. Meanwhile, the Campari Group will bring premium activations, signature cocktail experiences, and interactive brand engagements to Wet ‘N Wild with Magnum, Foul Play with J Wray & Nephew, and Xodus Remedy presented by Campari.

Festivalgoers can also look forward to high-energy experiences from Boom Energy Drink, whose touchpoints are designed to keep the excitement going throughout the weekend. Mother’s will round out the culinary experience with specially curated dishes prepared throughout the weekend, providing hearty, flavourful meal options to keep patrons fuelled while they enjoy the overall festival atmosphere.

Dream Entertainment says the collective investment by its corporate partners reflects a shared commitment to delivering a world-class entertainment experience, with immersive brand experiences carefully integrated into the festival to ensure patrons enjoy much more than just the performances onstage.

World.title: Safety or red tape?
World.content:
DALRYMPLE-PHILIBERT... said any organisation introducing a programme for children has a duty to satisfy itself that those involved are suitable.

A spirited debate erupted during a sitting of Parliament’s joint select committee reviewing the Child Diversion Act on Wednesday, after Government Senator Sherene Golding-Campbell questioned why licensed psychologists, who are already vetted by their professional regulatory body, must undergo additional background checks before being allowed to work with children in the Child Diversion Programme.

However, committee members, including chairman Delroy Chuck, argued that the additional scrutiny is essential because vulnerable children are involved, insisting that no safeguard should be overlooked when selecting professionals to work in the programme.

The disagreement emerged as the committee examined provisions of the Act dealing with how counsellors and psychologists are approved to provide services under the Child Diversion Programme, which seeks to rehabilitate children who come into conflict with the law rather than exposing them to the formal court system.

Under the existing law, the minister is empowered to approve counsellors and psychologists for use in the programme. The legislation also requires standards and procedures to be set for the operation of diversion services.

Golding-Campbell questioned whether that approval process was necessary for psychologists who are already licensed to practise under Jamaican law.

“If they’re registered under the Act, what is the purpose of a background check on a psychologist? I’m not understanding that,” she asked.

Director of the Child Diversion Branch in the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Venisa Clarke explained that the programme uses a range of mental health professionals, including psychologists, counsellors, clinical social workers, and guidance counsellors.

She said the background checks are carried out not because the professionals are unqualified, but because they will be working closely with vulnerable children.

“Every psychologist that touches base with the Child Diversion Office or contacts us, we have a list of things that are required. We have a checklist that they have to meet certain criteria. Once that is done, we indicate to them that we are now going to move to get the approval to engage. The first aspect of that approval is that a background check has to be done as well, and we have to see that they are certified,” Clarke explained.

She said the background check includes more than a criminal record search.

“For the mental health service providers, we engage a private member of society that does that for us. It includes a visit to their community, getting information from NIB [National Intelligence Bureau], as well as a sex offender registry, a whole list of things, and the report includes if they find any adverse traces or anything of that sort,” she added.

Golding-Campbell, however, argued that the process appeared to duplicate checks already carried out by the bodies responsible for licensing professionals. She also questioned whether the programme was making the best use of limited public resources.

“I appreciate that it’s children, but if these professionals are registered, they’re registered. If they have a valid registration under the Act, they’re registered. I’m not understanding why we would commit resources to a private investigator to find out whether or not they have convictions,” she queried further.

The senator also questioned why the minister should have the power to approve individual psychologists and counsellors if they have already met the legal requirements to practice in Jamaica.

Her concerns were met with resistance from several committee members.

Chuck acknowledged that professionally registered psychologists may require less scrutiny than other groups, but said the ministry still has a responsibility to ensure every person working with children can be trusted.

“You don’t know which of these personnel could abuse the child. And therefore, the background check is absolutely important… The last thing we would want is we put the child to interact with a mentor, and the mentor turns out to be a paedophile,” he said.

Member of Parliament for Portland Eastern Isat Buchanan also defended the practice, arguing that professional registration alone cannot guarantee that a person poses no risk to children.

“Background checks for the purpose of child diversion are about adverse findings. There are persons who have come in conflict with the law that have not been brought before the court because other things would have happened…So if we are protecting the child, Minister, respectfully, you sit in the chair right now. It is the approval by you, because if anything should happen I will be the first to say, ‘How could the minister make this happen? Heads should roll!’, and I will be the first to say ‘Resign, resign, resign’,” he expressed.

State minister in the Ministry of Justice Marisa Dalrymple-Philibert similarly backed the existing approach, saying any organisation introducing a programme for children has a duty to satisfy itself that those involved are suitable.

However, Golding-Campbell maintained that her concern was not with protecting children but with making sure the system is logical and consistent. She argued that if the programme believes extra vetting is necessary, then it should not happen only once at the beginning.

“If it is that you want to be satisfied that they are safe people for children separate and apart from their registration under law governed by another body, then it must be something that you’re telling me you’re satisfying yourself of periodically, because to satisfy yourself when they are approved does not hold for the entire time that they participate in the programme. Being good in 2022 doesn’t mean that I haven’t committed some offence that would disturb you in 2025,” she said.

That argument appeared to win some support from Chuck, who agreed that repeat checks should be considered.

Clarke also welcomed the suggestion, confirming that, while background checks are currently mandatory before a professional joins the programme, the ministry would consider introducing periodic reviews.

World.title: LEAPING TO HISTORY
World.content:
Tajay Gayle (Photo: AFP)

TAJAY Gayle created history on Wednesday when he won Jamaica’s first-ever men’s long jump gold medal at the Commonwealth Games (CWG).

Shot putter Lloydricia Cameron claimed a bronze medal at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland, as Jamaica’s medal tally went up to four — inclusive of three gold and a bronze — at the 23rd edition of the Games.

Romaine Beckford and Demario Prince had opened Jamaica’s medal account on Monday with gold medals in the men’s high jump and 110m hurdles, respectively.

Expectations are high for more medals on Thursday with finals in the women’s triple jump and discus throw competitions.

After placing fourth at the 2018 Commonwealth Games in Australia, Gayle jumped 8.15m (1.5m/s) to become the first Jamaican man to win a long jump competition. He is the first Jamaican man to win a medal at the Games since Wesley Clayton won back-to-back bronze in 1962 and 1966.

India’s Sreeshankar took consecutive silver medals after a best mark of 8.09m (1.3m/s), just ahead of Stephen Mackenzie of Scotland who was third with 8.08m (0.9m/s). Jamaican Jordan Turner was ninth with 7.65m (0.1m/s).

Cameron, who won her first national championships title this year, improved on her fourth-place finish from four years ago in Birmingham, England, taking the bronze with a best of 17.87m in the final round to eclipse Manpreet Kaur of India.

Canada’s two-time World Athletics Indoor champion Sarah Mitton defended her title with an effort of 19.88m. Nigeria’s 19-year-old Jessica Oji took the silver medal with 17.87m, getting the edge over Cameron with a better second throw.

National champion Ackelia Smith and NCAA winner Shantae Foreman are set to take on world leader and Olympic champion Thea Lafond of Dominica in the women’s triple jump on Thursday.

Jamaica’s Samantha Hall is the Commonwealth leader in the women’s discus throw and will start as pre-championships favourite going into the final.

There will also be qualifying in the 100m hurdles in which Kerrica Hill and Megan Simmonds are set to compete. In the men’s triple jump Jordan Scott, who is ranked number one, is also down to feature.

Kelly Ann Beckford qualified for the final of the women’s 800m after placing third in her semi-finals in 1:59.96, beaten to the finish line by Lilian Odira (1:59.39) of Kenya and Shafiqua Maloney (1:59.81) of St Vincent and the Grenadines.

Adelle Tracey was fourth in her heat in 2:01.54 for 10th overall.

Other Jamaicans, including 200m and women’s 400m hurdles runners, progressed past the first round of their respective events on Wednesday.

National champion Sanique Walker and Shiann Salmon, the latter who was second four years ago in Birmingham, topped the qualifying in the women’s 400m hurdles.

Walker won her heat in 54.83 seconds and Salmon topped hers in 55.30 to booked places in Friday’s final.

National champion Assinie Wilson was second in his first round heat in the men’s 400m hurdles in 49.19.

Lavanya Williams and Alana Reid were also the fastest in the women’s 200m first round.

Williams ran 22.91 (0.8m/s) to win heat five and national champion Reid clocked 22.95 (1.7m/s) to claim heat six as they made safe passage through to Thursday’s semi-finals.

All three Jamaican men also advanced in the 200m.

Christopher Taylor was second in his heat in 20.36 (1.6m/s), the same time given to Ghana’s Joseph Paul Amoah, who was declared the winner.

Roshawn Clarke won his heat in 20.56 (1/0m/s) and Jevaughn Powell recorded a wind-aided 20.28 (2.6m/s) to top his heat.

World.title: Chef Colin Brown’s HOMECOMING CHAÎNE FEAST
World.content:
Yellowfin tuna crudo with lime-ginger marinade, Scotch bonnet oil, ripe mango salsa and breadfruit crisp (Photo: Aceion Cunningham)

Sun-kissed afternoon, the hum of conversation, and the clink of glasses set the scene at Uncorked Ochi at Drax Hall on Sunday, July 26 as Chaîne des Rôtisseurs Jamaïque, Select Brands, and Uncorked hosted a celebratory bistro brunch showcasing the return of Chef Colin Brown to Jamaican shores. Brown — back from an international run of kitchens — teamed with Uncorked’s culinary team to present a lively fusion of island flavours and classic French techniques that won praise from members and guests alike.

The cold and seafood station opened the meal with refined island flair: Yellowfin tuna crudo brightened with a lime-ginger marinade, Scotch bonnet oil, ripe mango salsa, and a crisp of breadfruit; and an escoveitch conch paired with calabash lobster, spiced pickled vegetables, allspice, and lime zest that married Caribbean acidities with steely seafood sweetness.

The opening of the smoked and slow-roast station followed. A pimento-smoked salmon with a rustic salsa; golden goat, glazed with Appleton rum and finished with a nutmeg-thyme jus offered deep, caramelised rum notes; and Blue Mountain coffee-crusted pork belly, lacquered in a tamarind-molasses glaze balanced bitter, sweet and savoury. Braised oxtail croquettes, stuffed with a butter-bean purée with chive oil, provided a textural and flavourful nod to Jamaica’s comfort-cook traditions, while a live action station with pimento-smoked roasted leg of lamb, scented with rosemary, orange zest and tarragon, rounded out the roast offerings.

Side dishes and local provisions were treated with equal care: roasted sweet potatoes and breadfruit crowned with coconut butter and toasted pimento, herbed yam croquettes, creamy coconut rice with gungo peas, callaloo-pak choi sautéed with ginger, garlic and island five-spice, and an inventive green banana risotto studded with aged local artisan cheese. These accompaniments anchored the menu in terroir while supporting the international techniques on display.

Dessert showcased Jamaica’s signature ingredients in elegant formats: Wray & Nephew rum and gingerbread pudding bathed in warm coconut custard, a sorrel-hibiscus panna cotta with candied ginger, and a guava tart in flaky coconut pastry. Sweet finishes were complemented by a chilled limoncello cooler pairing that cut through the richness.

Select Brands curated the beverage pours, pairing the menu with a sparkling and wine line-up that included Veuve Clicquot Brut NV, Kettmeir Pinot Grigio 2024, Terra Alpina Chardonnay 2022, Aqua di Venus Rosé, Tassajara Pinot Noir 2022 and Dominio Fournier 2020. The thoughtful beverage selection underscored the brunch’s balance of celebration and culinary craft.

The event was both a welcome-home for Chef Brown and a statement of culinary collaboration — a tasteful fusion that celebrated Jamaica’s pantry while leaning into French technique and presentation, a thrust Brown is quick to emphasise in the Jamaican culinary space.

“We have to cook our own food, add our cultural perspective and use the techniques from France, Italy and we’ll become masters by taking an indigenous cuisine and refining it. For today’s menu we used the Seville orange, rice vinegar, Mirin, sushi ginger, ripe mango, tomato and we boiled the breadfruit in the skin, sliced thinly, fried it to make a nice crisp and this came out really well for the yellow fin tuna. escoveitch conch and lobster, we made a lobster bisque for the base, boil it and season only with Scotch bonnet powder, sear it, keeping it fresh and nice. For the conch we cooked it for hours and sliced it thinly, tossed and fried keeping it crispy,” Brown explained.

“The salmon was done of more a jerk style but with more kick to it. Everyone is more use to curry goat, but we slow-cooked the goat with Appleton rum, nutmeg and thyme, making it a well-balanced dish. The crispy pork belly was cooked in Blue Mountain coffee jerk for two and half hours and glazed with June plum and lime and dusted with Blue Mountain coffee, giving you the sweet, sour, coffee flavour and the jerk. The oxtail was also slow cooked and the lamb leg we marinated for three days,” Brown added.

World.title: Jamaica snatch last minute draw against Panama in U20
World.content:
Jaquan Brown of Jamaica celebrates his equaliser in the young Reggae Boyz' Concacaf Under-20 Championship match against Panama on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. The game ended 2-2. (Photo: Concacaf/Instagram)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica rallied from two goals down to earn a courageous draw against Panama in their Concacaf U20 Championships Group C at Estadio Universitario BUAP in Puebla, Mexico on Wednesday.

The result kept Jamaica’s hopes of advancing to the quarterfinals alive as they are on four points, one more than Canada who will play Honduras in the second game, while Panama are on one point from two games.

Jamaica are also third in the overall rankings that include teams from the other groups, only behind the USA and Mexico, both of who have won their first two games.

Desperate to earn a win after losing 3-0 to Canada on Sunday, Panama got off to a fast start and were ahead 2-0 after 22 minutes with goals from Moisés Richards in the 13th minute and Carlos Rodriguez in the 22nd minute.

It could have been worse had VAR not ruled out another goal for Panama in the 36th minute.

Jahmarie Nolan, who had scored the first goal in the 2-1 win over Honduras, pulled a goal back for Jamaica in the 62nd minute before Jaquan Brown headed home a freekick from second half substitute Jamione Lyle in time added.

It was the second time in a row that Jamaica scored on the final play of the game, in time added, after Brandon Bent had scored the winner against Honduras in time added.

The coaches had made one change to the starting team, Che Gardner of Stockport County replacing Sean Leighton.

World.title: Week Ender — Searing Contradiction: Wildfires and climate politics
World.content:
Wildfires may sound remote — something that happens deep in a forest or on an empty mountainside. But in Europe, there’s often very little distance between nature and major population centers. That’s why the fires near Bordeaux and Madrid have been so frightening: they’re not burning somewhere far away, but threatening homes, businesses and entire urban regions.

European countries are responding by sending planes, helicopters and hundreds of firefighters to help one another. But while Europe has built an effective system for reacting once the flames are raging, it’s still struggling with the less dramatic work of prevention.

POLITICO senior climate reporter Zia Weise joins host Sarah Wheaton, sustainability reporter Marianne Gros and Agnes Rønberg from the agriculture team to examine how abandoned land, poorly managed forests and disappearing livestock are making fires harder to control.

They also unpack the growing bill for homes, farms and businesses — and how the costs eventually spread to insurers and cash-strapped governments — while asking whether Brussels can prepare Europe for worsening climate disasters as it rolls back parts of the Green Deal.

World.title: Football and politics, brought to you by Big Business (and energy drinks)
World.content:
In “United Passions” — which really should have been called “Balls” — Blatter is played by Tim Roth, a fine actor who admitted he took the role to pay for his kids to go to college. If the movie was, heaven help us, ever updated to include Infantino’s tenure, surely the role would go to either Stanley Tucci or the ghost of late Wagner mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin.

Infantino has, you will doubtless be aware, decided to sell football off to the highest bidder, with FIFA publishing a proposal that would privatize the World Cup’s commercial operations. A venture capital firm headed by Josh Kushner, brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is lined up as the lead investor in the proposed deal. Of course it is. The scheme is known as FIFA Forward Enterprise or FFE — although FFS seems rather more appropriate.

I, for one, am looking forward to the Raytheon World Cup of 2038 in South Sudan, where the 18-karat gold trophy depicting two human figures holding up the Earth is replaced by a cheap plastic bobblehead of Trump with his pants around his ankles.

But not everyone is so keen on Infantino’s plan. Glenn Micallef, the EU’s sports commissioner, pointed out that football “isn’t baseball,” which is very perceptive of him. It’s also not cross-country skiing, knitting or a cauliflower.

Micallef’s point is, of course, that football hasn’t — and shouldn’t — reach the level of commercialization of American sports, although it had a damn good go during this summer’s World Cup with the introduction of hydration breaks sponsored by Powerade.

But the further monetization of sports feels inevitable; it is entertainment, after all. Will politics go the same way? When, for example, will we see EU summits sponsored by Red Bull, the European Commission midday briefing brought to you by Xanax, or Germany sponsored by sausages in a glass jar?

World.title: Why Andy Burnham is no ordinary Labour prime minister
World.content:
The Labour Party and the Co-operative Party are distinct organizations — but a pact agreed in 1927 allows candidates to stand on behalf of both parties.

In practice, Co-operative MPs tend to follow the Labour line — but the party has a distinct focus on mutual ownership, community businesses, and credit unions. It argues for democratic control of services and businesses by the people who use them — and supporters say this program offers up real hints about how Burnham will now govern.

Since returning to the Westminster frontline, the new prime minister has hardly been shy about his administration’s support for the co-operative drive.

“If people, in 1844, could form the co-operative movement in Rochdale to lower the price of food, then why can’t we act now, with similar courage, to make life better?” he asked in his first major speech after winning the Makerfield by-election. That was a direct callback to a group of working-class weavers — known as the Rochdale Pioneers — credited with founding the modern cooperative movement by pooling wages to set up a worker-owned store at a time of soaring food costs.

The Co-operative Party was “created for a slightly different purpose” to Labour, says International Development Minister Kirsty McNeill — a Labour and Co-operative MP like Burnham, It is about getting a better deal “as a consumer in the marketplace and where you live.”

“It’s going to be a moment of unprecedented opportunity for the co-operative movement,” says Caitlin Prowle, the party’s assistant general secretary. “I believe that this new team is very serious about rewiring our economy, rewiring society and shifting power.”

World.title: Russia’s Olympic win comes with a price for Putin
World.content:
But while Russia has been trumpeting its big diplomatic win, and the IOC has drawn international ire for its decision, what Moscow quietly agreed to in order to achieve its victory garnered far less attention — a quiet renunciation of what Moscow claims as “sovereign territory.”

What lies behind the IOC’s reversal was confirmation that the Russian Olympic Committee “no longer includes as its members any regional sports organisations in territories falling under the jurisdiction of the National Olympic Committee of Ukraine” — that means Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson.

A woman holds a sign with the text “Boycott Russian sport at the Olympics” during a march in memory of the hundreds of Ukrainian athletes killed since the Russian invasion of Ukraine, in Paris on July 13, 2024. | Remon Haazen/Getty Images

These four territories of great economic, industrial and historic importance for President Putin have been a major sticking point in ending the war since Russia annexed them in 2022 in defiance of international law. And this concession made on the global stage is now turning into a domestic political scandal, drawing criticism from the country’s influential pro-war commentators who see it as a betrayal of the Kremlin’s territorial claims.

“The Russian Olympic Committee gave up part of the country’s territory just to live it up in style at the Olympics,” wrote famous pro-war journalist Dmitry Steshin — just one of many discontented voices.

‘Sabotage at a state level’

This is not the first clash between the Kremlin’s international sports ambitions and its influential military bloggers.

Russia’s attempts to send its athletes to the 2024 Olympics under neutral status — a restriction imposed by the IOC after 2023 — had similarly triggered widespread backlash, with the country’s pro-war commentators accusing authorities of “betraying national interests.”

World.title: Italy and Spain clash over Schengen as Ceuta migration spat boils over
World.content:
“We are prepared to take action — including through extraordinary measures — to defend our borders and ensure citizens’ safety,” she added.

Meloni, along with Italian Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani — the most senior ministers from each of the parties in Italy’s ruling right-wing coalition — has called for the suspension of the Schengen agreement, or for Spain to be kicked out of the free-travel zone.

Under the agreement, people can move freely between the 29 European signatory countries. However, several countries have reintroduced checks on some of their borders, which is allowed under the treaty, citing migration risks. Italy has already temporarily reinstituted checks on the Slovenian border to clamp down on smuggling and terrorism.

A frame grab from an AFP video showing migrants reaching the shore of the Spanish north African exclave of Ceuta after swimming around the border fence between Morocco and Spain on July 30, 2026. | Lucía Diaz/AFP via Getty Images

Tajani went further than just calling for Spain to be shut out of Schengen, pinning the blame for the Ceuta unrest on Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s migration policy — which promises to legalize hundreds of thousands of unauthorized migrants — calling it “profoundly wrong” and claiming it “provides and incentive for human trafficking.”

That drew a stern rebuke from Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares, who has summoned the Italian ambassador — a mark of serious diplomatic displeasure — to answer for Tajani’s comments.

“This message is unbecoming of the foreign minister of a partner and friendly country from which we expect European solidarity, not partisan demagoguery,” he fired back in a public reply to Tajani on X.

World.title: Climate change made Spanish wildfires 20 times more likely
World.content:
The scientists had already found that climate change increased the likelihood of the record-breaking Western European heat wave in late June as well as the spring drought — both events that made land more fire-prone.

“These mega-fires show how fast climate-driven extreme heat and dry landscapes can turn wildfires into devastating national disasters,” said United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell in a statement responding to the findings.

“Humanity continuing to burn colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas is baking our planet, making these conditions more dangerous, and these megafires more deadly and destructive,” he added, calling for a faster transition from polluting fossil fuels to clean energy.

The researchers looked at a fire risk metric incorporating hot, dry and windy conditions, as well as landscape conditions during the worst fire week near Madrid and Bordeaux. They then compared this year’s situation to the worst conditions in previous summers and juxtaposed the current climate with a simulation of the planet’s pre-industrial state.

The study also established that in today’s climate, similar fire weather is expected to occur every 20 years in southwestern France and every six years in central Spain.

A key driver of the increased fire risk was weather whiplash earlier this year, with a dry spring following a wet winter, the scientists added. These conditions fueled excessive vegetation growth that then dried up, providing plenty of fuel for fires to spread.

“What we’re seeing in France and Spain isn’t just bad luck, it is a clear sign of the escalating impacts of anthropogenic warming,” said Clair Barnes, a climate scientist at Imperial College London and the lead researcher on the analysis.

"Every fraction of a degree of warming pushes us into unknown territory, and these fires show exactly what that risk looks like," she added.

World.title: Search called off for GB surfer who disappeared off coast of Portugal
World.content:
Authorities have called off a search for a British surfer who disappeared off the coast of Portugal earlier this week after failing to locate the missing man.

 

Arran Strong, who had competed in the World Surf League since 2016, went missing off of Arrifana beach in Portugal's southwestern Aljezur region on Monday.

According to Portugal's Autoridade Marítima Nacional (AMN), the 28-year-old had reportedly got into difficulty in the water while paddleboarding with a friend from Monte Clérigo beach to Carrapateira.

The friend, who has been identified as his coach José Maria Pyrrait, was rescued by a local fishing boat, per the AMN.

Pyrrait has shared details of the moments leading up to Strong's disappearance in a post on Instagram, writing that the pair had stopped for a drink and to take some photos as they made their way to Carrapateira.

"When we set off again, I let him go ahead," he wrote. "As I’m a faster paddler, I always did that – whenever I caught up with him and gained a short lead, I’d stop and wait for him. This time was no different, but when I stopped to wait, I saw his board drifting about 100 metres away.

Pyrrait said he then "paddled as fast as I could" to where Strong's board was and dived to look for him.

"But we were in very deep water and visibility was very poor, so I called for help from my partner on shore, who immediately alerted the rescue services," he went on. "A local fisherman picked me and the surfboards up, and we spent nearly two and a half hours scanning the entire surrounding area with the boat’s sonar."

Pyrrait added: "Arran was like a son to me; from the age of 10, he trained with me and spent his weekends and holidays with me."

"My love for him was like that for another son that life had given me."

In a post on Instagram, GB Surfing paid tribute to Strong, calling him a "fantastic teammate" and "respected competitor."

"His passing is a devastating loss to our sport and the wider surfing community, and he will be greatly missed," it said, adding: "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with Arran’s family, friends, teammates and all those whose lives he touched."

World.title: Italy calls for closing Schengen area to Spain over Ceuta migrant crisis
World.content:
Italy's foreign minister has called for the closure of the Schengen area to Spain after hundreds of migrants crossed into the North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco on Thursday.

 

In a post on X, Antonio Tajani said he was "in favour" of closing the free travel zone with Spain, arguing that "irregular and uncontrolled immigration poses a threat to national security."

"The images coming out of Ceuta show that the Madrid government’s decision to grant Spanish – and therefore European – citizenship to over 500,000 irregular migrants is profoundly misguided and encourages human trafficking," he added, apparently referring to the Spanish government's previous move to give legal status to some undocumented migrants. Spain's foreign minister said he had summoned the Italian ambassador over what he called Tajani's "inappropriate" comments.

Italian PM Giorgia Meloni echoed Tajani's words in another post on social media, saying Rome was ready to take "extraordinary measures" to defend Italy's borders, including through the "suspension of the Schengen area with Spain."

Migrants cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Thursday, July 30, 2026. Antonio Sempere/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

Madrid said on Thursday that it would deploy the army to Ceuta to reinforce security after the crossings, which saw many migrants swim around the border fence. Nine people reportedly died attempting to reach Ceuta.

It comes after the enclave's regional president urged Madrid to declare a national emergency and assume control of the situation in the autonomous city, warning that local authorities had become overwhelmed by the surge in illegal crossings.

The Spanish Interior Ministry had initially ruled out declaring a national emergency. It later announced the deployment of troops to help restore order and reinforce security in the territory. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is expected in Ceuta on Friday as political pressure grows from the opposition.

Meanwhile, the European Commissioner for Migration, Austria's Magnus Brunner, said he was in constant contact with the Spanish authorities and stressed that protecting the EU's external borders remains "a crucial part of our efforts to fight illegal migration".

The European Commission said it had offered operational support through Frontex.

The scenes recalled the 2021 migration crisis, when around 10,000 people entered Ceuta over the course of two days. While Morocco says it is cooperating with Spain and the EU to manage the latest arrivals, Rabat has previously been accused of using migration flows to exert political pressure on its European neighbour.

Spain and Morocco agree to speed up returns

Hundreds of people reached Ceuta from Morocco on Thursday, swimming or using inflatable devices to arrive at Tarajal beach, overwhelming Civil Guard officers.

More than 60 people have died attempting the crossing over the past 12 months.

Sánchez said his government was "fully committed to providing an immediate response to the situation in Ceuta" and pledged to work with the Moroccan authorities to "restore normality as soon as possible".

Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska is expected to travel to Ceuta to meet local officials and assess the situation. The two countries said they had agreed a procedure to accelerate returns, although no timeline or figures were made public.

The Spanish Interior Ministry also said human trafficking networks may be exploiting a recent court ruling to encourage undocumented migrants to attempt the crossing. Rabat blamed traffickers too, even-though its law enforcement also handles the border.

Moroccan diplomatic sources said the increase in irregular crossings did not reflect any intention by the authorities in Rabat to facilitate or promote illegal migration into Spain.

Spain's Civil Guard sources in Ceuta, however, questioned the level of Moroccan cooperation, arguing that support from the Moroccan Gendarmerie had been limited and insufficient to ease pressure at the border, despite the Spanish government's insistence that cooperation with Morocco remained active.

World.title: Italy: recipe for ancient elixir, possible Coca-Cola precursor, found in convent
World.content:
In the archives of the historic San Marco Pharmacy, in Florence, a mid-19th-century slip of paper has been found containing the recipe for an "Elixir vinoso ricostituente", described as a drink capable of easing physical and mental fatigue and weakness caused by age or exertion.

 

The person who found the recipe was Father Manuel Russo, rector of the San Marco convent.

"I stumbled across the old advert for this elixir while I was consulting our archive. I began delving deeper into the documentation kept in the convent and discovered that it was one of the most sought-after products in the friars' pharmacy," he told the weekly Toscana Oggi.

The composition and history of the recipe

What is most surprising is the composition of the tonic: thirty grams of kola nut and ten grams of Bolivian coca leaves, infused in a litre of alcoholic blend. It is the same mixture that underpins the medicinal compound which, in 1886, American pharmacist John Stith Pemberton is thought to have used to create his "French Wine Coca", the forerunner of modern Coca-Cola.

The only difference lies in the absence of alcohol, due to Prohibition in force in America at the time, which the pharmacist compensated for with carbonated water and syrup.

Father Manuel Russo told Toscana Oggi that the recipe dates back to the 18th century, but that it enjoyed its widest circulation between the late 19th and early 20th centuries. According to the weekly, during the period when Florence was Italy's capital, from 1865 to 1871, it was not uncommon for officials and office workers to stop at the San Marco convent during their breaks to sip the tonic.

According to the rector, this story, evidenced by the note with the recipe, some original labels and a few empty bottles, highlights the advanced pharmaceutical tradition of the Dominican friars.

As for any connection between the composition of the Florentine elixir and that of the American medicine, there is no proof whatsoever. What remains is a suggestion and a series of coincidences that arouse curiosity about the history of one of the world's most famous drinks.

The mystery of Coca-Cola's origins

Florence is not the only city where a recipe similar to that of the US beverage is hidden.

In Aielo de Malferit, a small town in Spain's Valencian Community, a very similar syrup was also produced in the 19th century, called "Nuez de Cola Coca", and it is still made today.

Originally its name was "Anís Celestial" and it was produced by the Aielo Liquor Factory, founded in 1880 by three friends, Bautista Aparici, Ricardo Sanz and Enrique Ortiz.

With their liqueurs, the owners won numerous prizes and took part in international events, including the 1889 Paris World's Fair and a drinks competition held in Philadelphia in 1885, just one year before the official birth of Coca-Cola.

"Aparici often travelled to the United States to open up new markets. In those years a blight destroyed our vineyards and he brought back a more resistant vine, the American one, which we still use today. In return he left bottles of Nuez de Cola Coca," says Juan Juan Micó, the factory's current owner, speaking to the BBC.

There is no further evidence of links between Aparici and America. What is known is that the following year pharmacist John Stith Pemberton created "French Wine Coca", which would later take the name Coca-Cola and go on to enjoy extraordinary success first in the United States and then around the world.

In the meantime, the Aielo liquor factory passed from hand to hand and, after being requisitioned during the Spanish Civil War, in 1953 it crossed paths again with the US multinational. When Coca-Cola arrived in Spain, it realised there was a similar drink hindering its expansion and it bought the patent.

Nuez de Cola Coca continues to be produced in its alcoholic version, and in Aielo de Malferit the question lingers: what if Coca-Cola really originated in a small town in the province of Valencia?

World.title: Europe wants to be a strong partner of the US in the Moon race, ESA astronaut says
World.content:
“We as Europeans, we as Italians, we want to be strong partners of the United States in this race,” astronaut Luca Parmitano told Euronews, talking about the current frontier in space exploration: returning to the Moon.

 

Parmitano, an Italian astronaut from the European Space Agency (ESA), was selected by NASA to take part in the Artemis III mission, designed to be a test mission for NASA’s Moon landing programme.

Set to launch in 2027, Artemis III will send three NASA astronauts and Parmitano to low-Earth orbit on the Orion spacecraft to dock with two lunar landers produced respectively by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company and Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin.

NASA has presented the mission as one of the most complex human spaceflights in recent history. As Parmitano prepares for it, he joined Euronews interview programme 12 Minutes With to share how he is getting on, the challenges ahead, and the current state of the space race.

Bringing the European identity into orbit

“The mission was not at all on my horizon,” said Parmitano, “I was speechless, which is quite unusual for me, and I was really grateful."

Parmitano was the first Italian commander on the International Space Station and spent over 366 days in space across two long-duration missions: Volare (2013) and Beyond (2019-2020). He was the first Italian to perform a space walk and now he will be the first European to go into orbit with the Artemis programme.

NASA publicly presented the crew for the Artemis III mission on June 9 at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. At the event, Parmitano gave an emotional speech, calling Italy his own “launch pad” and the ESA his “launch tower”.

Parmitano told Euronews he is grateful to the Italian public education system and aims to bring into orbit the spirit of determination — a characteristic of European identity for him.

“People of my age, we were not born Europeans. We became Europeans. This identity was desired, this identity has been a goal, something we wanted to achieve,” he said.

Artemis III crew member Luca Parmitano greets the crowd during a press conference at Johnson Space Center on Tuesday, June 9, 2026, in Houston. (AP Photo/Annie Mulligan) Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Artemis III: a complex mission toward the Moon

Despite the excitement, Parmitano is aware of the challenges posed by Artemis III. “We have three launches that have to happen in close proximity and from very different spacecrafts,” he explained.

Multiple factors will contribute to the success of the Artemis III mission, including the readiness and successful launches of the lunar landers and NASA’s Orion spacecraft as well as the critical orbital manoeuvers.

Astronauts will also have to live in the Orion spacecraft, with a habitable volume of just 8 to 9 cubic metres. It is built for deep space conditions, which are different to those at low-Earth orbit where the mission will be conducted.

To prepare for such a complex journey, Parmitano and his three NASA crew members, Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas, are now following an intense training schedule.

The programme involves practicing crucial skills, conducting simulations, and preparing for potential malfunction scenarios. “Our training is very complex and wonderfully different and varied,” Parmitano stated.

The state of the space race

If lately on Earth, relations between the EU and the US have been tense, in space, Parmitano claims, this is not the case. “We don't look at what's happening at the political level; we are operators.”

Parmitano said the Artemis III mission is part of the space race to return to the Moon and underlined that the EU-US relationship in orbit remains strong. “We all feel a common goal, which is that of the betterment of humankind on Earth, our life, and this is the next step."

The ESA has been playing an important role in the Artemis mission architecture. For example, it built the European Service Module to provide electricity, thermal control, oxygen, nitrogen, and water to the Orion spacecraft.

However, ESA's contribution to the programme was altered following NASA's decision earlier this year to pause work on the Lunar Gateway, a Moon-orbiting space station for which Europe had been building some key modules.

On the 2027 deadline, presented by many experts as far too ambitious, Parmitano argued that “to achieve complex objectives, you have to be ambitious and push hard”.

World.title: Copyright win: Sorry, ChatGPT won't help you write like Hemingway anymore
World.content:
If you thought a few keystrokes would turn you into Agatha Christie, Stephen King or Ernest Hemingway, ChatGPT has some bad news.

 

OpenAI has quietly reprogrammed the chatbot to reject direct requests to replicate or mimic a named author's voice, whether they are still alive to object or have been dead for decades.

Ars Technica was first to spot the change, running its own prompts through ChatGPT to confirm the pattern.

Engadget followed up with its own tests and got the same result, noting that a study by publication No Latency had found ChatGPT did not refuse these requests for dead authors as recently as a few months ago, suggesting this is a genuinely new restriction rather than something that slipped through the cracks.

The homage is dead, long live the vibe

Ask ChatGPT to rewrite your Facebook post in the visceral style of horror writer Stephen King, for instance, and the chatbot will not oblige.

Ars Technica's testing found much the same. It prompted for an opening scene in King's voice and ChatGPT said it could not closely imitate his distinctive style, offering an original piece built around small-town dread instead.

Try John Steinbeck and you get more or less the same brush-off, followed by an unprompted 750-word substitute story, a Depression-era tale built from "broader qualities such as stark naturalism, economic hardship, vivid rural landscapes, social inequality," rather than the real thing, according to testing by Fast Company.

The loophole that remains — for those who refuse to see this as a sign that they might want to use their own creative writing skills (i.e. brains) instead of relying on a machine — is that producing a prompt describing a certain author's style, instead of mentioning them directly, might still let you get away with it.

The change follows a wave of author lawsuits against OpenAI and a $1.5 billion (€1.29bn) copyright ruling against rival Anthropic, so blocking style mimicry lets OpenAI argue its tool inspires rather than reproduces.

Whether readers can tell the difference between "inspired by Steinbeck" and "actually Steinbeck" is another question entirely.

Early tests suggest the homage often reads flatter than the source material, all short paragraphs and none of the flow or punch that made the original worth stealing in the first place.

World.content:

07/31/2026 July 31, 2026 What is in Trump's 20-point peace plan for Gaza?

Donald Trump says the agreement on Hamas disarming is a "major milestone" in his 20-point plan for post-war Gaza.

The plan was unveiled in September last year.

Here's a reminder of some of the plan's main aims:

Creating a pathway to a Palestinian state, which Israel has consistently and vehemently opposed

Removing Hamas from power and securing a commitment from the militant group to disarm

Reforming the Palestinian Authority, which runs the occupied West Bank

Providing an economic plan for Gaza's post-war recovery and growth

Providing security guarantees for Gaza, which would be enforced by the US and regional powers

Ensuring that Israel halts all operations immediately upon an agreement, hands over any captured territories, and pledges not to occupy or annex Gaza

The plan had also called for the return of remaining Israeli hostages, in exchange for Palestinian prisoners

Those steps were fulfilled before the first phase of a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas

DW spoke to Palestinian-American humanitarian activist Ahmed Fouad Alkhatib in October about the prospects of Hamas fully disarming. Here's what he had to say:

Hamas 'very unlikely' to fully disarm, Gaza expert says To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the wake of Hamas' announcement on Friday, Alkhatib cautioned that the militant group's claims should be "treated with firm skepticism."

In a post on X, he said a Palestinian police force and a transitional government in Gaza is still "many months away," which will give the group "ample time" to shore up contingency plans and preserve its influence on the enclave's population.

"Just as there is no olive oil without olives, there is no Hamas without weapons and armed resistance. Some members may genuinely want to evolve and enter a political process, and they may; but they are unlikely to do so sustainably and successfully while still operating under the Hamas banner and identity," Alkhatib explained.

World.title: Are Iran and Ukraine wars getting tangled in Caspian Sea?
World.content:
Tehran has threatened a response after a Ukrainian strike on an Iranian cargo ship in the Caspian Sea that Kyiv says was carrying weapons to Russia. Still, Ukraine says it wants to avoid escalation with Tehran.

A recent Ukrainian strike on an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea has drawn concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine and the war in Iran are becoming entangled.

Ukraine has said the ship was carrying military equipment from Iran to Russia. Iranian state media, citing Iran's ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, reported that the cargo vessel "Anna" was anchored approximately 5 kilometers (3 miles) from the entrance of the Volga River when it was attacked by drones causing an explosion. One sailor was reported killed.

Iran summoned Ukraine's charge d'affaires and described the incident as an act of aggression.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said Ukrainian forces had carried out successful long-range strikes against a Russian warship and vessels that Kyiv says were transporting military cargo.

Ukraine has long accused Iran of helping Russia wage war through the supply and development of Iranian-designed drones.

Tehran has acknowledged earlier drone sales to Moscow but has rejected accusations that it supplied weapons specifically for use in the Ukraine war.

However, the Ukrainian military has extensive documented physical evidence that Iranian-designed Shahed drones have been deployed throughout the war that has dragged on for more than four years.

How Ukraine shoots down Russia's drones on a budget To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In March 2026, Russia launched nearly 950 Shahed, Gerber and other types of attack drones at Ukraine in a 24-hour period, according to Ukraine's Air Force.

Iran's Foreign Ministry has accused Ukraine of attempting to expand the geographical scope of its war with Russia. Kyiv, by contrast, presents its attacks in the Caspian Sea as part of an effort to disrupt military logistics supporting Moscow.

Will Iran strike Ukraine?

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a statement the attack "cannot go unanswered."

However, Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, told DW that Tehran is unlikely to respond immediately with a direct military strike against Ukraine.

"I believe the Islamic Republic will avoid an emotional reaction and choose a diplomatic response instead of a military one," he said, pointing to Tehran's summoning of the Ukrainian diplomat and the possibility of raising the matter at the UN Security Council.

On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha posted on X that Iran's accusations were "unjustified and groundless."

"The regime in Tehran is a direct accomplice to Russian aggression against Ukraine, fueling Moscow's criminal war with weapons that have killed Ukrainians since 2022," he wrote.

A day later, in a call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Sybiha softened his tone and said that Ukraine wants to avoid unnecessary escalation with Iran.

Ukrainian Middle East expert Ihor Semyvolos considers the likelihood of an Iranian retaliatory attack on Ukraine to be very low.

"Attacks on ships or ports in the Caspian Sea are one thing, since this is related to Russia," which attacked Ukraine.

"However, an Iranian missile attack on Ukrainian territory is an entirely different matter. That would be a direct act of war," said Semyvolos, adding that such an attack "would only complicate the situation for Iran."

Austrian military expert Markus Reisner told DW that an Iranian missile attack on Ukraine is unlikely, even though Tehran possesses medium-range missiles.

Reisner said it would make little sense for Iran to actually launch a missile at a target on Ukrainian territory when there could be more important or higher-value targets elsewhere.

No 'new front' in Iran war

Reisner, currently head of research at Austria's Theresian Military Academy, added that the attack in the Caspian Sea does not indicate that Ukraine is now a participant in the Iran war.

Reisner points out that the Ukrainian military has been increasing attacks on maritime facilities, particularly in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, since May. Around 200 Russian ships, tankers and tugboats have already been hit.

Ukraine's goal is not "to open a new front against Iran, but rather to disrupt supply routes between Iran and Russia in the Caspian Sea as well," said Reisner.

Moscow-based analyst Vakhshiteh said, however, that the attack "can be seen as a signal and an indication that the geography of the Ukrainian war is expanding from the Black Sea to the Caspian Sea."

Ukrainian Middle East expert Ihor Semyvolos agrees. He finds it logical that Ukraine would expand its strategy to control sea lanes for arms deliveries and attempt to impose a general economic naval blockade against Russia in the south.

Ukrainian coordination with the US?

There is no direct evidence that the operation in the Caspian Sea was coordinated with the US, and the issue has not been publicly discussed, Semyvolos said.

"But it's obvious that Ukraine uses American intelligence data. Therefore, the Americans were most likely aware of it," Semyvolos believes.

Austrian military analyst Reisner emphasizes that the timing of Ukraine's attack plays a crucial role.

"Zelenskyy wants to clearly demonstrate here that Kyiv and Washington share a common enemy in Iran," Reisner said.

The Ukrainian attack could also be seen as a demonstration from Kyiv that it is actually a better ally in fighting Iran than some NATO countries, he added.

Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump in Washington this week, as ties between Kyiv and the Trump administration have turned positive along with Ukraine's advances on the battlefield.

Zelenskyy and Trump had perhaps their most cordial meeting so far this week in Washington Image: Zelenskyy Social Media Account/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Will Ukraine's Caspian Sea attacks continue?

As Ukrainian Foreign Minister Sybiha's statement on X indicates, Kyiv increasingly sees Iran and Russia as part of the same military ecosystem.

And Ukraine has also demonstrated tactical momentum in carrying out long-range drone strikes deep inside Russian territory.

Ukrainian analyst Semyvolos expects Ukraine to continue its operations in the Caspian Sea. He explains the timing of the operation by noting that the Ukrainian military now has the technical ability to carry out long-range strikes.

However, if Ukraine again targets Iranian vessels, Tehran faces an uncomfortable strategic choice.

Moscow-based analyst Vakhshiteh argues that a direct Iranian military response against Ukrainian territory risks creating a new front at a time when Tehran is already confronting attacks now concentrated in southern Iran.

Vakhshiteh also suggested that Iran could instead look for indirect ways to impose costs on Ukraine, including measures against shipping connected to Ukrainian interests.

However, such options would carry their own considerable escalation risks and there is no indication that Tehran has decided to pursue them.

World.title: Spain will send troops to Ceuta to help with border security
World.content:
Authorities in the Spanish city of Ceuta asked Madrid to declare a national emergency and send military assistance. Crowds of people breached the border of the territory next to Morocco as police lost control.

Officials in the Spanish territory of Ceuta on the northwestern tip of Africa on Thursday asked the government in Madrid to declare a national emergency and send the army to help secure its border with Morocco.

The call came as video footage showed crowds of people trying to walk around the breakwaters separating Moroccan and Spanish territory or otherwise scale the border fence. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez pledged an "immediate response."

Spain's Interior Ministry said later on Thursday that its armed forces would send personnel to Ceuta to support the border guards.

"The Armed Forces will reinforce the Guardia Civil in the exercise of its powers and any others that may be necessary to maintain civil security in the city of Ceuta," the ministry said.

What had happened in Ceuta during the day?

The Guardia Civil said that crowds broke through the fences into Spain after overwhelming police at the city's breakwater. Video footage showed hundreds swimming across from the Moroccan side, using inflatable inner tubes and other flotation aids.

"The situation is absolute chaos," Rachid Sbihi, head of the association that represents Spain's Guardia Civil in Ceuta, told the Associated Press. "It's not possible to give precise numbers but there are thousands of migrants crossing," he said, adding that the border had "totally collapsed."

The AFP news agency cited a spokesperson for the Spanish government's delegation in Ceuta as saying that nine people had died amid the offshore rush.

The scenes were reminiscent of a similar flashpoint at the border crossing in May of 2021 when more than 8,000 people entered the territory in just two days.

In recent days, rescue parties had already noted increased numbers of people trying to swim around the border checks.

An official from Spain's Guardia Civil policing the border described the situation as 'absolute chaos' Image: Atlas/REUTERS

What did the regional government say?

Juan Jesus Vivas, head of the Ceuta regional government, called for the Spanish government in Madrid to declare an emergency on grounds of national security, asking for more police and for the army to be deployed on the border. This followed a meeting of the city's board of spokespeople, who reached a unanimous agreement.

"Yesterday, I spoke out to warn of the extreme gravity of the migration crisis we are enduring," Vivas wrote online. "Today, mere hours later, the situation is even more critical: another night of mass arrivals, nearly a thousand people waiting outside the CETI [Temporary Migrant Reception Center], our reseources completely overwhelmed, and another life lost at sea."

The head of the regional government said its migrant reception center known as CETI had nearly a thousand people waiting outside. Here you see a much smaller crowd outside the facility on Sunday. [FILE: July 26, 2026.] Image: Antonio Sempere/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

He said that the small city was facing "a humanitarian and social emergency" of national proportions.

"We cannot face this pressure alone — pressure that has resulted in the arrival of between 1,500 and 2,000 people in just 10 days, equivalent to 2% of our population."

He wrote that "with every passing hour, the situation becomes more difficult" in the territory of around 85,000 people.

How did Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez respond?

Soon after the call for help from Ceuta, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the government in Madrid was "fully committed to providing an immediate response" to the situation.

"We are mobilizing all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necesssary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible," Sanchez wrote, adding that he had just said as much directly to Vivas.

"This is the moment to build solutions, with responsibility and cooperation," he said, not going into specifics in the post.

Sanchez's Interior Ministry said that the Moroccan government was "closely cooperating" with Spain to handle the situation and that Moroccan police were stopping "numerous people" trying to cross the border. It said that both countries had agreed to work together "for the return, as soon as possible, of all the people who entered Ceuta illegally."

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska made plans to visit Ceuta on Friday and evaluate the situation, the ministry said.

Why is the rush happening now?

It's not yet clear why large groups are suddenly seeking entry to Ceuta in the past few days, even though a couple of relatively recent developments at least bear a tangential relationship to the issue.

Earlier in July, the Spanish Supreme Court ruled that migrants arriving by sea could not immediately be pushed back across a border in the same way as they could at a land border crossing.

The Ceuta and Melilla enclaves in North Africa bordering Morocco do present exceptional cases where this ruling is concerned, in that it is technically possible to enter them "by sea" despite the fact that you are essentially circumventing a border crossing on land, not crossing the Strait of Gibraltar or the Mediterranean.

One less recent development that attracted international attention, meanwhile, is the Spanish government's offer of amnesty and residency permits to migrants who can demonstrate that they had already entered the country without legal authorization. However, that rule only applies to people who can prove they were already in Spain when it came into force, so it does nothing to improve the prospects of staying for people entering by irregular means now.

Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, at least, drew a parallel between the amnesty and Thursday's events, calling for the EU's open-border Schengen area to be "closed to Spain," and alleging that the amnesty had encouraged human trafficking.

Tajani's Spanish counterpart, Jose Luis Albares, condemned the Italian minister, saying it was "improper" for "a partner and friendly country from which we expect European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery."

World.title: Kenya: 15 dead elephants likely poisoned by cyanide
World.content:
The elephants ate contaminated tomatoes from nearby farms. It was unclear if the poisoning was deliberate or accidental.

Wildlife officials in Kenya said on Thursday that 15 elephants found dead this month in one of the country's best-known wildlife parks were likely poisoned by cyanide.

Authorities said the poison likely originated from pesticides used on farms. The elephants lived in Amboseli National Park near the Tanzanian border.

Kenya Wildlife Service spokesperson Duncan Juma Wanyama told the AFP news agency that investigators suspect the elephants ate tomatoes contaminated with "very strong pesticides."

Officials say tomatoes were found in the stomachs of several elephants from the same herd. The animals were likely attracted to unripe plants growing on nearby farms, Wanyama added.

Unclear whether poisoning was deliberate

At least one elephant died on a farm after consuming tomatoes, while other elephants traveled towards a water source before dying days later, despite receiving treatment by vets.

Cyanide is "a toxic substance... which is very lethal, very poisonous," Wanyama said, adding that "whenever the elephant consumed it, it affects their lung and the liver."

Officials did not say who they suspected was responsible for the contamination of tomatoes at farms neighboring the Amboseli National Park.

Kenya turns to drones in elephant conservation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But it all comes as farmers have been suspected of deliberately poisoning elephants in the past, in order to prevent them from eating their crops.

Wildlife officials are investigating whether other farmers in the area use the same chemicals.

Kenya Wildlife Service has warned that such contamination could have wider consequences for livestock that also graze in the area.

"Other than the elephants and the wildlife that may be feeding in those fields, we have the local livestock. We have the goats. We have the cattle that are there. Eventually, if this is truly what is in the system, then we are going to see a bigger impact,” Kenya Wildlife Service Director General Erustus Kanga said.

'Major setback' for conservation

Amboseli National Park is particularly known for its herds of elephants, as well as its breathtaking savannah landscapes, with Mount Kilimanjaro visible across the border in Tanzania.

The International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) charity said the elephant's poisoning was "a major setback" for one of Africa's key elephant populations.

IFAW said the incident highlighted the devastating impact toxic substances can have on wildlife, livestock, people and ecosystems.

"Those responsible must be held fully accountable under the law," IFAW Kenya director Ben Wandago said.

"This tragedy also underscores the urgent need for the strict control and responsible handling of highly toxic substances to prevent them from entering the natural environment," Wandago added.
