"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018834/The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.title: The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018834/The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.content:
From “don’t come,” to “the more customers, the better.” These were the refrains made by the owner of a chicken hotpot restaurant in southern China famous for shirking fame and which has recently drawn criticism for perceived hypocrisy due to its rapid expansion.

In April, “Mo’s Chicken Hotpot,” in the southern Guangdong province’s Foshan City, went viral after the recommendation of a popular food vlogger. The eatery drew crowds for its signature medicinal hotpot made from freshly slaughtered chickens — and whose healing properties included causing diarrhea, according to notices in the restaurant.

During the initial vlogger’s visit, the restaurant’s owner, surnamed Mo, insisted that customers should “not come” as he would not be able to handle the popularity. Nevertheless, the restaurant began drawing thousands of customers a day, including celebrities and influencers.

But the restaurant’s expansion to five branches in Guangdong and Shanghai — with another expected to open in the southern city of Shenzhen next year — and frequent online s in the months since have drawn ridicule, domestic media reported this week. Social media users argue the restaurant’s current activities contradict Mo’s previous rejection of fame.

Earlier interviews quoted Mo as saying he had no plans to raise prices or open new outlets, leading some online to question whether his indifferent persona had been a marketing strategy from the beginning.

As of this month, Mo said the restaurant has hired a 20-person livestreaming team and broadcasts twice a day. “We can’t afford not to livestream,” he told domestic media. “The pressure is just too great.”

The eatery’s official account on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, now has around 500,000 followers. It posts two to three times a week, mainly skits promoting its signature chicken hotpot alongside health tips. Several videos have garnered tens of thousands of likes.

The restaurant also sells meal kits, Chinese medicine, herbal teas, and local specialties such as salt-baked chicken via its online store.

The rating for Mo’s Chicken Hotpot on review platform Dianping has fallen from a peak of 4.8 out of 5 in April to 3.7, according to domestic media. Negative reviews mention inconsistent food quality, flies and poor hygiene standards in the restaurant, and high prices.

Visitor numbers have also fluctuated. In June, domestic media reported that sales at the original restaurant had fallen from 200 to 400 orders a day to fewer than 20 a day by the end of the month. However, Mo told domestic media in mid-July that the restaurant handles no fewer than 150 orders a day.

In a video interview with domestic media, Mo responded to the criticism, saying, “At first, when we suddenly became so popular, I really didn’t want the attention. We were so busy, it made me want to throw up.”

“Now I actually want the business to be even better,” he added. “When fortune gives you an opportunity like this … and there’s money to be made, why wouldn’t I try to make money? I’d be a fool not to.”

Mo also admitted that despite the restaurant’s expansion and livestreaming business, profits remain limited.

“Traffic comes quickly, and it disappears just as quickly. After a month or two, how do you sustain it? It’s really hard,” adding that if another wave of popularity were to come, he would “honestly close shop and stop.”

Mo also joined the second season of popular domestic cooking competition show “The Divine Dish,” which premiered Wednesday. He was eliminated in the first round.

“The ingredients (he used) were good, but his technique was poor,” one of the show’s judges said of his signature chicken hotpot.

On his Douyin account, Mo responded to his elimination, saying, “I will continue to use the finest ingredients and simplest methods to cook you the familiar chicken hotpot that warms your heart.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Weibo, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018835/Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.title: Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018835/Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.content:
Editor’s note: The theme of the third Shanghai Public Relations Academic Symposium on Irish Literature, held on July 26, was playwright George Bernard Shaw’s eight-hour visit to Shanghai in the 1930s, when China’s cultural and anti-imperialist movements were gaining momentum. The following is an account of the writer’s time in the city and its impact on Chinese intellectuals.

When George Bernard Shaw, the Irish playwright and novelist, paid a brief visit to Shanghai as part of his global voyage in 1933, the city’s intellectuals were thrilled.

Before his arrival, articles about Shaw had been published in various newspapers and magazines. Some discussed his Communist advocacy in Hong Kong, while others talked about how his satirical writing style had influenced European society.

According to a biography of Soong Ching Ling, the Chinese politician and wife of Sun Yat-sen, sometimes called the “father of modern China,” Shaw arrived at Wusongkou port — today the Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal in northeastern Shanghai — at 6 a.m. on Feb. 17 aboard the Empress of Britain, accompanied by his wife, the political activist Charlotte Payne-Townshend. At 5 a.m., Soong went to Wusongkou with Yang Xingfo, a social activist and patriotic democrat, to welcome the couple. At Shaw’s invitation, she joined him on board for breakfast.

More than 200 reporters rushed to Wusongkou early that morning, but Shaw initially refused to go ashore, telling Soong that apart from her, there was no one in Shanghai he wanted to meet, nor anything he wanted to see. But in the end, Soong persuaded him to pay a visit to the city. They took a steamship to Lanlu Wharf in today’s Yangpu District, where he finally went ashore. The reporters waiting at Wusongkou left empty-handed — not a single photograph of Shaw was taken.

At 10:30 a.m., Soong and Shaw disembarked and set out for the city’s downtown. Shaw met and talked with several left-wing Chinese intellectuals, including Yang, former Peking University president Cai Yuanpei, literary icon Lu Xun, writer and linguist Lin Yutang, and the American journalists Harold Isaacs and Agnes Smedley.

Later, at the invitation of the Chinese branch of PEN International, a global association of writers founded in London in 1921, Shaw and other Chinese intellectuals visited the World College on Route Ferguson (now Wukang Road) to attend a gathering with local PEN members. When Shaw met Mei Lanfang, the renowned Peking opera artist and founder of Shanghai’s Left Theatre Club, he expressed his puzzlement over the differences between Eastern and Western theater.

“Will you please tell me how a Chinese actor can do anything in the midst of such infernal uproars as one hears on your stage?” he asked. “In our theater, they put a man out if he sneezes. But you have gongs and cymbals and the competition of half the audience and innumerable vendors. Don’t you object?”

Mei explained that Peking opera was a folk art first performed in the open air, and drums and gongs were then used to attract people to the show. This tradition had simply endured.

Around 3 p.m., Shaw finally spoke with some Chinese and foreign reporters in the garden of Soong’s residence, discussing socialism, national oppression, Eastern culture, and revolutions, among other topics. Afterward, Soong accompanied Shaw back to the Empress of Britain, which then carried the playwright northward to Beijing.

Although Shaw spent just over eight hours in Shanghai, his visit sparked considerable discussion and reverberations among the city’s left-wing intellectual circles. The writer and poet Yu Dafu wrote in Free Talk, a supplement of the Shun Pao newspaper, that he hoped Shaw could tell the world, in his own sarcastic tone, about Japanese imperialism and its invasion of China.

At the time, intellectuals including Lu Xun and the poet and translator Qu Qiubai were working to build a central stronghold for China’s left-wing cultural movement. After Shaw’s departure, they, along with partners Xu Guangping and Yang Zhihua, began compiling reports from various newspapers and periodicals about the Irish novelist’s short visit. The collection was published in March 1933 by Yecao Shudian, or Wildgrass Bookshop, under the title “George Bernard Shaw in Shanghai.”

In the preface, Lu wrote: “Those who truly welcomed him were the Chinese people, as well as the literary and artistic circles that stood by the people. The Chinese people did not regard him as a ‘revolutionary leader’ or a ‘thoroughgoing socialist writer,’ much less as an idol. They regarded Shaw as a loyal friend of the oppressed people of the world, and of China.”

Editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Visuals from the Shanghai Lu Xun Museum, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018830/How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.title: How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018830/How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.content:
This is the first article in a two-part series exploring how Chinese culinary terms came to be included in the Oxford English Dictionary (OED).

For more than two decades, I have studied how Chinese words enter the English language, particularly through food. So when the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) released its second batch of updates this past June, one updated entry felt especially meaningful to me: “Cantonese.” For the first time, the dictionary formally recognized the word as a culinary term, defining it as food prepared in the style of Guangzhou and the surrounding region in southern China, as well as the restaurants that serve such cuisine.

The entry is accompanied not just by a simple definition, but by a timeline of citations tracing the term’s culinary history. The earliest example dates back to April 6, 1892, when New Jersey’s Trenton Times referred to “Fashionable Cantonese dishes.” This phrase shows that the term was already being used in relation to food more than a century ago, long before the era of modern globalization.

Western interest in Cantonese cuisine also stretches back to the late 19th century. The OED cites an 1894 report from The Washington Post describing a dim sum dumpling as “shaped exactly like a fishing creel.” By 1908, The New York Herald was explaining the dish to its readers by comparing it to a “second cousin to steamed sponge cake.” These early descriptions reveal how unfamiliar foods were introduced to Western audiences through comparisons with things they already understood.

Over the following decades, Cantonese cuisine continued to leave its mark. A 1950 publication by the Hong Kong Young Women’s Christian Association highlighted “Cantonese specialties” such as turnip pudding, while a 1997 culinary memoir recalled dining at a large “Cantonese restaurant” where dim sum was served from rolling trolleys. More recently, a 2015 article in The Guardian recommended Wong Chi Kee in Hong Kong for its “traditional Cantonese congee.”

These citations connect to a broader ecosystem of existing terms. The Cantonese practice of yum cha, literally “drinking tea,” the social meal of dim sum and tea traditionally enjoyed in the morning, was added to the dictionary in 2016, while dim sum has appeared in the dictionary since 1989.

Today, my research shows that the dictionary contains a vocabulary of 25 Cantonese culinary terms. Beyond the widely recognized dim sum and yum cha, the list includes char siu, wonton, chop suey, hoisin sauce, egg foo yung, and moo goo gai pan. These are no longer treated as foreign concepts requiring lengthy explanations; they have become established English words.

Yet this lexicographical milestone is not simply a retrospective look at history; it also reflects a living culture. Just months earlier, in March 2026, three new additions expanded the OED’s Cantonese culinary vocabulary: dan tat (egg tart), pineapple bun, and yin yeung (a Hong Kong drink combining milk tea and coffee). Their inclusion highlights that Cantonese cuisine is not a static relic of the past. It continues to evolve, innovate, and influence the English language. This ongoing linguistic exchange shows that the relationship between East and West remains an active and continuing process.

The contrast with other regional Chinese cuisines highlights that global influence is not simply a product of modern international presence. Shanghai, for instance, is one of China’s most globally connected cities, yet its local Benbang cuisine has left far fewer traces in the English language. Cantonese cuisine’s deep roots in English developed instead through generations of migration, trade, and everyday use.

Etymologically, “Cantonese” derives from “Canton,” the former English name for Guangzhou, which was first recorded by Portuguese traders in the 16th century. Over time, the term evolved from a geographic reference into a marker of a distinct cultural and culinary identity. This reflects a broader historical reality: Cantonese cuisine established an overseas presence earlier than many other regional Chinese cuisines, spreading through centuries of maritime trade and migration.

Historically, because the vast majority of early Chinese immigrants to many Western countries came from Guangdong, Cantonese restaurants dominated many Chinatowns. Iconic establishments such as New York’s Port Arthur Restaurant, which opened in 1897 and introduced upscale Cantonese dishes to Western diners, and San Francisco’s Shanghai Low, a Cantonese restaurant that adopted a Shanghai-inspired name to appeal to Western customers, did more than serve food. They became gathering places for immigrant communities and helped establish Cantonese cuisine’s prominence in Western societies.

As a linguist, I often argue that translation is not merely a tool for communication between languages; it is also a means of cultural understanding. The inclusion of these terms shows that English speakers are capable of adopting culinary vocabulary from other languages on its own terms.

For readers interested in exploring this vocabulary, here are eight popular Cantonese culinary terms currently included in the OED, with condensed definitions for clarity.

Many of the early Cantonese restaurants that introduced these dishes to Western audiences have since disappeared. Yet the vocabulary they helped popularize has endured, and a new generation of Cantonese restaurants continues to thrive in Chinatowns and communities around the world. The OED’s recognition of Cantonese cuisine reflects this longer history of cultural exchange: carried across borders by generations of immigrants, Cantonese food has become a lasting part of the global culinary vocabulary.

(Header and in-text images: Visuals from VCG, edited by Ding Yining/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018828/China's Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.title: China's Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018828/China's Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.content:
Chinese state-owned bookstore chain Xinhua Bookstore is partnering with food delivery giant Meituan to roll out a nationwide same-day book delivery service, promising to deliver books in under an hour.

The agreement, signed on Friday at the 34th National Book Expo in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, will connect the more than 10,000 Xinhua stores across China to Meituan’s instant retail network, Instashopping. Customers ordering through the network will be able to receive books in as quickly as 30 minutes.

The initiative marks the expansion of multiple pilot initiatives in the last two years comprising several regional Xinhua branches, including in Zhejiang, Shanghai, and the southern city of Shenzhen.

Founded in 1937, Xinhua is China’s largest and oldest bookstore chain.

Instant retail combines online ordering with inventories from nearby physical stores and a network of couriers to deliver products rapidly, typically in under one hour. China’s instant retail market is expected to surpass 1 trillion yuan ($150 billion) in 2026 and double to 2 trillion yuan by 2030, according to a report by the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation.

The push into instant retail comes amid intensifying competition between China’s e-commerce platforms and weakening demand for printed books. The country’s book retail market totaled roughly 110 billion yuan in 2025, down 2% from 2024, according to a report by Chinese analytics firm OpenBook.

Jiang Chuanyang, chairman of Xinhua’s Zhejiang branch, said at the event that China’s book market is evolving to comprise e-commerce, local instant retail, and physical bookstores. More than 100 stores in the province were active on Instashopping throughout 2025, generating combined sales of several million yuan, according to domestic media.

But the picture is more mixed for independent bookstores.

Su Shanna, brand manager of Yinxu, a chain of five bookstores in the eastern coastal city of Xiamen, told Sixth Tone that instant delivery orders account for roughly 15% of the company’s monthly revenue. The store joined Instashopping in May 2025, and also accepts on-demand orders through its WeChat mini program, fulfilling local deliveries through courier services such as SF Express and JD Logistics.

“It’s more of a bonus than a lifeline,” Su said, noting that demand for instant book delivery remains limited to a handful of scenarios. These include parents ordering extracurricular reading materials or textbooks for their children, tourists ordering books to their hotels, and patients looking for something to read during hospitalization.

Instant retail fills the gap where consumers need a book immediately and traditional e-commerce can’t meet the demand, according to Jiang Han, a senior researcher at Beijing-based think tank Pangoal.

But books are a low-profit business. Because instant retail platforms take a cut of bookstore sales, instant delivery is unlikely to become a major profit driver, he said.

The service’s real value isn’t in generating significant new revenue, but in generating new revenue sources, Jiang added. “Its significance should be on how it helps bookstores reconstruct their connection to readers.”

Jiang said that bookstores are increasingly trying to become “cultural service hubs” by diversifying their revenue sources, selling tourism-related products, and integrating with the local community. Instant retail is part of this trend.

In the case of Yinxu, members pay an annual fee of 188 yuan, which gives them discounts on books, book delivery services, and tickets to local performances, as well as access to various community activities.

“The key to success depends on whether bookstores can offer irreplaceable cultural experiences and emotional value,” Jiang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from iNueng/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018827/China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.title: China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018827/China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.content:
One graduate trained to restore ancient artifacts now generates AI video clips for short dramas. Another, schooled in landscape design, builds virtual scenery instead of physical sets.

Both are part of a hiring surge across China’s film industry, as AI creates demand for hybrid creative roles and cuts production timelines from months to days. Recruitment for AI video editors jumped 179% year over year in June, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

At one cultural communications company in Zhengzhou, capital of China’s central Henan province, monthly production of AI-generated short dramas has risen from a handful to nearly 100, according to CCTV. The expansion has created demand for AI video editors and “card pullers,” who write prompts, generate footage, and select clips that fit a production’s characters and plot.

The shift is drawing workers from fields including design, animation, digital media, and information technology, according to recruitment platform Zhaopin. AI film roles typically pay between 8,000 and 20,000 yuan ($1,100 to $2,800) a month, depending on experience.

“This indicates that AI is not simply a substitution, but a technological enabler that is driving the transformation of traditional professions and roles,” Li Qiang, a vice president at Zhaopin, told CCTV.

AI is also changing how short dramas are made. Some productions that once required crews of dozens can now be completed by a few people, or even one creator handling scripts, storyboards, visuals, and effects. CCTV reported that AI has compressed some production cycles from months to days, with certain episodes completed in hours and effects and previsualization work becoming three to 10 times faster.

Director He Ziqiang, an early adopter of AI filmmaking tools, has added AI storyboard artists, image generators, card pullers, and editors to his team, many without formal film training.

“Anyone can make their own film, as long as they have ideas,” He told CCTV. “This will greatly enrich artistic creation and vitality, enabling more talented ordinary people to express themselves through AI.”

The hiring surge comes as China’s short-drama industry’s annual output value approached 90 billion yuan in 2025, nearly double the previous year, while some AI-generated productions have reported net profit margins above 50%.

Li Yuan, who is not related to Li Qiang, founder of a Henan-based AI film company, told domestic media his firm had cut the cost of producing a drama from 300,000 yuan to 50,000 yuan while increasing output.

“We thought large models would take longer to nail video fluency, but they got it done in the first quarter of this year,” Li told state media.

But he also cautioned that AI short dramas remain at an early stage, with both the technology and audience tastes still evolving. “Only when the market stabilizes can creators and platforms offer better products,” he said.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Staff at a short-drama production company use AI tools during post-production in Jiaxing, Zhejiang province, July 21, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018823/China’s Classic Storytellers Recapture the Magic With Harry Potter
World.title: China’s Classic Storytellers Recapture the Magic With Harry Potter
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018823/China’s Classic Storytellers Recapture the Magic With Harry Potter
World.content:
As he starts his livestream, Qi Jingchuan looks every inch the classic Chinese storyteller — loose-fitting robe, pair of walnut shells in one hand, gavel and folding fan on the table just in front of him.

The only thing that doesn’t fit the scene is Hedwig, the snowy owl from the blockbuster “Harry Potter” series, who is perched on Qi’s shoulder.

Qi has been performing pingshu — a form of oral storytelling tracing to the Song dynasty (960–1279) — for more than a decade, originally entertaining audiences with folk tales about epic battles and wandering swordsmen.

However, to attract younger listeners on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, his livestreams now more often focus on the adventures of the boy wizard from J.K. Rowling’s best-selling fantasy novels.

Qi is among a new breed of performers of quyi — the umbrella term for China’s many ancient storytelling traditions — who have racked up hundreds of millions of views on social media after switching up their repertoires to include global hits such as “Harry Potter” and the Japanese manga series “One Piece” and “Naruto,” as well as modern Chinese online literature.

For younger people in China, quyi — such as pingshu; xiangsheng, or crosstalk; pingtan, storytelling through song; and kuaiban, narration with bamboo clappers — is more associated with their grandparents’ generation, with most regarding it as intangible cultural heritage rather than entertainment.

Performers like Qi are attempting to change that perception and breathe new life into traditional arts.

“More than anything, I want younger generations in China to understand what pingshu really is,” Qi told Sixth Tone, adding that he believes the art shouldn’t be confined to just antiquated centuries-old stories.

Zhao Luping, associate professor of journalism at Shanghai’s East China Normal University, believes that this fusion of ancient art forms and digital-era content could be an effective way to sustain the vitality of this heritage.

The “Harry Potter” series, for example, is already available as novels, audiobooks, movies, and soon as a television show, “but when retold as pingshu, it can still capture young people’s attention,” she explained. “That’s what makes this phenomenon so interesting. Various quyi genres possess distinct artistic charms.”

Serving the right dish

For 43-year-old Qi, the decision to experiment with modern narratives stemmed from pure frustration.

Historically a staple of teahouses and marketplaces, pingshu was among China’s most-loved forms of entertainment after radio broadcasts brought the art into millions of homes in the 1950s. Its popularity peaked in the ’80s, when classic storytellers like Shan Tianfang and Tian Lianyuan became household names.

Qi developed a fascination with the art form at an early age. After graduating from university, he began studying pingshu and eventually became a professional performer.

By that time, however, interest in pingshu had long since waned. The arrival of TV, followed by the internet and then short-video platforms, had transformed people’s tastes for entertainment.

As long-form storytelling struggled to compete with the endless stream of rapid-fire online content, Qi noticed a widening gap: performers were still telling historical epics and martial arts classics that older generations knew by heart, but younger audiences were turning elsewhere.

To mix things up, Qi tried reaching more listeners via livestream, which at first brought attention but not income. His audience was still mostly older people accustomed to listening to pingshu for free on the radio.

He realized that to preserve their art and make a living, quyi performers needed to go beyond their core audiences and seek younger fans willing to pay for content.

“Maybe we just weren’t serving the right dish,” Qi said. “These centuries-old plots can feel remote, making it harder for listeners to form a connection.”

In April, he started regaling his followers with storylines from “Harry Potter,” an instantly recognizable brand. Although the tales have changed, he said the performance remains unmistakably pingshu, characterized by a combination of narration, character portrayal, and commentary.

In Qi’s retelling, Albus Dumbledore, the mysterious headmaster of Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, becomes “Grandpa Deng,” a figure who speaks with the wisdom and authority of a Chinese martial arts master, while the antagonist Lord Voldemort takes on the dramatic flair of a Peking opera villain.

He also incorporates jokes and internet slang to bring this magical world closer to contemporary Chinese audiences, at one point suggesting that Harry Potter’s Nimbus 2000 flying broomstick should really be called Su7, like the Xiaomi electric car model.

One of Qi’s fans, 27-year-old Zhang Cheng, grew up listening to pingshu stories with his grandfather, but gradually drifted away as he grew older. He said that hearing Qi’s “Harry Potter” adaptation immediately drew him back.

“The humor comes from the contrast,” he said. “A centuries-old Chinese storytelling tradition telling a Western fantasy story feels so unexpected that you naturally want to hear what comes next.”

When he started his livestream, Qi was typically attracting 20,000 to 30,000 viewers a night with classic pingshu tales. That figure increased fivefold after he switched to “Harry Potter,” and in June it climbed to around 200,000 for his adaptation of “Naruto,” a long-running manga series about a teenage ninja.

The makeup of his audience also changed, with ages now ranging from 20 to 50, while overseas Chinese living as far afield as the United Kingdom, New Zealand, and the United States are tuning in and sending virtual gifts in various local currencies.

Most evenings, Qi will livestream for about three hours, often pushing the limits of his stamina. “My goal is to generate around 3,000 yuan ($440) in revenue each night,” he said, referring to his income before Douyin takes its cut, about 50%.

Broader revival

This is not the first time quyi performers have attempted to innovate — Chinese artists have been adapting foreign classics for more than two decades.

Experimental theater troupes have reimagined William Shakespeare’s “Othello” as Pu opera, while “Hamlet” has been staged as Peking opera and Yue opera productions under the title “The Prince’s Revenge.”

However, as each traditional art form has its own rhythm, performance conventions, and aesthetic language, the challenge lies in deciding what can be adapted to appeal to modern audiences and what must remain unchanged for the sake of preservation.

Liu Hechun, who performs with China’s best-known crosstalk company Deyunshe and specializes in Xihe Dagu — a traditional storytelling art from northern China that combines narration, singing, and drums — recently began adapting “One Piece,” another popular Japanese manga series about pirates and hidden treasure. He said that he often starts with the most dramatic scenes, drawing audiences into the action before revealing the characters’ backgrounds and motivations.

Foreign names that might be difficult for Chinese audiences to grasp are replaced with familiar cultural references. For example, the naval officer Helmeppo becomes “Meng Yanei,” as yanei in China conjures images of the archetypal spoiled son of a powerful official, famously depicted in the classic novel “Water Margin.”

Xihe Dagu is based on a musical structure that allows performers to adjust rhythm and melody according to a story’s pace and emotion. “The art’s signature techniques — the drum patterns, alternation between speaking and singing, and the methods used to introduce characters — remain the same,” Liu said.

Peng Xicai, another veteran quyi performer, added that a similar approach is emerging across other traditional arts. He points to Suzhou, in the eastern Jiangsu province, where embroiderers are replacing the classic imagery of peonies, birds, and landscapes with popular anime characters and bubble tea logos.

While artisans see their work as a way to preserve Chinese heritage by giving it contemporary relevance, the growing trend of adapting global franchises has drawn scrutiny over the use of copyrighted plots and characters.

“Whether adapting popular intellectual property into traditional performing arts infringes copyright depends on how the original work is used,” said Wang Yu, a lawyer based in the southern city of Shenzhen for the Beijing Yingke Law Firm.

If performers directly retell an original story or quote its dialogue, they need permission from the copyright holder, she explained. “Even if the expression is entirely original, retaining the same plot, character development, and sequence of events may constitute an unauthorized adaptation.”

The legal risk is lower when performers create an original story and make only limited references to existing IP for comparison, inspiration, or artistic effect. However, even then it’s a tightrope, Wang added. “Performers must credit the original author and the title of the work, and the quotation must not have a material impact on the normal commercial exploitation of the original work.”

As contemporary adaptations become popular, artists are seeking to move beyond the legal gray area. Rather than rely on unofficial productions, pingshu artist Qi has begun approaching copyright holders and production companies to secure authorization for their work.

Meanwhile, Liu sees these adaptations as only the beginning. “It’s just the first step,” he said. “The goal is for people to fall in love with the traditional art form itself through these stories. If we take away these familiar stories, and young audiences are still willing to watch the performances of traditional Chinese tales or other stories, then we’ve succeeded.”

For him, traditional storytelling shouldn’t depend on pop culture franchises, but they can serve as a bridge — one that leads audiences back to the enduring appeal of the traditional format.

Editor: Hao Qibao

(Header image: Performers merge global blockbusters with traditional Chinese arts. From Douyin)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018809/Love’s Labor’s Found: The Beijing Scholar Speaking Up for Hired Hands
World.title: Love’s Labor’s Found: The Beijing Scholar Speaking Up for Hired Hands
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018809/Love’s Labor’s Found: The Beijing Scholar Speaking Up for Hired Hands
World.content:
Editor’s note: Over eight years, Cong Rui’an, a doctoral student in political science at Beijing’s Tsinghua University, regularly sought work as a day laborer in Majuqiao Town, one of the capital’s largest informal labor markets. In May, he published the book “Majuqiao Time: My Days as a Day Laborer,” offering his insights into the lives of these often-stigmatized workers. Here, Cong talks with The Paper about his experiences.

The Paper: What makes Majuqiao different from Shenzhen’s Sanhe job market, which attracted widespread attention a few years ago?

Cong: Majuqiao and Sanhe are often mentioned in the same breath, but they differ in many aspects. Sanhe was a relatively centralized day-labor market dominated by a handful of large staffing agencies, making it easier to regulate and shut down. Majuqiao, by contrast, is essentially an urban village: hiring takes place on the streets, and labor brokers operate in small, dispersed clusters, making the market more flexible and harder to eliminate. Sanhe has disappeared, but Majuqiao remains. The government has slated Majuqiao for transformation — from an old urban village for temporary workers to one designed for white-collar workers. And it’s worth noting that Beijing is the capital, so the political considerations are different, which naturally shapes the government’s approach to regulation.

Next is the people. At first glance, Sanhe seemed to draw a younger crowd. Majuqiao has plenty of young people, but fewer wait for work on the streets. The same goes for rough-sleepers, who were more common in Sanhe. Shenzhen (in Guangdong province) lies farther south, so the weather makes sleeping outdoors more feasible. Majuqiao is also an urban village rather than just a hiring market — long-term workers and local residents live alongside day laborers, so the street scene feels less like a “spectacle.”

Another issue that is often overlooked is long-term employment. A friend told me that although Sanhe was known for its day laborers, many people there were actually looking for steady jobs — they just didn’t attract the same curious stares. Sanhe lies in the Pearl River Delta, home to a great many small enterprises with high and flexible hiring needs. Beijing has far fewer businesses of this kind. As a result, workers chasing a freer life will naturally gravitate toward southern China rather than the capital. Many of those who come to Majuqiao are farmers looking for short-term work during the agricultural off-season, which helps explain why the workforce here skews older. In this sense, Majuqiao reflects the broader aging of rural China.

The Paper: What kinds of day labor have you done, and have you found anything that went against your expectations?

Cong: I’ve worked as a waiter, porter, parcel sorter, landscaper, factory worker, and in all kinds of temporary security jobs. If I get the chance, I’d like to work at an electronics factory or a construction site.

I try to keep an open mind, but what might surprise people is the laborers’ attitude toward work. Outsiders often fall into one of two extremes: some assume day laborers are drifting through life, unwilling to work seriously, while others romanticize them as tireless strivers fighting for survival. In reality, they are a bit of both. It’s true that some slack off — but that’s just part of the picture. Many take genuine pride in what they do, finding a source of self-respect in their speed, strength, and skill. In their circumstances, the ability to work is one of the few things they can call their own, and it’s a kind of social currency among their peers.

Another misconception is that only intellectual work is mentally exhausting. In fact, the psychological toll of manual work can be equally heavy, especially as many workers routinely face harsh and often degrading treatment from their supervisors. Physical fatigue can fade after a night’s sleep. Mental exhaustion is much harder to shake off. Over time, that constant emotional strain wears people down. They grow numb to hardship because, to make a living, they have little choice but to adapt. Yet beneath that numbness lies an uncomfortable question: how can we expect people who have long lived without dignity to suddenly live up to society’s expectations? Of course, people have to take responsibility for themselves, but the environments they live in matter. We act upon our surroundings, and they inevitably shape us. None of us becomes who we are in a vacuum.

The Paper: In what role did you interact with the workers? Did they or the employers and labor brokers ever sense you were different?

Cong: I’ve always approached them as fellow workers. Sometimes I’d say I was a student doing day-labor gigs. I’m quite introverted and rarely initiate conversations with strangers. But when I became just another worker, talking with people felt more natural. Whether we were waiting for work or had some downtime on the job, people were happy to chat. Putting those informal conversations alongside my formal research often led to the greatest insights.

As for whether anyone ever figured me out, no one ever brought it up. I’m sure some workers and brokers had their suspicions, but hardly anyone cared. We were all there to work. Who had the time or reason to pry?

The Paper: Are there any workers who have particularly stayed with you?

Cong: There are so many that it’s hard to know where to begin. Many struggle to make a living and work hard for their families. At the same time, there are moments when they feel lost, living one day to the next. These experiences are real, and they often coexist within the same person. I’d like to share a story that has little to do with work but reveals something essential about the people in Majuqiao.

One day, I witnessed a violent assault on the street. Arguments are common in Majuqiao, and fights break out. But it’s by no means a lawless place where people are indifferent. That day, two men had been drinking, a conflict flared, and one man struck the other with a brick. There was blood everywhere. The attacker stood a short distance away, expressionless and making no attempt to flee. By then, a crowd had gathered, and there was nowhere for him to go anyway. The police arrived a little later and took him away. As he sat in the back of the police car, surrounded by onlookers, he struck me as surprisingly young. But he was scruffy, with an overgrown beard and hair. He had probably been out of work for some time. Looking like that, he would have had little chance of finding work — recruiters rarely trust someone who looks so unkempt.

Then the ambulance arrived. They were short-handed, so I helped lift the injured man onto the stretcher. The moment I took hold of him, I was struck by how extraordinarily light he felt. He carried no bag, and the only thing that fell from his pocket was a phone charger. I slipped it back into his pocket and felt a wave of sadness. As we carried him, it occurred to me that he, too, must once have had dreams. He must have worked hard, struggled, and refused to give up easily. But life had slowly ground him down. In the end, a night spent drinking alone led to a fight, leaving him on a stretcher. And I couldn’t help thinking that the man who struck him had probably lived much the same kind of life.

After the injured man was taken away, all that remained on the ground was a brick and a pool of blood. A little while later, a dog wandered over and began sniffing at the blood. Instantly, the workers gathered nearby began shouting to drive the dog away. They probably didn’t even know the injured man, and they were not people you would describe as gentle, but at that moment they simply couldn’t bear to watch.

Was this some act of nobility? No. It was merely the most basic human instinct. Yet it was that instinctive compassion that made me realize we are all the same. It is only life that carries us to different places.

The Paper: What does Majuqiao mean to you now?

Cong: Maybe I should begin with some criticism I received recently. Some point out that in eight years I have visited Majuqiao just over 20 times, arguing that my research can hardly be taken seriously. Others say I’m just another Ph.D. student looking down on people at the bottom of society and using their lives for my benefit. I understand those criticisms, and I welcome them. But if those doubts become a reason to reject this kind of work altogether, then many important stories will never be told, and many realities will go unseen. Somewhere there’s a balance to be found — and it can only emerge through continued discussion.

I think much of the criticism comes from a particular idea of what fieldwork should look like — that the amount of time you spend somewhere is the only measure of how seriously you engaged with it. But Majuqiao was never a project for me. I didn’t have a research plan. No supervisor sent me there. I kept going because I wanted to understand the place and the people. Over time, it became part of my life — an anchor, really. Even when I wasn’t working there, I kept following what was happening: the workers’ group chats, recruitment posts, and anything I could find about Majuqiao online. It was a different kind of engagement — quieter, but no less continuous. As a result, my relationship with Majuqiao has stayed the same. Projects end, but life doesn’t. And that’s why I’ll keep paying attention long after this book.

Sometimes, going back to Majuqiao feels like going home. That isn’t because I love the place. In truth, Majuqiao isn’t somewhere you’d call comfortable or beautiful. It’s noisy, chaotic, and often weighs heavily on you. Yet I feel deeply attached. I know its smells and rhythms. I know what kind of people I’ll run into at certain intersections, and what kinds of work appear with the changing seasons.

At the end of the day, I don’t think it’s ever possible to fully understand another person’s experience. I’d rather acknowledge that limitation than pretend it isn’t there. All I can do is try not to distort people’s lives, not to turn them into commodities or spectacles. I want readers to encounter them as they are — as ordinary people, seen with the dignity and respect they deserve, rather than swallowed up by narratives that burden them with symbolism or moral judgment. But I also have to admit that complete justice is impossible. To imagine otherwise is arrogance.

I’ve never thought of the people in Majuqiao as “source material” or “tools.” Most of them I met only once, yet a single sentence or look has stayed with me. Majuqiao opened my eyes, and it has forced me to rethink things I’ve always taken for granted, to ask myself where I’ve come from and where I’m going.

But if you ask what I mean to Majuqiao, the answer is very little. The place doesn’t need me. Life there goes on, with all its warmth and hardships. But as this book has already had some social impact, I intend to put that to good use. The workers in Majuqiao have their concerns and demands, but too often they go unheard. If this book can carry their voices a little farther, then I hope to keep doing that — not only for them, but for working people everywhere.

Reported by Zhong Yuan.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Chen Yue; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Day laborers gather at the Majuqiao labor market in Beijing, July 2023. Andrea Verdelli via VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018819/China Mourns Volunteer Who Died Carrying Aid to Flooded Villages
World.title: China Mourns Volunteer Who Died Carrying Aid to Flooded Villages
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018819/China Mourns Volunteer Who Died Carrying Aid to Flooded Villages
World.content:
A 29-year-old volunteer died of heart failure caused by overexertion after carrying supplies on foot to villages cut off by flooding in southern China’s Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.

According to domestic media, Dang Xinrui collapsed July 14 while returning from Heyuan Village in Hengzhou, where he and other volunteers had spent six hours carrying about 15 kilograms of medicine, vegetables, and other supplies along flood-damaged routes.

His death has prompted an outpouring of tributes online, with many praising Dang for leaving a vacation in neighboring Yunnan province to join the relief effort.

Flooding triggered by Typhoon Maysak beginning July 6 washed away roads and bridges across parts of Guangxi, cutting off villages and communities. As of July 9, authorities had reported 39 deaths, nine people missing, and at least 375,000 residents affected.

With vehicles unable to reach some areas, hiking enthusiasts from across China formed volunteer teams to carry supplies on foot, sometimes trekking for as long as 10 hours.

Dang, an operations controller at Meishan East Railway Station in southwestern China’s Sichuan province, had taken up hiking about a year earlier. He was on annual leave in Yunnan when he saw appeals for volunteers and traveled to Guangxi to join the relief effort.

He and his teammates set out from a supply depot at 5 a.m. on July 14 and hiked six hours to Heyuan Village. After eating porridge offered by villagers and resting for less than 30 minutes, they began the return journey.

On the way back, Dang became dizzy but continued for another 300 meters before collapsing. His teammates performed CPR while waiting for rescue teams.

Flood-damaged roads prevented an ambulance from reaching the site, forcing medical workers to carry emergency equipment on foot for more than 20 minutes. They arrived at 6:04 p.m., but Dang was pronounced dead after more than three hours of resuscitation efforts.

“These volunteers spent 2,000 to 3,000 yuan ($300 to $450) of their own money to travel here from all over China,” one villager told domestic media. “They didn’t know us, yet they worked harder than our own relatives. They were all good people.”

On the microblogging platform Weibo, hashtags about Dang’s death drew more than 13 million views, with users paying tribute to his kindness and mourning his loss.

Videos filmed before the journey showed volunteers packing supplies into Dang’s hiking backpack. When another volunteer said it was full, Dang adjusted it and asked for more. After five cucumbers were added, he could be heard saying, “Add a little more.”

Photos recovered from his phone showed him drenched in sweat and later lying on the ground with fellow volunteers, their shoes and legs covered in mud.

Family members and colleagues described Dang as generous and quick to help others. In 2021, he found a handbag containing 4,800 yuan in cash, tracked down its owner and returned it intact, earning an award from his employer.

After Dang was cremated on July 19, his father accompanied his ashes home on a high-speed train that passed through Meishan East Railway Station, where Dang had worked. He chose the route so his son could “be a railway worker one final time.”

As the train crossed the station, Dang’s colleagues lined the platform and saluted, many in tears.

“I knew he would join the disaster relief, but I never imagined I would lose him,” his father, Dang Qing, told state broadcaster CCTV. “What comforts me most is that he spent his final days doing something he truly loved and something meaningful. That makes me proud.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Left and right: Photos from Dang Xinrui’s phone show the volunteers on their way into the mountains. Center: A selfie taken by Dang before setting out. From The Paper)

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Smart City Strategy Enters New Phase Through Global AI Partnerships
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has taken a new step in its digital transformation agenda by signing an agreement with the Global Digital Economy Cities Alliance (DEC40), an international organization promoting cooperation in smart city development and the digital economy, on July 28, to advance collaboration in smart cities, artificial intelligence and regional innovation.

The partnership between the Kazakh Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development and DEC40 provides opportunities to exchange international expertise, attract technology companies and investors and introduce advanced solutions in artificial intelligence, digital governance and Smart region/Smart city development.

Its success, however, will depend on how effectively international cooperation is converted into practical projects that improve public services, urban efficiency and quality of life.

Astana as a model for AI-driven urban management

Astana is becoming the main testing ground for Kazakhstan’s smart city ambitions. The capital is developing an integrated digital ecosystem combining AI, video analytics, intelligent transport systems and data-driven public administration.

A major initiative is the city’s partnership with UAE-based Presight AI. The $190 million six-year project aims to modernize existing infrastructure, expand AI-powered monitoring systems and create a digital twin of Astana by 2030.

The initiative will connect urban data systems, improve traffic management, strengthen emergency response and support more efficient city operations. At the same time, the expansion of AI-based technologies will require strong safeguards for data protection, transparency and public trust.

Creating a national smart region ecosystem

The DEC40 agreement expands Kazakhstan’s focus beyond the capital by supporting regional smart city projects. As one of the first practical steps, Kazakhstan plans to compile a list of priority Smart region/Smart city projects and present them to the DEC40 international community to attract technological solutions, strategic partners and potential investors.

This fits into Kazakhstan’s wider digital transformation agenda, which includes AI development, GovTech modernization, cybersecurity, digital infrastructure expansion and the use of technology in sectors such as energy, agriculture and logistics.

For global technology companies, Kazakhstan’s advantages include a strategic location between Europe and Asia, growing digital infrastructure and state support for innovation.

Alatau City and future urban models

Kazakhstan is also developing Alatau City as a future-oriented innovation hub. The city’s plans include AI-driven urban management, digital twins, smart city technologies and Web3 solutions.

Projects such as K-Smart City and Alatau AI-Driven City aim to create an urban environment where artificial intelligence and big data support planning, services and investment growth. Authorities have identified 53 investment projects worth around 2 trillion tenge (US$4.2 billion), expected to create approximately 51,000 jobs.

Unlike the modernization of existing cities, Alatau represents an opportunity to design a new urban ecosystem around emerging technologies from the beginning.

Turning ambition into results

Technology alone will not determine the outcome of Kazakhstan’s smart city strategy. Skilled specialists, effective governance and investment will be essential, with results ultimately measured through safer streets, improved transport, faster government services and stronger economic opportunities.

Kazakhstan’s cooperation with DEC40 is a global shift toward AI-powered urban development. The next stage will be whether these partnerships produce measurable results and help position Kazakhstan as a regional leader in smart city innovation.

World.title: Kazakhstan-China Oil Pipeline: Alternative Route as Export Risks Mount
World.content:
ASTANA – Twenty years after the first Kazakh crude reached China, the Atasu-Alashankou pipeline has evolved from an infrastructure project into one of Eurasia’s most strategically important energy corridors. More than a transportation route, the pipeline has strengthened economic ties between neighboring Kazakhstan and China while providing an alternative export corridor at a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty.

The Atasu-Alashankou pipeline, the first phase of the Kazakhstan-China oil pipeline system, marked a turning point for Kazakhstan’s energy sector. Stretching nearly 965 kilometers, including 962.9 kilometers across Kazakhstan and 2.2 kilometers inside China, the pipeline passes through the Ulytau, Karagandy, Zhetisu and Abai regions before crossing the border. It transports crude from western Kazakhstan, the Aktobe Region and the Kumkol oil fields while also carrying Russian oil in transit to China.

According to the KazMunayGas national oil and gas company, the Atasu-Alashankou pipeline has transported more than 200 million metric tons of crude oil since commercial operations began in 2006. Another key segment of the network, the Kenkiyak-Kumkol pipeline, has transported more than 100 million metric tons over the same period. Together, the two pipelines form an integrated eastbound export system that has become a cornerstone of Kazakhstan-China energy cooperation.

The corridor has taken on greater strategic importance as geopolitical tensions have reshaped global energy markets. Unlike maritime shipping, pipelines offer uninterrupted overland transportation with lower operating costs and fewer geopolitical chokepoints. For Kazakhstan, the eastern route has become an important element of export diversification.

Reliable partnership

The pipeline also aligns with China’s long-term energy strategy. As the world’s largest crude oil importer, China continues to diversify its supply sources and transportation routes to strengthen energy security.

According to OilGasLook, a Kazakh Telegram channel specializing in oil and gas industry analytics, China imported 247.6 million metric tons of crude oil worth $151 billion from 35 countries during the first quarter of this year. The country’s broad supplier base reflects both the scale of its energy demand and its efforts to reduce exposure to geopolitical risks that could disrupt supplies.

Within that strategy, Eurasia occupies a central position, and Kazakhstan has become one of China’s most important partners thanks to its abundant natural resources, geographic proximity and established pipeline infrastructure.

While oil and gas remain central to bilateral relations between the two countries, cooperation has steadily expanded into manufacturing, transportation, digital technologies and infrastructure. Bilateral trade reached a record $49 billion last year. Over the past 35 years, China has invested more than $30 billion in Kazakhstan’s economy, while more than 8,500 companies with Chinese capital now operate in the country, including major corporations such as CNPC, CITIC and Huawei.

The partnership continued to deepen in July, when President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Chinese President Xi Jinping met in Shanghai. Following the talks, the two governments signed a trade and economic cooperation program and a roadmap extending through 2030.

More than 70 commercial agreements worth over $15 billion were also concluded, covering the automotive industry, artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure, transportation, manufacturing and education. The agreements reflect the continued deepening of Kazakhstan-China cooperation and reinforce the two countries’ long-term strategic partnership.

The future of Kazakhstan’s oil exports increasingly depends on the continued development of eastern export routes. Growing geopolitical uncertainty has reinforced the importance of diversification, making the Kazakhstan-China pipeline not simply an alternative route but a strategic asset that enhances export resilience and reduces dependence on traditional western corridors.

At the same time, Kazakhstan still accounts for a relatively modest share of China’s crude imports, leaving considerable room for growth. Expanding that position will require continued investment in production capacity, pipeline infrastructure and cross-border logistics, as well as closer trade and investment cooperation.

Alternative export routes are gaining strategic importance as traditional corridors come under increasing pressure.

World.title: Drone Attack on CPC Facility Threatens Critical Route for Kazakhstan’s Global Oil Supplies
World.content:
ASTANA – A tanker loading Kazakh oil at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) marine terminal was attacked by drones on July 30, causing a fire on board and suspending loading operations. No casualties or oil spill were reported.

According to CPC, the tanker Nissos Sifnos under the flag of the Marshall Islands, carrying crude oil from Tengizchevroil, was targeted at the CPC Single Point Mooring Unit No. 3 while receiving oil.

The attack caused a fire in the manifold area on the vessel’s cargo deck. The fire was extinguished by the tanker’s crew with assistance from three CPC support vessels. The tanker remained afloat, and specialists are assessing the damage.

No CPC employees, contractor personnel or crew members were injured. Medical assistance and evacuation were not required. Oil loading operations were stopped, while CPC pipeline facilities continue operating normally.

Another tanker, Marathi, flying the Isle of Man flag and approaching the CPC marine terminal for loading, was also attacked in territorial waters approximately six nautical miles from the facility.

CPC stated that the incident disregarded previous calls by Kazakhstan and other CPC shareholders, including through the U.S. State Department, against the use of force targeting international energy infrastructure.

The attack poses risks to global energy security, international energy trade and the economic interests of Kazakhstan, CPC shareholders and oil companies using the route, including Chevron, ExxonMobil, Eni, TotalEnergies and Shell.

“Such terrorist attacks also endanger the lives of international tanker crews and create significant environmental risks in the Black Sea, as a strike on a tanker near loading facilities could have resulted in the vessel catching fire and caused a major oil spill,” reads the CPC statement.

The incident comes amid ongoing Kazakhstan-US discussions on energy cooperation and the security of the CPC route. On July 29, Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev held a telephone conversation with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, during which the officials discussed bilateral cooperation, preparations for President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s upcoming visit to the United States for the G20 Summit and the situation surrounding the CPC.

On July 30, Kazakhstan’s Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov also met with U.S. Ambassador to Kazakhstan Julie Stufft to discuss energy cooperation, regional energy security, reliable export infrastructure and the stability of global energy supplies.

World.title: What CPC Disruptions Reveal About Energy Security, Kazakhstan’s Balanced Foreign Policy
World.content:
ASTANA – The Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which exports around 80% of Kazakh oil, has been shut down for a week following Ukrainian drone attacks on July 17 and 19. The recurrent attacks renew questions about the country’s energy security, export dependence and the growing challenge of preserving its balanced foreign policy.

The tankers Asia and Nissos Ios were loading oil produced in Kazakhstan when they were attacked at the CPC terminal on the Black Sea.

In a statement, the Kazakh Foreign Ministry condemned the attacks, describing them as an “unacceptable infringement on Kazakhstan’s economic interests” and said they amounted to deliberate attempts to destabilize legitimate international trade, global energy markets and transport and logistics chains. The ministry called for an immediate end to the attacks and urged Kazakhstan’s partners to condemn them unequivocally and work together on practical measures to protect infrastructure used to export Kazakh hydrocarbons.

Kazakhstan resumed crude oil exports via CPC on July 27.

Unlike previous disruptions, the latest attacks forced a complete suspension of operations along the export route, significantly raising the stakes for Kazakhstan and its international energy partners, and threatening nearly 1.5 million barrels per day of oil exports.

On July 30, the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Nissos Sifnos was attacked by drones while loading Tengizchevroil crude at one of the CPC terminal’s offshore moorings, according to a statement released by CPC press service. The strike caused a fire near the vessel’s oil-receiving manifolds, but the crew, assisted by three CPC support vessels, extinguished it. No casualties or oil spill were reported, and the tanker remained afloat while its damage was assessed.

The CPC pipeline is Kazakhstan’s primary crude oil export route, transporting the majority of the country’s oil exports from western Kazakhstan to the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk for shipment to international markets. Among its key shareholders are Russia (24%), KazMunayGas (19%), Chevron (15%), and Lukoil (12.5%)

In 2025, the CPC system shipped 64.8 million tons of Kazakh oil, accounting for 82.3% of the country’s total crude exports. Overall, 70.52 million tons of oil were transported through the 1,511-kilometer Tengiz-Novorossiysk pipeline, including 36.6 million tons from Tengiz, 17 million tons from Kashagan and 9.2 million tons from Karachaganak.

“What this means for energy security more broadly is that it highlights how suddenly vulnerable export systems become when they depend on a narrow set of transit corridors. Even a major producer can be exposed if its routes to market run through suddenly politically fragile territory,” said Alexander Cooley, Claire Tow Professor of Political Science at New York-based Barnard College, in a comment to The Astana Times.

Short-term options

Experts say in the short term, there are no viable alternatives for Kazakhstan. Aruzhan Meirkhanova, a senior analyst at Outpost Eurasia, said the key task now is adaptation.

“Existing routes cannot absorb comparable volumes, are more expensive and involve more complex logistics. Realistically, the immediate priority is adaptation,” Meirkhanova told The Astana Times.

“This means strengthening contingency planning, redirecting limited volumes through alternative routes where feasible, and deploying broader anti-crisis measures to mitigate the economic consequences of disruptions domestically,” she said.

Most of the oil shipped from Novorossiysk originates in Kazakhstan’s Tengiz, Kashagan and Karachaganak fields, which are developed by international energy companies.

“Its uninterrupted operation, physical security and resilience are a shared interest and responsibility, not solely Kazakhstan’s,” she added.

Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev spoke by phone on July 29 with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to discuss bilateral ties and the situation surrounding the CPC was on the agenda.

“The CPC is an international project involving major Western energy companies and supplies significant volumes to the EU. Kazakhstan has therefore consistently raised the stability of the corridor in its discussions with both the United States and the European Union,” Meirkhanova said.

Cooley also said Astana’s options are limited in the short term.

“The country’s alternative routes are simply too small and too expensive to replace CPC volumes [about 80% of Kazakhstan’s exports] quickly, so the practical response is likely to be more diplomatic than logistical. Kazakhstan can keep working to expand trans-Caspian and other eastern export routes to China, but those are longer term strategic goals, not immediate substitutes,” he said.

What comes next

Meirkhanova named diversification of export routes as a key long-term priority, an issue that has long been on the government’s agenda.
