“Kazakhstan’s policymakers understand this and have pursued it across diplomatic, economic and energy-policy tracks. Among others, this includes comprehensive engagement with Azerbaijan and Georgia, efforts to increase shipments through the BTC [Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan] pipeline, and investments in Caspian port, tanker and related transport capacity,” she explained.

She cautioned that even if expanded, alternative export routes were unlikely to replace the CPC because they also remained constrained by capacity, infrastructure and commercial viability.

“The realistic objective is to reduce concentration risk gradually and create additional flexibility. Broader economic diversification and a gradual reduction in the country’s fiscal dependence on hydrocarbon revenues are also necessary to strengthen its economic resilience,” she added.

Cooley said the best strategy is to “preserve the balancing act it has pursued so far, but become even more vocal and visible internationally in its protests over attacks that threaten its energy interests.”

“It [Kazakhstan] should maintain working channels with Kyiv, Moscow, Western and Gulf partners, and press all conflicting parties to pledge that commercial shipping and export infrastructure be kept out of the conflict,” Cooley said.

Efforts to maintain balanced foreign policy

For decades, Kazakhstan has relied on a balanced foreign policy to manage relations with its partners. The war in Ukraine and growing concerns about regional trade and energy infrastructure have made that balancing act more difficult, but not necessarily unsustainable.

“There is a meaningful room for Kazakhstan to maintain a balanced foreign policy, although the external environment has clearly become more difficult. As a middle power, Kazakhstan has strong incentives to preserve strategic autonomy and maintain constructive relations with its key partners through diplomatic engagement. This has long been the essence of its multi-vector foreign policy,” said Meirkhanova.

Cooley said that the policy had never amounted to a concrete security guarantee for Kazakhstan’s strategic assets.

“Moreover, we now have two conflicts. Russia and Ukraine and the U.S. and Iran, whose geographic scope is increasing to include the Caspian and adjacent areas involving Kazakhstan. This expansion will require Astana to transition to a more visible diplomatic role, perhaps affording more opportunities for it to act as a mediator,” he said.

Meirkhanova also mentioned President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s recent call to end hostilities and a return to negotiations under what he described as the Istanbul Formula 2.0.

“It should be understood primarily as a humanitarian position aimed at stopping the loss of life. At the same time, it also reflects Kazakhstan’s interest in reducing risks to regional security, civilian infrastructure, trade and energy flows. The emphasis on diplomacy is pragmatic, since negotiated settlement remains the most realistic path towards reducing long-term geopolitical and economic risks,” she explained.

Global oil market under strain

The consequences of a prolonged disruption would extend beyond Kazakhstan. The country is one of the European Union’s key suppliers of petroleum oil. In the first quarter of 2026, it accounted for 9.6% of EU imports, according to Eurostat. A year earlier, its share stood at 12.7%.

In 2024, Kazakhstan ranked as the EU’s third-largest supplier of petroleum oil in 2024, behind the United States and Norway, with exports totaling 52.4 million tons.

Any sustained reduction in Kazakh shipments would therefore add pressure to European energy supplies and to a global oil market already strained by instability around the Strait of Hormuz, and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Infrastructure as a geopolitical instrument

The CPC case also exposes a broader weakness in the idea that connectivity necessarily produces stability. Cooley noted the same infrastructure that links economies in peacetime can become a pressure point during conflict.

“For over two decades in the post-Cold War era, we often assumed that transnational infrastructural projects such as energy pipelines would inevitably promote cooperation by giving countries shared commercial and geoeconomics interests. This was often the logic, for example, cited by supporters of the Nordstream 2 pipeline between Russia and Germany,” he said.

In Central Asia, connectivity has similarly been promoted as a source of trade, transit revenue and economic integration.

“This year’s events suggest that such infrastructural connections, in times of crisis or suddenly expanding conflicts, also create new points of exposure and vulnerability,” Cooley added.

World.title: Can Kazakhstan Balance Cheap Toll Roads With Modernization?
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan continues to operate one of the world’s most affordable toll road systems, with passenger vehicles paying an average of 207 tenge (US$0,44) per 100 kilometers on Category I highways, the country’s highest-standard roads, using prepaid accounts. According to national road operator KazAvtoZhol’s release from July 28, comparable toll roads in China, France, Japan, Russia and Türkiye cost 15 to 40 times more.

The figures raise a broader question: can Kazakhstan maintain exceptionally low tolls while financing the infrastructure needed to support its ambitions as a major Eurasian transport hub?

Affordable tolls support competitiveness

Kazakhstan’s pricing policy aligns with the country’s broader economic priorities, rather than an effort to maximize toll revenue. Low charges help reduce transport costs across the country’s vast territory and strengthen its competitiveness as a transit corridor linking China, Central Asia, the Caspian region and Europe.

Passenger vehicles pay tolls only on Kazakhstan’s highest-standard Category I highways, while commercial vehicles are charged according to their weight because of their greater impact on road wear. Tariffs are approved by the government and linked to the monthly calculation index (MCI) rather than set independently by KazAvtoZhol.

Road quality remains the bigger challenge

Low tariffs, however, do not resolve the challenge of maintaining road quality. KazAvtoZhol has acknowledged this by suspending toll collection on road sections where defects affect safety until repairs are completed. This year, this mechanism is applied to sections of 14 toll roads.

The government has invested heavily in road upgrades, with more than 34,000 kilometers repaired in 2019-2025. Today, 94% of national roads and 91% of local roads meet official standards. Yet growing public concerns show that maintaining roads across Kazakhstan’s vast territory remains a major challenge, even as infrastructure expansion continues.

Transport Minister Nurlan Sauranbayev has attributed part of the challenge to the gap between the country’s extensive 95,000-kilometer road network and available maintenance funding.

Engineering may determine long-term sustainability

Experts say the durability of Kazakhstan’s roads depends not only on funding but also on modern engineering.

Boris Asmatullayev, Doctor of Technical Sciences and science director at Kazroadinnovation, says some road designs still rely on approaches developed decades ago, despite heavier freight traffic and increasingly demanding climatic conditions. Kazakhstan’s highways experience temperature swings exceeding 100 degrees Celsius, from severe winter frosts to intense summer heat, accelerating pavement deterioration, according to Kazinform.

Kairat Mukhambetkaliyev, a senior researcher at the Kazakhstan Road Research Institute, says road construction is increasingly tailored to regional conditions through internationally recognized pavement design standards and climate-adapted materials. Updated standards and longer maintenance cycles, he argues, could improve durability while reducing long-term costs.

Alongside engineering improvements, the government is introducing digital tools to strengthen road management. At a March 3 government meeting, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov instructed relevant agencies to launch a unified digital platform for monitoring road conditions by the end of this year, enabling faster detection of defects and more efficient maintenance planning.

What to watch next

Kazakhstan’s low toll policy demonstrates that road infrastructure is viewed as a strategic economic asset. Keeping tariffs among the world’s lowest may strengthen domestic mobility and regional transit competitiveness, but long-term success will depend on whether engineering standards, maintenance practices and digital monitoring improve road quality as traffic volumes continue to grow.

World.title: From Screens to Stadiums: Games of the Future 2026 Kicks Off in Astana
World.content:
ASTANA – The Games of the Future will become another golden bridge of unity, friendship and solidarity among countries, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said as he opened the international tournament in Astana on July 29.

The tournament brings together more than 800 participants representing over 50 nationalities. They will compete through Aug. 9 across eight disciplines that combine traditional athletic performance, competitive gaming and major esports titles.

“This tournament brings together what may appear to be incompatible. At its core is a reasonable and realistic balance between two worlds – physical and virtual. (…) The main mission of the Games of the Future is to truly unite people and inspire them toward new achievements. I am sure that the Games of the Future will become another golden bridge of unity, friendship and solidarity among our countries,” said Tokayev at the opening ceremony of the Games of the Future Astana 2026 powered by Samruk Kazyna.

The ceremony formally launched 12 days of competition at four major sporting venues across the Kazakh capital. Laser effects, aerial acrobatics, live music and performances by leading Kazakh artists were combined with national cultural motifs in a production centered on the connection between physical sport and digital innovation.

The ceremony was attended by Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov and Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, along with official delegations and representatives of the international sports community.

Daniel Merkley, Phygital International CEO, said the opening represented more than the start of another international competition.

“It is a celebration of ambition, innovation and collaboration. It is an opportunity to bring together nations, communities and innovators from around the world, united by a shared belief that the future is created by those prepared to embrace new ideas,” said Merkley.

Where physical and digital competition meet

Unlike a conventional multisport event, the Games of the Future place digital and physical abilities within the same competitive system.

In the phygital disciplines, athletes begin with a video game before moving into a related physical contest, such as basketball, football, fighting or dancing. The results of both stages contribute to the final score, allowing teams to recover from a digital-stage deficit during the physical competition or extend an advantage established on screen.

The format requires athletes to switch between different rules, skills and tactics within a single match. Strong gaming performance must be supported by physical preparation, while experience in traditional sports may not be enough without equally strong results in the digital stage.

Merkley said the competition reflects the evolution of sport for a generation that moves naturally between physical and digital environments.

“Over the coming days, Astana will become the center of the phygital world, as elite athletes, leading esports organizations, innovators, partners, media and supporters from across the globe come together to celebrate the Games of the Future. Together, they will showcase a new era of sport – one that brings together physical excellence, digital competition and technological innovation on a truly global stage,” said Markley.

Basketball launches competitive program

The competitive program began at the Qazaqstan Athletics Sports Complex, where 16 clubs opened their group-stage campaigns in Phygital Basketball Presented by Halyk Fund. The discipline combines the 3on3 FreeStyle basketball video game with a fast-paced basketball match on the court. Teams carry their score from the digital stage into the physical contest, with the combined total determining the winner.

Croatia-based Zagrebacki mališani NITUI, the reigning champions of the Phygital Contenders qualifying tournament held in the capital in June, opened the main competition with a 34-17 victory over Kazakhstan-based GTB KZ.

GTB KZ player Yesset Zharkylov, who is also a member of Kazakhstan’s national 3×3 basketball team, said the unfamiliar digital stage intensified the pressure of playing the tournament’s opening match.

“We were the first to begin. It was exciting, and as the teams opening the tournament, we were very nervous during the digital part. It is a new game that none of us had played before, so there was a lot of tension. The physical part was better because we had played basketball before, and overall, the tournament is very entertaining and interesting,” Zharkylov told The Astana Times.

For Zagrebacki mališani NITUI, the opening victory provided a positive start to a campaign in which the team has set its sights on the title.

“We didn’t know exactly what to expect because it was the first game of the tournament. Getting the first win is important. We came here to win every game, and that’s still our goal,” said Zagrebacki mališani NITUI athlete Jure Gunjina.

His teammate Jan Kroflin said the players’ basketball background gave them confidence once the contest moved onto the court, but the digital component required considerably more preparation.

“We are all basketball players, so that part comes naturally. The digital stage took much more work because none of us had played the game before preparing for this competition. We wanted to make sure we didn’t fall behind there,” Kroflin told The Astana Times.

Eight disciplines across 12 days

Beyond basketball, GOTF 2026 program includes hybrid versions of football, fighting, tactical shooting and dancing, along with tournaments based on some of the world’s most established competitive video games.

The first group of disciplines comprises Phygital Football UFL Presented by Samruk-Kazyna, Phygital Basketball Presented by Halyk Fund, Phygital Shooter CS 2 Presented by Yandex GO, and Phygital Dancing Presented by Solidcore Resources.

The program also includes Phygital Fighting Presented by Kazzinc, MOBA PC Dota 2 Presented by Bank CenterCredit, MOBA Mobile MLBB Presented by FREEDOM, and Battle Royale – PUBG: BATTLEGROUNDS Presented by Alatau City Bank.

Alongside the competitions, visitors can take part in interactive activities, enter prize draws and attend autograph sessions with athletes and esports players competing at the tournament. The field features prominent names from global sport and gaming, including PUBG star James Giezen, known as TGLTN and players representing internationally recognized organizations such as Xtreme Gaming, Vici Gaming, Boca Juniors and Valencia Basket. The program continues across Astana through Aug. 9.

World.title: Kazakhstan Faces Growing Health Risks as Rising Temperatures Intensify
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is facing increasing climate-related risks as temperatures rise at around twice the global average, putting growing pressure on public health systems and communities. Experts warn that more frequent and intense heatwaves require stronger adaptation measures, including a national Heat-Health Action Plan.

According to Kazhydromet, 2025 was the warmest year in Kazakhstan’s recorded history, with average temperatures exceeding the 1961-1990 climate norm by approximately 2.9°C. Nine of the country’s ten warmest years have occurred since 2000, reflecting a long-term warming trend.

Heatwaves are becoming more frequent and prolonged, notably in western and southern regions, where the number of days above +30°C is increasing by 4-7 days every decade. In July, Kazakhstan recorded new temperature highs, including +40.0°C in Almaty and +45.2°C in Shymkent, reported the Central Asia Climate Foundation on July 27.

Heat impact on public health

Extreme temperatures are already affecting health outcomes. According to the Kazakh Ministry of Health, emergency-treated cases of arterial hypertension increased by 26% in June compared with the same period in 2025. While Kazakhstan does not yet calculate heat-related mortality using WHO methodology, international assessments indicate rising risks.

The World Bank estimates that heat-related mortality in Astana and other major Central Asian cities currently stands at around 19-21 deaths per 100,000 people annually and could increase significantly by 2090 without additional adaptation measures.

The ministry said the country is developing climate-resilient healthcare approaches, including improved monitoring, medical training and integration of climate risks into national health policies. However, experts stress the need for a comprehensive Heat-Health Action Plan aligned with WHO recommendations.

Global heat risks increase

The country’s rising heat risks are consistent with global climate trends. Europe, the fastest-warming continent, has experienced record-breaking heatwaves, with temperatures rising at around twice the global average. A recent heatwave in Western Europe was linked to more than 10,000 excess deaths, while the UK recorded around 2,700 premature deaths from May and June heat events, with scientists attributing more than 40% of these deaths to human-caused climate change.

The WHO is urging countries to strengthen heat preparedness through early warning systems, climate-resilient healthcare facilities, public awareness and urban cooling measures.

World.title: Kazakhstan Housing Company Launches Analytics Platform as Housing Sector Reforms Advance
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan Housing Company (KHC), a subsidiary of the Baiterek national management holding, has launched the beta version of KHC. Analytics, a platform designed to provide comprehensive data on Kazakhstan’s housing market and the shared-equity construction sector.

Centralized housing market data

The platform consolidates housing market information into interactive dashboards, offering data that the company says has not previously been available through a single public source. Its launch comes as Kazakhstan introduces reforms to make the construction sector more transparent and efficient.

KHC.Analytics comprises six thematic sections, with selected content available free of charge and advanced analytical tools offered through a paid subscription, Kazakhstan Housing Company reported on July 27.

The platform combines data on shared-equity housing projects, residential prices, developer activity, financing, construction progress and regional market trends with broader housing and macroeconomic indicators, including residential completions, property transactions, inflation and household incomes. According to KHC, the platform is intended to provide journalists, analysts, investors and homebuyers with a standardized source of market information.

KHC Chair Altai Kuzdibayev said the platform provides exclusive data on the shared-equity housing market with regional comparisons and is intended to become a common industry reference.

Construction Code strengthens oversight

The platform’s launch coincides with Kazakhstan’s implementation of its new Construction Code, signed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Jan. 9 to strengthen regulation and accelerate digital transformation in the sector.

The legislation introduces digital oversight of urban planning through a unified cadastral system, limits amendments to detailed development plans to once every two years, strengthens seismic safety requirements and expands state construction supervision. It also establishes a National Institute for Technical Standardization, introduces professional certification for engineers, creates a unified electronic register of licensed construction companies and extends minimum building warranty periods from two to five years, with at least 10 years for structural elements, roofs and facades.

A unified digital construction portal, Qportal.kz, will integrate planning, design, project review and construction into a single system, with each project assigned a unique identification number.

Record housing construction

Addressing a joint session of Parliament on June 30, Tokayev described the Construction Code as strategically important for the sector. He noted that Kazakhstan commissioned more than 20 million square meters of housing last year, the highest annual figure in the country’s history, enabling thousands of families to acquire homes.

Kazakhstan’s construction sector remains a key driver of economic activity, supported by infrastructure projects, road development and residential construction. In January-May, construction output exceeded 2.4 trillion tenge (US$ 5 billion), rising 13.4% year-on-year. The sector continues to support investment, job creation and business activity while contributing to expanded housing supply and improved living standards.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Amy V. Diaz appointed Chargé d’Affaires at US Embassy in Georgia
World.content:
The US Embassy has announced that Amy V. Diaz has been appointed Chargé d’Affaires ad interim in Georgia. The announcement was published on the embassy’s official website.

According to the embassy, Diaz is a senior career member of the US Foreign Service and has served in the role since July 2026.

Who is Amy V. Diaz?

Amy V. Diaz has held a range of diplomatic and leadership positions throughout her career. Before her current appointment, she served as Chargé d’Affaires ad interim and Deputy Chief of Mission at the US Embassy in Lilongwe, Malawi.

Earlier, she worked at the US State Department’s Bureau of European and Eurasian Affairs, where she was Deputy Director of the Office of Policy and Global Issues.

Diaz also headed the consular section at the US Embassy in Harare, Zimbabwe, and led the counternarcotics team at the US Embassy in Afghanistan.

Her previous assignments also include serving as rule of law adviser and coordinator for the Summit of the Americas at the US Embassy in Panama, chief of the internal political unit at the US Embassy in Tbilisi, and vice consul at US diplomatic missions in Harare and Monterrey, Mexico.

US Chargé d’Affaires ad interim to Georgia Amy W. Diaz

Diaz joined the US State Department in 2002 through the Presidential Management Fellows programme and has been a career member of the US Foreign Service since 2005.

She holds a bachelor’s degree from St. John’s College in Annapolis, Maryland, and a Juris Doctor degree from the University of Arizona. According to the State Department, she has received multiple Superior Honor Awards and Meritorious Honor Awards in recognition of her distinguished service.

The post of US ambassador to Georgia has remained vacant since July 2025, when Robin Dunnigan stepped down. Since then, the embassy has been headed by a series of Chargés d’Affaires ad interim. Alan Purcell initially led the mission, before Amy W. Diaz was appointed US Chargé d’Affaires ad interim to Georgia in July 2026. Washington has yet to nominate a new ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to the country.

Amy W. Diaz named acting US envoy to Georgia

World.title: Foreign visitor numbers and tourism revenue decline in Georgia
World.content:
The number of foreign visitors to Georgia and the country’s tourism revenue both declined in the second quarter of 2026, although visitor satisfaction and the average length of stay increased, according to a new report by the National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat).

Official data show that 1.3 million foreign visitors travelled to Georgia between April and June, down 5.2% compared with the same period in 2025.

Most visitors — 81.5% — were tourists, meaning they stayed in Georgia for at least one night. Same-day visitors accounted for 14.8%, while 3.8% made both same-day and overnight visits.

According to the statistics, neighbouring countries continued to account for the largest share of international visitors to Georgia. Russia remained the biggest source market, with 328,900 visitors, or 25.1% of the total. It was followed by Turkey (16.9%) and Armenia (10.8%).

The largest age group among visitors was people aged 31 to 50, who accounted for 45.6% of the total. Men made up 57.1% of visitors, while women accounted for 42.9%.

Nearly half of all visits to Georgia (49.6%) were made for holidays, leisure and recreation. Visiting friends and relatives accounted for 25.6% of trips, while 12% were made for transit purposes.

Tbilisi and the Adjara region remained the most popular destinations. The capital accounted for 36.9% of all visits, while Adjara attracted 26.2%.

The decline in visitor numbers was reflected in tourism revenue. According to Geostat, foreign visitors spent a total of 3 billion lari (around $1.11 billion) in Georgia during the second quarter of 2026, down 13.3% compared with the same period last year.

Average spending per visit also fell by 9.2% over the same period, to 1,922.1 lari (around $711.9). Visitors spent the largest share of their budgets on food and drinks (27.3%), shopping (25.2%) and accommodation (24.3%).

Despite the decline in both visitor numbers and tourism spending, foreign visitors continued to rate their experience in Georgia highly. Some 54.4% of respondents described their trip as “very satisfying”, while 38.7% said it was “satisfying”, bringing the combined satisfaction rate to 93.1%.

The Geostat report also showed that the average length of stay increased from 5.30 to 5.48 nights. Meanwhile, 81.8% of visits were made by repeat visitors, indicating that most foreign travellers who have visited Georgia at least once return to the country.

Tourism in Georgia

World.title: Tbilisi to demolish landmark Rike Jugs complex. VIDEO
World.content:
The landmark Rike Jugs architectural complex in central Tbilisi, on Europe Square, is being demolished after the city authorities granted permission for the work.

The site, which has remained unused for nearly 15 years, will be redeveloped into a hotel. Most of Rike Park — an area of around 15,000 square metres — will now pass into private ownership.

The complex, known as the Rike Jugs, consists of a music theatre and an exhibition centre. It was built in 2011–2012 in one of the busiest tourist areas of the Georgian capital. The project was conceived by then-President Mikheil Saakashvili and designed by Italian architect Massimiliano Fuksas.

The complex was never used for its intended purpose. Construction was completed just as power changed hands in Georgia, and the new ruling Georgian Dream party took a dim view of the Rike Jugs, along with other architectural projects associated with the Saakashvili era. Party members described the complex as a “dump” and said it was an eyesore.

After years of standing empty, the Rike Jugs were eventually put up for sale. Several auctions failed before the complex was sold in 2022 for 10 million lari (about $3.7 million) to businessman David Khidasheli, an associate of Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili. After Khidasheli’s relationship with the authorities deteriorated — leading to the loss of parts of his business and several licences — he decided to sell the property.

The complex changed hands again in 2025, when it was acquired by Rike Domi, a company registered on 25 April that year.

Under the terms of the deal, the company must build a hotel on the site by 2030, investing 44 million lari (around $16.3 million) in the project.

Urban planning experts and anti-corruption researchers say the sale bears signs of corruption. They argue the complex was sold for well below the market value of comparable property in Tbilisi, particularly in a prime tourist area in the city centre. When it was first offered at auction, the asking price for the Rike Jugs was 95 million lari (about $35.2 million)..

Tbilisi demolishes Rike Jugs complex

World.title: Russian lawmaker makes another bid to enter South Ossetian politics
World.content:
North Ossetia parliament member Dzambolat Tedeyev, who represents the A Just Russia – Patriots – For Truth party and is a former head coach of Russia’s national freestyle wrestling team, is officially returning to South Ossetian politics. What role he intends to play, however, remains unclear. His previous attempts to establish himself in the region’s political scene have all ended in failure.

A native of South Ossetia, Tedeyev once even sought to become the region’s president.

At the recent third congress of the Patriots of Alania party, which was already under Tedeyev’s influence, he was elected its chairman. The high-profile move in Tskhinvali coincided with the party’s nomination of Murat Valiyev — a serving officer in the State Protection Service and former KGB officer — as its presidential candidate.

Tedeyev said the party’s main goal would be to ensure that the views of South Ossetian citizens are heard by the republic’s leadership.

“Our position has never changed, but now we have our own platform from which we can defend the interests of our citizens and our country. Today, we see people leaving because they cannot find work. Despite an investment programme aimed at creating new businesses, unemployment remains a serious problem.

There are many issues to address. But today we have hope because, thanks to you, we now have a party where we can make our voices heard. We must unite and build the future of our republic together,” he told delegates at the party congress.

Commenting on the nomination of little-known State Protection Service officer Murat Valiyev as the party’s presidential candidate, Tedeyev appeared to acknowledge that Valiyev was being put forward as a “technical candidate.” He urged acting president and election frontrunner Marat Kambolov to “rely on” Valiyev and his allies.

Tedeyev also recalled his own failed presidential bid in 2011, when the Central Election Commission refused to register him as a candidate.

“There was a time when I wanted to run, but I wasn’t allowed to. Today, I see that Marat has greater potential, stronger connections, and is capable of achieving more. Why shouldn’t he rely on me? That’s why I decided that even if we nominate Murat Valiyev today, Marat should rely on him, on us, on all of us.

And let’s all put our ambitions aside a little. We all know what we’re capable of.”

Tedeyev’s remarks have prompted mixed reactions in South Ossetia. Local analysts say it remains unclear whether he genuinely intends to challenge for power or is instead demonstrating loyalty by putting forward his ally as a “technical candidate” in the hope of negotiating with Kambolov after the election.

The events of 2011, when Dzambolat Tedeyev unsuccessfully challenged the outgoing president, Eduard Kokoity, for power, remain fresh in South Ossetia’s collective memory.

After the Central Election Commission refused to register his presidential candidacy, Tedeyev threw his support behind former education minister Alla Dzhioyeva. Although the former official had been accused of corruption and placed under house arrest, her alliance with Tedeyev helped unite the protest vote and secure victory in the election.

The pair, however, were never allowed to take power. The Supreme Court annulled the election results, triggering days of street protests. The opposition, led by Dzhioyeva and Tedeyev, unsuccessfully sought to defend what they said was their electoral victory.

The standoff ended in a compromise that ultimately fell short of Tedeyev’s ambitions. Kokoity announced his resignation, even though his second and final term was already nearing its end, while the opposition agreed to end the protests. A repeat presidential election was scheduled for March 2012, but Dzhioyeva did not take part.

Since then, Tedeyev has periodically sought to influence political developments in South Ossetia, but without much success. Ahead of the 2024 parliamentary elections, for example, he formed an alliance with the parliamentary People’s Party, whose members were once supporters of former president Eduard Kokoity.

According to local analysts, in exchange for Tedeyev’s financial backing, the party agreed to include his allies on its electoral list. However, the alliance ultimately failed to secure a majority of seats in parliament.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Dzambolat Tedeyev takes over South Ossetia party

World.title: ‘Moscow will only push Armenia out of Russian-led blocs’: Reaction to Russia’s foreign intelligence claim
World.content:
SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

“Brussels understands that Armenia will face a severe economic crisis if Yerevan leaves the Eurasian Economic Union,” Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service said on the previous day.

The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) is a Russia-led economic bloc. Its members are Russia, Armenia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.

“Brussels should not expect the EAEU countries to keep Yerevan’s political crew afloat or bankroll its marathon swim toward the European Union,” the SVR said.

In Armenia, observers noted that the statement followed a phone call between Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin on July 27. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said one of the main topics was a referendum in Armenia on European Union membership or continued participation in the EAEU.

“We stressed the need for Armenia to hold a referendum as soon as possible so Armenians can decide which direction they want to take,” Peskov said.

The Kremlin’s readout of the call did not mention Pashinyan’s response. However, the Armenian prime minister’s office said he told Putin:

“Holding such a referendum would only become possible after Armenia submits an official application to join the European Union and the issue takes on practical significance.”

The Armenian authorities have given Russia the same response on several previous occasions.

Local analysts viewed the Kremlin’s remarks and the SVR statement as another attempt to pressure Armenia.

In their view, the crisis in bilateral relations continues, and “there is still no solution in sight”. They also questioned why Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, rather than the EAEU itself, had spoken on the bloc’s behalf.

The Armenian prime minister’s office said that, during the call, “Pashinyan stressed that restrictions on exports of Armenian-made goods to the Russian market violate the legal framework governing Armenia-Russia relations and Eurasian Economic Union regulations. He asked Russia to take steps to resolve the issue.” Pashinyan appears to have called Putin primarily over Russia’s ban on imports of numerous Armenian food products and other goods. Russia introduced the restrictions at the end of May.

Statement by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service

The SVR titled its statement, “The EU Lures Armenia but Cannot Help It.” The statement argues that Armenia would face a severe economic crisis if it left the EAEU.

“Armenia will lose the income it currently receives from Eurasian integration. The remaining EAEU members will not bankroll the Armenian authorities as they row toward the European Union. EU institutions acknowledge that the bloc’s worsening economic problems, driven by anti-Russian sanctions and what they describe as Brussels’ obsession with supporting the war in Ukraine, will leave the EU unable to offset Armenia’s multi-billion-dollar losses. Several European countries have already told EU leaders they are unwilling to open their markets to Armenian goods at the expense of domestic producers.”

Russia’s foreign intelligence service also claims the EU will continue to assure Yerevan of its unwavering support.

“The EU plans to explain the lack of tangible assistance by arguing that accession depends entirely on Yerevan and on its own ‘progress’ toward European integration.”

According to the SVR, the EU has already presented Pashinyan’s government with the following demands:

reduce the presence of Russian businesses in strategic sectors;

sever humanitarian ties with Russia;

suppress domestic opponents who resist those policies.

The statement adds that the EU will encourage Armenia by “holding out the prospect of visa liberalisation for Armenian citizens and promising that, at some distant point in the future, Armenia will become a ‘prosperous crossroads of peace.’

How Armenians View European Integration: Poll Results

Against the backdrop of Russia’s call for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether to remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership, local broadcaster Factor TV conducted an online poll. Participants answered the following question: “If a referendum on choosing between the EAEU and the EU were held this Sunday, which would you vote for?”

According to the broadcaster, more than 3,300 people have already taken part in the poll. The results are as follows:

74% said they would vote for EU membership;

said they would vote for EU membership; 21% said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU;

said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU; 5% said they were undecided.

Reactions

Political analyst Samvel Melkisetian said:

“Statements like these from Moscow are nothing new. They fit a long-established Russian pattern. The aim is to show both domestic and international audiences that Russia remains actively involved in regional developments. They also seek to expose what they portray as the EU’s and the West’s ‘hidden mechanisms’ of harmful influence across the post-Soviet region.”

He also noted that Moscow’s rhetoric often portrays Armenia not as a sovereign state making its own decisions, but as an object of external influence.

Political analyst Hovsep Khurshudyan said:

“What does Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service have to do with the EAEU that allows it to speak on behalf of the bloc’s member states? Has the SVR become the press office for the EAEU or its members?”

Khurshudyan also questioned Russia’s intelligence service:

“How can Brussels be accused of driving Armenia’s economy into crisis when it is Brussels that is compensating for the losses caused by the sanctions Russia has imposed?”

He was referring to EU support programmes launched after Russia restricted imports of Armenian goods.

Khurshudyan argues that, in the end, Russia’s actions will only accelerate:

Armenia’s withdrawal from Russian-led integration structures, including the EAEU and the Collective Security Treaty Organization;

the withdrawal of Russian border guards from Armenia’s borders with Iran and Turkey;

the termination of the concession agreement under which a Russian company operates Armenia’s railways.

Khurshudyan believes Armenia still has room to take further steps, while Russia has already exhausted most of its leverage.

SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

World.title: Imam of Georgia’s Akhaltsikhe mosque and family members brutally beaten
World.content:
Georgia‘s Interior Ministry has launched an investigation into an attack on the family of a Meskhetian Muslim in the city of Akhaltsikhe. According to the victims, more than 10 people assaulted the imam of the local mosque, Shevket Dvalidze, and members of his family during the incident on 18 July.

The attack was first reported by the news outlet Batumelebi. According to the publication, the assault began after the imam’s son and an underage relative visiting from Turkey were heard speaking Turkish to each other.

Meskhetian Muslims, also known as Meskhetian Turks or Ahiska Turks, are a Turkic ethnic group originating from the historical region of Meskheti in southwestern Georgia.

Shevket Dvalidze, imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque

According to the imam’s family, the group initially confronted them verbally, hurling insults over their use of the Turkish language, before the argument escalated into a physical assault.

The victims said the attackers followed them to their home and brutally beat them in the courtyard. Shevket Dvalidze, the imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque, sustained the most serious injuries and was later taken to hospital.

Batumelebi reported that Dvalidze was also urged to withdraw his police complaint.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry said it had opened an investigation under Article 126 of the Criminal Code, which covers physical violence.

The Georgian-based Social Justice Center responded to the incident by calling on the authorities to conduct a prompt and effective investigation and to properly assess whether the attack was motivated by discrimination.

According to the organisation, the victims said that between 10 and 12 people took part in the assault, and that most of them had been identified. However, only two suspects were arrested and were later released on bail by a court.

The Social Justice Center said the circumstances suggested the case could constitute not only an act of violence but also a hate crime, as the attack may have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation said investigators should examine whether the assault was motivated by the victims’ ethnic, religious or linguistic identity and ensure those circumstances are properly reflected in the legal classification of the case.

According to the Social Justice Center, correctly classifying the attack as a hate crime is important not only because of its legal consequences, but also because it acknowledges the true nature of the offence and helps prevent similar incidents.

The organisation called on the Interior Ministry and the Prosecutor’s Office to identify all those involved in the attack, rather than limiting the investigation to the two detained suspects. It also urged investigators to examine allegations that pressure had been put on the imam to withdraw his police complaint.

The Social Justice Center also called on the government and the Office of the State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality to publicly condemn the violence against the Meskhetian Muslim family, which it said appeared to have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation further urged the authorities to strengthen policies promoting equality, rebuilding trust and supporting cultural diversity in Akhaltsikhe’s Meskhetian Muslim communities, while reviewing barriers related to the repatriation and citizenship of Meskhetian Muslims.

Imam beaten in Georgia after speaking Turkish

World.title: Nauru cuts diplomatic ties with occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The Pacific island nation of Nauru has cut diplomatic ties with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, Georgia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

According to the ministry, Nauru’s cabinet decided on 21 July 2026 to terminate diplomatic relations “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of South Ossetia, also known as the State of Alania,” and “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of Abkhazia.”

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation based on shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions to be independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to back the Moscow-backed move.

Nauru is a small island nation in the Pacific Ocean, in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 square kilometres, the country is smaller than several districts of Tbilisi, while its population is estimated at around 12,000 to 13,000 people.

Nauru ends ties with Abkhazia and South Ossetia

World.title: Families of men killed in Taipan army helicopter crash launch class action
World.content:
A class action has been launched against the Commonwealth and Airbus, over a fatal army helicopter crash that killed four men during a training exercise in July 2023.

It is expected to allege failings led to their deaths.

Lead applicant, Caitland Lyon lost her husband, Captain Danniel Lyon in the crash.

He was flying an MRH90 Taipan helicopter over waters near Lindeman Island during an exercise for exercise Talisman Sabre, one of the defence force's largest military exercises.

The families of the four men killed in the crash have launched a class action, expected to allege failings by the Commonwealth and Airbus. (Supplied: ADF)

While flying in a four-helicopter formation, his aircraft, which had the call sign Bushman 83, suddenly dipped and plummeted into the ocean.

Captain Lyon and his three colleagues, Lieutenant Maxwell Nugent, Warrant Officer Class 2 Joseph Phillip Laycock and Corporal Alexander Naggs died.

This week marked three years since the crash, and the families of the four dead aviators returned to Airlie Beach, near the crash site, for the erection of a permanent memorial.

A permanent memorial honouring the four men was unveiled earlier this month. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

The class action, which the ABC understands includes around 10 family members of the airmen, is expected to allege reasonable care was not taken in relation to the safety of the Taipan aircraft, its systems and configuration, the planning and authorisation of the mission, the management of visual degraded conditions, fatigue and workload, warnings and risk controls and providing information and support to aircrew.

Taipan crash memorial A permanent memorial honouring the four men has been unveiled near the place where part of their helicopter was dragged from the water.

Ms Lyon said she and other affected family members were running up against a time limitation period under Queensland law and needed to stop the clock, after hearing "alarming" evidence at an independent inquiry into the crash.

"We are deeply concerned by the airworthiness of the [MRH90] and how it was brought into service, as well as the TopOwl system," Ms Lyon said.

The TopOwl 5.10 software has been at the centre of examination during the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force (IGADF) inquiry, after former test pilots revealed they had deemed the technology too dangerous for service and that it posed an "unacceptable risk" to pilot safety.

That inquiry also heard the men, and their regiment were sleeping next to an active airport and fire station, in hot and noisy tents.

The Taipan wreckage was pulled from the water off the coast in the days following the crash. (ABC News)

One expert who analysed the men's apparent sleep schedules gave evidence to the inquiry and said the men were so fatigued, it would have been like flying over the legal alcohol limit.

The IGADF is set to hand down its findings and recommendations imminently, after a mammoth inquiry.

A probe by the Senate is set to hand down a separate report into the crash in September.

The Department of Defence and Airbus has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Mother-daughter 'ISIS bride' pair plead not guilty to slavery crimes
World.content:
A mother and daughter charged with slavery crimes while living under Islamic State rule in Syria have pleaded not guilty, fast-tracking their cases to Victoria's Supreme Court.

Kawsar Ahmad, 54, and Zeinab Ahmad, 31, faced the Melbourne Magistrates Court via videolink and formally entered the pleas, meaning their cases will now proceed to trial.

The women were part of a group, dubbed the "ISIS brides", who returned to Australia in May having spent years held in a Syrian detention camp.

Prosecutors allege members of the Ahmad family moved to Syria about a decade ago and kept a slave in their home while supporting Islamic State.

Kawsar Ahmad is charged with enslavement, possessing a slave, using a slave and engaging in slave trading.

Zeinab Ahmad is facing two charges: enslavement and using a slave.

Zeinab Ahmad, 31, remains in custody following a failed bid for bail. (Supplied: Anita Lester)

The pair have opted to fast-track the case to the Supreme Court, skipping a committal hearing where prosecution evidence would be assessed by a magistrate.

The first Supreme Court directions hearing will take place on August 21.

Further pre-trial hearings will need to occur before a trial date can be set.

The Australian Federal Police allege Kawsar Ahmad taught religious studies to the alleged slave, a Yazidi teenager part of an ethnic group persecuted by the Islamic State terrorist group.

She was granted bail last month by Victoria's top magistrate Lisa Hannan.

Her daughter Zeinab Ahmad was denied freedom however, with the same magistrate finding she had not established that "exceptional circumstances" existed to warrant her release on bail.

Since returning home in May, lawyers for both women have said they do not support Islamic State or terrorist ideology.

In June, Zeinab Ahmad's defence barrister Grace Morgan accepted there had been no "explicit" renunciation but said her client despised IS and the "men who enforced its ideals on her".

Members of the Ahmad family spent years in the Al Roj detention camp in Syria after the fall of Islamic State and made impassioned pleas to the Australian government to be brought home.

World.title: 'A bit rude': Barristers bicker as gangland figures discussed at CFMEU inquiry
World.content:
A top silk who investigated the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) has refused to withdraw claims that a notorious Melbourne gangland figure controls a network of labour-hire companies, under tense cross-examination at a Queensland inquiry.

Lawyer Geoffrey Watson SC authored a bombshell report titled Rotting from the Top which laid bare allegations of a culture of violence, intimidation and bullying in the union's Queensland branch.

He also alleged widespread corruption and bikie infiltration in the Victorian division under ousted leader John Setka.

Mr Watson fronted the inquiry in Brisbane on Friday and faced combative questioning by Simon Wilson KC, acting for the M1 Trades Group, a Victorian labour-hire and traffic management firm linked to underworld identity Mick Gatto.

In his report, Mr Watson alleged companies within the M Group network used "dummy directors" such as Tony Paragalli and Michael Portia to mask the involvement of Mr Gatto.

He also alleged Mr Gatto's denials of owning the businesses were "transparently false".

Mr Watson declined to withdraw any findings relating to Mr Gatto and the M Group.

Mick Gatto and his associates Tony Paragalli and Michael Portia have all strongly denied any improper ties. (ABC News)

"It is my view all the evidence points to Mr Gatto controlling the M Group companies," he said.

"It was a business which was commenced by an act of corruption."

The inquiry has heard M1 Traffic Control Qld Pty Ltd, a recently-established Gold Coast company, is owned by Mr Paragalli and Mr Portia.

Mr Portia, Mr Paragalli and Mr Gatto have all strongly denied any improper ties, ownership or front arrangements.

Courtroom clash

The two senior barristers repeatedly clashed during the hours-long cross-examination.

"If you want to challenge my competence, go straight for it," Mr Watson said.

Mr Wilson replied: "I'm about to."

"I think you're being a bit rude," Mr Watson said.

"I'm going to be ruder later," Mr Wilson replied.

Report author Geoffrey Watson faced combative questioning at the CFMEU inquiry on Friday. (Supplied)

The courtroom duel continued, prompted Commissioner Stuart Wood KC to intervene, warning Mr Wilson to rein it in.

"Do we really need all this theatre?" Commissioner Wood asked.

"We don't need all the abuse," he said.

'They were suggesting I made it up'

Mr Watson told the inquiry that "nobody" from the Victorian government had contacted him about his explosive report, despite it fuelling a political firestorm in the state.

Former premier Jacinta Allen was ousted this week amid the fallout of Labor's handling of alleged CFMEU corruption, with her replacement Ben Carroll swiftly announcing a royal commission into the construction sector.

Qld CFMEU commissioner takes aim at police Commissioner Stuart Wood took aim at the police response to a 2024 CFMEU blockade in which he said police "took the side of law-breakers".

Mr Watson's allegations of criminal behaviour on the state's Big Build program was heavily criticised by the former premier and other ministers, including attorney-general Sonya Kilkenny, who called the assessment "reckless" and "lacking evidence".

"They made those statements to the press without asking me about how I arrived at the report … what I'd done to achieve the report," Mr Watson said.

"They were bitterly critical remarks. It's hard to read them as being anything less than they were suggesting I made it up," he said.

Earlier this year, lawyers for ousted CFMEU leaders Michael Ravbar and Jade Ingham also challenged the "veracity" of Mr Watson's findings, citing concerns over his research methods and record-keeping.

The inquiry heard Mr Watson relied on handwritten notes and chose not to tape interviews. However, he defended that approach, arguing witnesses "clam up" when being recorded.

World.title: Indonesian court bans use of education funding for free school meals
World.content:
Read the story in Bahasa Indonesia

Indonesia's Constitutional Court has ruled the country's flagship Free Nutritious Meals program, designed to combat under-nutrition, cannot be funded through the national education budget.

The free meals program, or MBG, was launched in 2025 with the aim of feeding 83 million school children and expectant mothers that year.

On Thursday, Indonesia's chief judge Suhartoyo ruled that the budget for educational needs and the free meals program must be separated within two years.

"Funding for the Free Nutritious Meals program, which is currently classified as a component of education spending, must be separated from operational education funding," the court said.

The ​ruling came after students and educators filed petitions against this year's state budget law, arguing that counting the free meals program as an educational provision violated Indonesia's constitution.

The court found while the provision did not breach the constitution this year, it must separate the funding allocations by no later than the 2028 state budget, but ideally earlier.

Teachers worry ruling will not be implemented

Under the constitution at least 20 per cent of Indonesia's state budget must be allocated to education.

In the 2026 budget, education spending accounted for 20.1 per cent of total expenditure.

At the centre of the case was the government's decision to allocate almost one-third of Indonesia's Rp769.1 trillion ($61.5 billion) education budget to the free meals program.

Sources of funding for the Free Nutritious Meals program. (ABC News: Jarrod Fankhauser; Indonesian Ministry of Finance)

The petitioners argued that if MBG spending were excluded, education spending would fall to about 14 per cent — well below the legal requirement.

They asked the court to ensure all of the education budget was directed to core learning functions like school facilities, teachers' salaries, classroom learning and scholarships.

The Education and Teachers' Association was one of the groups behind the challenge.

Iman Zanatul Haeri at the Constitutional Court. (ABC News: Ari Wu)

Iman Zanatul Haeri, head of teacher advocacy at the association, welcomed the court's decision but described it as "a grey area ruling".

"This kind of ruling is usually used by the government to keep a program going while making a few adjustments so it can continue operating while still complying with the constitution," Mr Haeri told ABC Indonesia.

"With this decision, the constitutional court must ensure that education funding is used for the welfare of educators, including university lecturers.

"But we also know that even in the best-case scenario there is no guarantee that the government will implement the ruling."

Mr Haeri said it was possible the government already had a plan to preserve the MBG, which it considered a priority initiative.

"We will continue to speak out until the government realises that using education funding for MBG is a fundamental constitutional mistake," he said.

Riga Felix was one of the petitioners for education funds to the Constitutional Court. (ABC News: Ari Wu)

Rega Felix, another petitioner who attended the Constitutional Court hearing, described the ruling as a "victory" for educators because it means "the education budget can no longer be interfered with by the MBG program".

He said some concerns remained.

"There are two key phrases in the ruling. Funding for MBG from the education budget is considered constitutional for 2026, but not for subsequent years," Mr Felix said.

"So I feel the Constitutional Court has still taken a middle path that remains somewhat grey. But in principle, our petition has been granted."

Mr Felix also said the court's decision to allow up to two years for the ruling to be implemented could be open to differing interpretations.

"We would prefer to see the political will start now because, in principle, this is not education spending," he said.

Some teachers paid less than $43 a month, association says

The Indonesian government plans to appoint tens of thousands of MBG's core kitchen workers as government employees. (Supplied: Nur Zaid, Kompas.com)

The test now will be whether the government fully implements the decision and redirects education funding towards schools, teachers and students.

The Institute for Demographic and Affluence (IDEAS) has previously said that the amount of money currently allocated to MBG was enough to provide free basic education for all Indonesian children, scholarships for nearly 3 million low-income university students and salary increases for more than 2 million contract teachers.

Teachers paid $170 per month as education funds go to free meals Temporary teachers in Indonesia paid low wages criticise a government decision to direct one third of yearly education funding to the president's flagship free meals program.

The Indonesian Teachers Association (PGRI), citing data from IDEAS, told parliament earlier this year that Indonesia still had at least 700,000 contract teachers.

According to the organisation, 74 per cent of those contract teachers earned less than Rp2 million ($170) a month, while some received less than Rp500,000 ($43).

"For example, in Dompu, West Nusa Tenggara, salaries are far below a decent standard, at just Rp139,000 ($11)," a PGRI representative told parliament.

Petitioners vow to see change enforced

President Prabowo Subianto inspecting the distribution of free meals in Bogor, West Java, last year. (Supplied: Presidential Secretariat Press Bureau, Cahyo)

Although the Constitutional Court has partially granted the challenge, Mr Haeri of the Education and Teachers' Association said he did not believe it would guarantee change and there was work to do.

"We will formally hand over the Constitutional Court's ruling to the state secretariat, the National Nutrition Agency, and the ministries and institutions involved in administering MBG," he told the ABC.

"We want to ensure that the executive branch truly implements the constitutional mandate, and hopefully that will lead to changes in the 2027 State Budget Law."

Petitioners celebrated the Constitutional Court's ruling prohibiting the use of education funds for MBG. (ABC News: Ari Wu)

Mr Haeri said the ruling represented an important test of the Constitutional Court's willingness to defend constitutional principles.

"We can see now whether these judges are truly guardians of the constitution or not, because a constitutional mandate is not a matter of whether it can or cannot be carried out, but a matter of obligation," he said.

" A constitutional mandate must be implemented, full stop. "

Prasetyo Hadi, Indonesia's minister of the state secretariat, said the government had received the court's ruling and would respect the decision.

"We will need to review it because budget matters are not decided by the government alone," he told reporters.

"The budget is drafted together with parliament, so please give us some time."

A group of people demonstrated in front of the Constitutional Court demanding that the government comply with the decision. (ABC News: Ari Wu)

MP Yahya Zaini, part of the ruling coalition, said the ruling should be acted on quickly, with policymakers finding a way for the MBG program to continue.

"The National Nutrition Agency must undertake major efficiency measures," Mr Zaini said.

"That includes refocusing spending, limiting the construction of new kitchens and improving the governance of the MBG program."

Meals program faces ongoing scrutiny

The National Nutrition Agency (BGN), which oversees the MBG program, has been under the spotlight in recent months.

In the lead up to the ruling there was a string of controversies involving the agency including allegations of corruption involving former BGN head Dadan Hindayana, the resignation of his successor Nanik S Deyang, and the closure of hundreds of MBG kitchens.

Indonesia's free meal program poisons thousands of children The key election commitment of President Prabowo Subianto is facing mounting backlash over its poor oversight, questionable food sourcing and unhygienic kitchens.

The government also reduced the program's budget on two occasions and said more cuts were possible.

Mr Haeri said those developments appeared less like a genuine internal review and more like an effort to adapt to the legal challenge.

"Whether this is predictive or something else, throughout the hearings we saw BGN continually trying to improve itself in line with the direction of the proceedings," he said.

"That is actually not good news, because they should have been conducting evaluations without needing to be challenged first, without us having to go to the Constitutional Court.

"The government is … revising things here and there, even though the root of the problem is that the design of BGN was flawed from the very beginning."

World.title: Pregnant wagyu cows and calves worth $200,000 stolen from station
World.content:
Pregnant cows and calves are among 142 wagyu cross cattle believed to have been stolen from a central Queensland station.

Greenlake Station manager Madeline Price said she noticed the cattle were missing during the second round of weaning, when young cattle are separated from their mothers.

"We ran the cows through at weaning and we got an accurate count on the 3rd of April," she said.

"We ran them through again on the 28th of May … after counting, double counting and triple counting and thinking we must be wrong. We weren't.

"That's when we realised that they were missing."

The stolen cattle are valued at more than $200,000. (Supplied: Madeline Price)

Valued at more than $200,000, the group included 97 cows and 45 weaner heifers, which are female cattle less than a year old.

Ms Price said among them were pregnant cows from the station's main breeding stock that were close to giving birth.

"It does make you feel pretty sick to ring your dad who's given you this amazing opportunity and tell him you're down 142 head of cattle," she said.

" It does make you lay in bed and think, 'What could I have done differently?' "

The Price Cattle Company runs 3,000 head across a 7,500-hectare operation about 50 kilometres north of Rockhampton.

Ms Price said it had taken some time to realise the cattle were stolen because of the size of the herd and property.

"It's like throwing 1000 grains of rice on your kitchen floor and saying which [group] has 900, which one has 1000?" she said.

The theft comes during a strong cattle market, where cows and weaner heifers have sold for as much as $2,000 a head, depending on weight and quality.

Stock squad detectives investigating the theft said anyone who saw unusual stock movements in the Todds Road and Rossmoya Road areas of Greeenlake during April or May should contact them.

"The cattle … were branded with a GL under half-circle symbol, a yellow management tag 'Greenlake' and NLIS devices," a spokesperson said in a statement.

AgForce Queensland, the state's peak producer body, also urged anyone with information on the matter to contact police.

"Stock theft can be difficult to detect and prosecute, and producers tell us it is more widespread than reported figures suggest," they said in a statement.

"Beyond the financial loss, stock affects producers' wellbeing and their sense of security on their own properties."

Madeline Price still has a couple of thousand cattle needing her care. (ABC Capricornia: Jessica D'Souza)

Ms Price said her focus was now on getting the remainder of the herd through winter.

"I guess you can't just sit under your desk rocking back and forth thinking about it," she said.

"There's thousands of other cattle on this place that day in, day out, that need you to keep up to them."

World.title: Jewish artist 'cancelled' after group chat leak, royal commission hears
World.content:
A Jewish Australian artist has said she was "cancelled", dropped from her residency and lost friends after the leaking of a private message in which she described terrorist group Hamas as "animals".

Representatives of Australia's arts and creative industry are fronting the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, which has been considering the use of education and training to combat hate.

The inquiry has previously heard evidence about hundreds of creatives whose information and messages were leaked in the doxxing of a private chat group in early 2024.

Nina Sanadze was involved in the collection of floral tributes following the Bondi attack. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

Melbourne artist Nina Sanadze told the inquiry a private message in which she described terrorist group Hamas as "animals" in the wake of the October 7, 2023 attack in Israel was released in the leak.

Ms Sanadze said she was immediately "dropped" from friendship groups and was told by the art institution she was attached to that it would be "inappropriate" for her to come to the studio.

She said she had told her employer before the doxxing event she would leave the studio, due to the increase in antisemitic sentiment in the community post-October 7, 2023.

"I said 'let me leave'. They were concerned it would look antisemitic … don't leave," she said.

Ms Sanadze said she was subsequently "interrogated" about her political beliefs by the art institution after the doxxing event in early 2024.

"I was told that if I did not leave the studios, there would be more … information released by unknown people, they wouldn't mention who, to discredit and damage my reputation. So I was threatened with that unless I left," she said.

Ms Sanadze went on to open the Goldstone Gallery in early 2025, saying there was "no other place for people like [her] to exhibit" their art.

The inquiry heard the gallery had hosted public events, poetry readings, live music and discussions between Palestinian and Israeli women.

The gallery is currently closed, with Ms Sanadze saying Jewish artists were hesitant to publicly exhibit their work.

"There's no funding, there's no security, it is very hard," she said.

"The artists are scared to exhibit, and it's getting worse after [the terror attack in] Bondi.

"People fear, not only for their safety but for their reputational damage."

Ms Sanadze was involved in the collection of three tonnes of floral tributes left at Bondi Pavilion after the shooting on December 14, 2025.

The vigil established at Bondi Pavilion following the December 14 terror attack.

The flowers have been transported to Melbourne, where they are being used to create an exhibition for the Sydney Jewish Museum.

Ms Sanadze said the flowers were a visible demonstration of the "outpouring and support" for the Jewish community.

"The flowers meant for me and for the Jewish community … they symbolise cohesion and empathy and standing together," she said.

Comedian told he didn't 'look Jewish'

The inquiry heard from a Jewish comedian, who used the pseudonym CGM, who shared some of the material he performs at festivals and gigs.

"Earlier this year, I was outside a bar speaking to a non-Jewish friend who said to me, 'you don't experience antisemitism do you? You don't even look Jewish'," he said.

"I asked him, 'what does Jewish look like, horns?'"

"It's true, I don't look like [Jerry] Seinfeld, but that didn't stop my synagogue in Melbourne from being … set on fire recently, or the synagogue where I did my bat mitzvah from being rammed by a car.

"Nor did it stop my workplace from being firebombed and graffitied to depict my Jewish boss with horns."

A witness described feeling "fear and shame" after the October 7, 2023 attack. (Suppied: Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion)

The comic said his peers had helped him when he started to isolate himself after October 7, 2023.

"After a few weeks, a comic with a Muslim background reached out to me and said 'where have you been?' I said I just feel like staying in … I feel so much fear and shame," he said.

"[The other comic] said to me 'brother, I've seen your act, you should have been feeling fear and shame the whole time.'

"He said 'don't be stupid, come and tell jokes.' He gave me a spot at his gig, which is a very generous thing for a comic to do."

CGM said he later told the other comic he felt "[Jewish] blood is cheap to people".

"He said [the Muslim community] feel the same," he said.

"I think there's a lot of feelings and a lot of pain. But we didn't hurt each other, we made each other laugh.

"That is one example of the best of the industry and what I hope people would want out of their arts industry.

"It is interesting to be in that nuance and that connection rather than the binary I think that's what makes great art."

World.title: Screening missed bus driver's opioid use before deadly wedding crash
World.content:
A breakdown in safety systems was a contributing factor to the lethality of a bus rollover in the NSW Hunter Valley that killed 10 passengers and injured dozens more, according to a new safety report.



The group was travelling home from a wedding in 2023 when the bus crashed in Greta, marking one of the deadliest coach crashes in the state's history.

Brett Button was sentenced to a prison term of 32 years after he was convicted of dangerous driving occasioning death over the crash.



The Office of Transport Safety (OTSI) report into the crash found the systems for detecting Button's drug use did not work.

"The driver should not have been behind the wheel that night, given a history of likely misuse of the opioid prescription painkiller tramadol, including likely impairment at the time of the crash," he said.

" The applicable system of driver health oversight and standard drug testing did not appropriately identify this issue or escalate it to the driver licensing authority. "

He said passenger complaints about his conduct were also not disclosed.



The investigation also found passenger protection systems, including seatbelts, were unable to prevent passenger ejections, which contributed to the extent of fatalities and injuries.



The report has handed down a total of 41 recommendations to improve safety across the state's bus and road network.



The state government has accepted in full or in principle the 21 recommendations that were handed to Transport for New South Wales.



It has proposed new legislation that includes a new set of safety duties for bus operators, company officers, procurers, bus safety workers and drivers, as well as a strengthened compliance and enforcement framework.

World.title: NSW minister reports 'vile' online threats to police
World.content:
NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty has referred "vile" comments made about her on the Facebook page of a political party to police.

The misogynistic and violent comments were posted on the Facebook page of the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers (SFF) Party in response to an announcement about a feral pig eradication program.

"I do think there needs to be consequences for serious threats that are made against anybody," Ms Moriarty said.

"Some of the comments are pretty vile.

"My team have met with the police … they've indicated they will follow up and I hope they do."

In a statement to the ABC, NSW Police said its inquiries into the matter were ongoing.

"Officers from Sydney City Police Area Command are aware of social media posts targeting a member of parliament," a spokesperson said.

Mark Banasiak says he was not aware of the threatening Facebook posts. (ABC Illawarra: Charles Rushforth)

SFF MLC Mark Banasiak was questioned about the posts on ABC Sydney's 702 Mornings program.

"When we see those comments, they are removed and deleted," he said.

"If we feel any of them warrant further referral, we do."

Mr Banasiak said he had not been made aware of the posts and could not recall the last time he referred commentary on either the party's or his professional Facebook page to the police.

Ms Moriarty said all politicians and parties had "a responsibility to monitor what's happening on our social media feeds".

Some of the posts, viewed by the ABC, are now no longer appearing on the SFF Facebook page.

Chris Minns says Tara Moriarty should be able to do her job without being vilified. (ABC News: Julia Andre)

Mr Minns said Ms Moriarty should be able to do her job without abuse or vilification.
