"I thought it was appalling; no-one deserves that," he said.

"Twenty or 30 years ago you never saw that sort of abuse; people would be too ashamed to label someone like that.

"Now they feel like they've got impunity to do it online and it's disgraceful."

Minister says 'it's not on'

Ms Moriarty said it was not the first time she had received a violent threat this year.

"People should be able to have robust debates online, but there's no need at all to threaten anybody at any time with violence," she said.

"It's not on."

Mr Banasiak himself spoke about politicians being subjected to threats in NSW Parliament in October 2024.

"What many of us did not 

NSW Farmers vice president Rebecca Reardon said although she had not seen the online threats, making derogatory comments was "not the way to behave with people".

"It's not the way to talk to people and it's certainly not the way to get the best results on things," she said.

"Generally speaking, I do not hear that sort of rhetoric … [farmers] do not go around representing themselves in that manner."

World.title: There can only be one Taylor Swift. For the rest of us, there’s life
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsCelebrity life Opinion There can only be one Taylor Swift. For the rest of us, there’s life Our young companion had given up on fame. Who was I to argue? Anson Cameron Spectrum columnist, The Age July 31, 2026 — 1:57pm

July 31, 2026 — 1:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The rain had closed the roads, and we were stranded on the far side of the Flinders in a remote shearers’ quarters cooking outside on an open fire waiting for the wind to dry the country and set us free. Stuck with us on this far-flung station was a young woman, travelling by herself – an independent soul, edgy tattoos, doing yoga in the morning before lone walks to ephemeral waterfalls. She had a purposefully serene bearing that reminded me of someone who has recently faced down troubles and is minute-by-minute ignoring the pain, deciding to play life like it’s someone else’s problem. Nothing would excite her too much now ... she was too distant to be hurt. It was like she’d chosen to be old. We got talking, and it turned out she had been a musician, and had gained some traction in that world – she was Googleable, I found videos and songs online. But it had ended now, she said. At 17 she’d given herself 10 years to make it and that 10 years was up. It hadn’t worked, so she was putting the dream behind her. “No teenager knows what a decade is,” I said. “You made a bet with an unknown currency.” Photo: Robin Cowcher I thought of telling her no dream was over until you called it over, but I couldn’t do it. She was right – her dream of living as a musician was likely behind her now. For most people, their belief in their own exceptionality is as comforting as a god on their shoulder – but at some stage, tasting piquant daily truths, the fantasy sickens, loses pace, dies ... and they have to live on after its death.



Which makes me wonder about the value of the dream, and of dreaming, of believing you’ll be Taylor Swift, Bad Bunny, Banksy, Picasso, Hunter Thompson, Cate Blanchett, Anais Nin ... of becoming a musician, an artist, an actor, an influencer. Fame has always been a big sell at school, and an easy one to the young, with them wanting the adumbration they see of it. At 15, no one hears the siren song of accountancy or bureaucracy. They eagerly opt to be the next Springsteen, and there is no shortage of adults telling them it’s doable, not far-fetched at all. But your stories are rejected, your tunes called derivative, you fluff the audition, your art doesn’t sell. It’s a risky thing, the dream, if you’ve invested heavily. Is it wrong for the adult world, the kindly chaperones and trained educators, to enliven the dream, it being so unlikely, so distracting and, eventually, so injurious? Or is the dream a necessary belief for many young people, a crucial bridge spanning that decade from the nihilist teens until the acceptance of the mortgage and the pram? Related Article Opinion I no longer tell people I’m from Victoria. They can get their laughs elsewhere I think a certain type of kid needs the dream. Some kids are Springsteen for just as long as they need to be, until their imaginations tire and their egos temper to fit the likelihoods, and it no longer hurts not to be Springsteen. What else was going to get those kids through the preposterous disappointments of youth but the dream? The idea of being a repeat of your parents is way harder to stomach at 17 than at 27, when you’ve made a grudging peace with the everyday. Maybe kids need the dream as a vaccination against despair, until the realisation that this is it, and that your parents weren’t so urgh after all – they were just people who held their heads up and got on with living life by the day, carrying water, chopping wood, after their dreams had died.



There’s life after the dream, I wanted to tell this achingly ex muso. Without the responsibility of being the next Taylor Swift, you’re freed to take pleasure in a picnic, a baby’s foolery, a new bike, love, swimming, making bread, cutting deals ... any of the run-of-the-mill labours and micro-splendours that school around us to make a worthwhile world. We last saw her wandering in a red stone gorge. She’d taken “shrooms” and was entranced by the tumbling water and kaleidoscopic trees, all given licence for high jinks by psilocybin. They say that drug is a powerful tool for self-discovery. I know getting lost is. She’d been lost already that day, she told us, and we thought she probably would be again. She seemed determinedly adrift in the ruins of an imagined life. Next week, once the roads had dried, she’d be back in her city signing on to a happy enough afterlife, I hoped.

World.title: The five-star Melbourne luxury hotel that sits dusty and abandoned
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life The five-star Melbourne luxury hotel that sits dusty and abandoned Cara Waters Updated July 31, 2026 — 1:51pm ,first published 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The luxury Shangri-La hotel overlooking Carlton Gardens is set to be shelved with the developer applying to turn what was going to be a five-star hotel into apartments. What should be 500 rooms in the gleaming tower remain dusty concrete shells without fittings or fixtures even though it was first supposed to open in 2024, with the opening then pushed out to 2026. A proposed Shangri-La hotel overlooking the Carlton Gardens is set to be scrapped. Ruby Alexander There has been no progress in four years at the 61-level hotel with the entrance blocked by temporary fencing and piles of dead leaves beside the shuttered doors. The Shangri-La is one half of a $600 million twin-tower structure at 308 Exhibition Street that was completed by builder Multiplex in August 2023.



No progress has been made at the 61-level hotel for four years. Ruby Alexander Its neighbour, a 59-level residential tower called Sapphire by the Gardens, is connected to the empty Shangri-La tower by an arching bridge on level 46. Billionaire Adrian Portelli owns the $39 million penthouse in Sapphire by the Gardens into which he famously craned his McLaren Sena GTR sports car. However, Portelli is unlikely to have to share his view with Shangri-La guests after the hotel’s developer, Setia (Melbourne) Development Company, a subsidiary of Malaysian conglomerate Setia SP, filed an application with the government seeking a planning permit to convert the hotel shell into 393 residential apartments. Shangri-La Melbourne was supposed to open in 2024 but the rooms are still empty shells. Arsineh Houspian



Related Article City life ‘Lambo guy’ Adrian Portelli’s light party keeps the city awake A spokesperson for the Department of Transport and Planning said the proposal would be considered in accordance with the relevant planning scheme. “Any proposal will be considered on its merits – as this application is currently under assessment it would be inappropriate to comment further,” he said. Setia (Melbourne)’s financial report filed last week recorded a $14.4 million loss for the financial year. “Construction for the hotel tower has not started and the company continues to assess strategies in relation to the completion of the development,” the report states.



Green Street News, which writes on commercial real estate, has reported that disagreement over construction costs scuppered the hotel deal, with Shangri-La wanting Setia to deliver the fitout for the cost that was quoted pre-COVID. The twin gleaming glass towers cover half a city block at the northern end of Melbourne’s CBD opposite the gardens that house the historic Royal Exhibition Building, the site of Australia’s first parliament. Billionaire Adrian Portelli inside his penthouse apartment in Sapphire by the Gardens with Zeher Khalil of Site Inspections. YouTube/Site Inspections Setia sold the management rights for the hotel complex to the global luxury brand Shangri-La in 2017, and in 2022 the incomplete hotel was unsuccessfully offered for sale for $500 million for the empty building – effectively $1 million for each room key. The plans for the hotel include a grand ballroom with a 2500-person capacity, function rooms and event spaces, a health club, spa and wellness centre, as well as restaurants and bars.



The Age has previously reported the cost of the hotel fitout before the COVID-19 pandemic had been budgeted at about $60 million, but inflation and cost increases for materials and labour have since inflated that estimate to $80 million. That puts a $580 million price tag on the fully furnished and fitted-out hotel. The plans for Adrian Portelli’s $39 million Melbourne penthouse at Sapphire by the Gardens. Wentao Zhang lives in the adjoining Sapphire by the Gardens tower and said in his three years as a resident, there had been no progress on the fit-out of the Shangri-La. “It’s completely empty inside and neglected, some of the windows are broken,” he said. “I’ve heard they’ve run into financial difficulties.”



Zhang said residents of Sapphire by the Gardens have no access to the sky-bridge floor on level 46 which is supposed to connect the apartments to the hotel. Related Article Commercial real estate The Melbourne luxury hotel that needs just one thing Cancelling Shangri-La’s Melbourne hotel means that the luxury brand will only have two sites in Australia: the Shangri-La Sydney and the Shangri-La the Marina in Cairns. André Jacques, regional director of marketing at Langham Hospitality Group and director of the Victorian Tourism Industry Council, said it would be disappointing if Shangri-La’s Melbourne hotel was abandoned and turned into apartments. “It would be a shame, considering how many apartments there are already in Melbourne,” he said. “From an international hotel brand standpoint, and a luxury hotel brand, it’s very positive to have another brand like Shangri-La in the market.”



Jacques said 6500 new hotel rooms had opened in Melbourne in the last six years, but occupancy rates were strong and there was still demand for luxury hotels. Setia SP, Setia (Melbourne) and Shangri-La declined to comment on whether plans for the hotel have been permanently shelved. World.title: ‘There are people still waiting to be rescued’: Foreigner among victims as Japan quake toll rises
World.content:
WorldAsiaEarthquakes ‘There are people still waiting to be rescued’: Foreigner among victims as Japan quake toll rises Mari Yamaguchi Updated July 31, 2026 — 1:38pm ,first published July 30, 2026 — 3:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kumamoto: Soldiers and emergency workers combed through a badly damaged shopping mall and collapsed houses looking for trapped survivors on Wednesday after a powerful earthquake that killed at least 34 people, including a foreigner, in south-western Japan. The 7.1-magnitude earthquake that hit a day earlier in the Kumamoto area on the southern main island of Kyushu also left at least 86 people injured, five of them seriously, the prefectural government said. The tally has been steadily growing, fanning fears it may continue to rise. Loading Some of the most serious damage was at the Aeon Mall shopping centre in the town of Kashima, which was bustling with thousands of people when the quake happened. The company said some 3000 customers were evacuated to a parking lot before a gas explosion happened in another part of the mall, where some people were still working. Fumika Ono was shopping at a mall with her older sister when the ground shook so fiercely she lost her balance and ducked. Children began screaming and goods scattered on the floor.



The 19-year-old was among the crowd of shoppers who managed to escape safely. Related Article Updated

Earthquakes Race to find survivors of deadly Japan quake as death toll rises The sweltering weather heightened worries about the survivors as rescuers braved the heat. It remained unclear how many people might still be missing. The mall’s second floor collapsed, trapping people. Witnesses said the explosion shook the area as much as the quake. Three people remained missing, while four deaths were confirmed at the mall site, according to Aeon President Akio Yoshida.



“We take it seriously that an explosion happened and precious lives were lost,” Yoshida told a news conference in Kumamoto, where he bowed deeply along with two other executives. Japanese media footage of the mall showed that part of the ceiling had caved in, and metal pieces and other debris were scattered about as helmeted and masked rescue workers searched the area. The rescue operation inside Aeon mall. Japan's Fire and Disaster Management Agency via AP The explosion followed the 7.1-magnitude earthquake. Getty Images Kiyoshi Matsunaga, 74, who lives in the mall’s neighbourhood and was at a supermarket just a few blocks away, said Tuesday’s quake reminded him of a deadly quake 10 years ago that hit Kumamoto and killed 50 people.



He stopped in his tracks when the shaking began while he was pushing his cart toward a cash register. Things scattered from the shelves. He could not move, he recalled. “I was frightened,” he said. Japan is one of the most quake-prone nations in the world. In the Nuyamazu district, a pair of temple gates at a 16th-century Buddhist temple collapsed. They had just been repaired five years ago.



Yuki Kiyozumi, deputy chief priest at the temple, recalled how she had to crawl on the floor because the shaking was so violent. She had just returned home from a meeting and was about to feed her cat. “I don’t even know if or how we can rebuild them again,” she said, while cleaning up damaged ornaments and furniture. A man helps clean the damaged gate of Jofukuji Buddhist temple in Kumamoto. AP Photo/Hiro Komae The fallen torii gate near a shrine in Yatsushiro. Yu Nakajima/Kyodo News via AP In nearby Yatsushiro, a chimney collapse at a Nippon Paper Industries factory killed five people while seven others were rescued from the debris, according to the Kumamoto prefectural government disaster team.



Four people were still believed to be trapped there, it said. A smokestack at Nippon Paper Industries’ Yatsushiro Mill collapsed in the earthquake. undefined/Kyodo News via AP In the first reported death of a foreign national, a Vietnamese technical intern was killed after a crane fell on him at a factory where he worked, according to the Vietnamese government. He had arrived in Japan in January. Seven other Vietnamese technical interns at the factory evacuated safely. Separately, a Vietnamese woman married to one of the workers was injured when a wall collapsed and was being treated at a hospital. Nearly 34,900 homes were still without electricity and some 15,000 homes without running water, Kumamoto officials said. More than 8800 people left their homes to stay in over 400 shelters, where power sources were being added to provide air conditioning.



Aerial police footage showed some homes in residential areas were completely flattened, including a few that crumbled into a nearby river. Japan’s Self Defence Forces joined rescue workers in the search and rescue operations. Hundreds of professionals were helping with the effort, including firefighters from Taiwan. Related Article Explainer

Earthquakes Scientists know where the big earthquakes will hit. They just don’t know when “There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it’s a race against time,” Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said. “We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can.” Takaichi said the government was preparing to deliver food and other necessities to hard-hit areas. She also offered her condolences to the victims and sympathy to their relatives, while urging those affected by the quake to take care of themselves under the hot weather.



Bullet train services remained suspended. Although operations at Aso Kumamoto Airport resumed Wednesday, some airlines cancelled flights as a precautionary measure. AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Local transmission of H5N1 declared as alarm sounds for local birds, sea lions
World.content:
PoliticsFederalBird flu Local transmission of H5N1 declared as alarm sounds for local birds, sea lions Mike Foley Updated July 31, 2026 — 1:30pm ,first published July 29, 2026 — 12:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dreaded local transmission of the deadly H5N1 bird flu has been declared in South Australia, sounding the alarm for avian species around the country and sparking fears for a colony of endangered sea lions, which are also susceptible to the virus. The South Australian government said on Wednesday that 11 new cases of the virus had been detected among greater crested terns, a local species that does not leave the country. CSIRO national laboratory testing underway is expected to confirm the SA results. It is likely that migratory seabirds from the Antarctic brought the virus to Australia and it then spread among terns. Australian sea lions are endangered, and the Kangaroo Island colony of 1000 is one of the country’s largest. David Whitley Seven detections were made on South Australia’s south-east coast, and four on Kangaroo Island.



SA Primary Industries Minister Clare Scriven said results showed it was “very, very likely” the birds were infected with H5N1 virus. Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the virus was believed to be spreading in terns and that with the onset of local transmission, it would spread in local populations. “We do expect with this local transmission there will be further transmission in Australian wildlife,” Collins said. Australia’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Beth Cookson, said little could be done to stem the virus moving around the country. “In the natural environment there are limited feasible actions to contain the spread,” Cookson said.



Bird flu viruses have circulated around the globe for decades. H5N1 is a particularly deadly variant and has killed hundreds of millions of birds around the world. It is believed that an outbreak in Australia could spark an environmental disaster, risking extinction of dozens of species including marine mammals such as dolphins and seals that also suffer from infection. Related Article Bird flu Deadly bird flu puts 100 species of Australia’s ‘isolated’ wildlife at risk of mass deaths Scriven said popular beach tours to the colony of about 1000 sea lions at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island had been halted. The virus has not been detected among the marine mammals, but tours were halted to stop any potential disturbances that could harm the colony. There are also about 100,000 long-nosed fur seals on or around Kangaroo Island. These animals can also contract the virus. “Everyone knows how susceptible the [sea lion] population is, and they are an endangered species,” Scriven said.



H5N1 arrived in South America in 2022 and killed more than 30,000 South American sea lions, 17,000 southern elephant seal pups and unknown numbers of porpoises, dolphins and otters, as well as at least 650,000 native birds. More than 13,000 seal pups were killed by the virus on Australia’s sub-Antarctic Heard Island territory, which was more than three-quarters of new births on the island. Conservation groups are calling for the immediate deployment of a $200 million fund to boost wildlife resilience. They argue that while the virus cannot be stopped from spreading among wildlife, investment in habitat restoration and programs to cull feral predators can help native animals survive the outbreak. “With only 12,000 individuals left, the Australian sea lion simply cannot absorb the kind of losses we have seen bird flu inflict on marine mammals overseas,” said Australian Marine Conservation Society campaign director Alexia Wellbelove. “Every colony, every pup, every individual matters when a population is this small. We cannot afford to wait.”



Invasive Species Council senior advocate James Johnston said emergency wildlife funds were critical. “We can’t stop bird flu reaching every corner of Australia, but we can give our wildlife a much better chance of surviving it,” he said. Related Article Biodiversity ‘Finish line in sight’ for world-leading cat eradication on Kangaroo Island The Albanese government committed $113 million to preparations to deal with an H5N1 incursion, with an emphasis on planning to identify an outbreak swiftly and a response to limit its spread. This includes funding to prepare biosecurity officers to respond to an outbreak in farmed poultry, which may involve quarantining farms or districts and restricting transport between locations.



Tens of millions of dollars have also been committed to environmental measures such as building pup shelters on Kangaroo Island to help reduce infant mortality in sea lions, removing weeds from islands to improve habitat for seabirds, and funding pre-existing captive breeding programs for endangered species such as the Tasmanian devil, orange-bellied parrot and regent honeyeater. The funds would also pay for teams to remove carcasses of infected animals swiftly to prevent further spread and limit contact between wild and farmed birds. Australia’s unique wildlife, which has evolved in isolation for millions of years, could be particularly vulnerable to H5N1. But little is known about native species’ vulnerability. There have been no detections of the virus in farmed poultry. An outbreak would cause a significant impact on chicken meat and egg production. H5N1 in the United States has caused more than 170 million birds to be culled since 2022, while egg prices had tripled by 2025. H5N1 is not considered a significant risk to human health. However, pet birds and cats usually become extremely ill and die when infected.



Dogs are more resistant to the virus and rarely die or become severely ill. The same is believed to be true for rabbits and guinea pigs as well as cows, sheep, pigs and horses. People are encouraged to look out for possible infections in birds and marine mammals. Signs include sudden death or difficulty breathing, standing, walking or flying. Sick animals should not be touched, but their location should be noted, with photos and videos, before calling the bird flu hotline on 1800 675 888. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

CLARIFICATION A previous version said the new strain of bird flu threatened otters, which are only found in Australian zoos. The closest native animal is the otter-like rakali.

World.title: Fresh data backs Amplia push against pancreatic, ovarian cancer
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Fresh data backs Amplia push against pancreatic, ovarian cancer Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright July 31, 2026 — 1:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Amplia Therapeutics has received encouraging lab results which highlighted the use of its lead drug narmafotinib, saying it can attack several of the nastier features that make the cancer so hard to treat. The research, led by Professor Paul Timpson and colleagues at Sydney’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research, was the results of extensive laboratory work on narmafotinib in pancreatic cancer models and was posted online on the biology preprint server bioRxiv. Amplia Therapeutics’ says fresh preclinical research data has strengthened the case for its drug candidate narmafotinib against pancreatic cancer cells, pictured. Amplia says the work adds further evidence that narmafotinib, a focal adhesion kinase (FAK) inhibitor, may improve outcomes by targeting tumour fibrosis, chemotherapy resistance and metastatic spread - three big hurdles in a disease that remains one of cancer medicine’s toughest assignments. FAK is a protein inside cells that acts like a control switch for movement, survival and attachment. It sits where cells anchor to their surrounding environment and helps tell them whether to grow, move or shut themselves down.



‘The research conducted by Professor Timpson’s team over recent years is now being shared with the broader scientific community.’ Amplia Therapeutics chief executive office and managing director Dr Chris Burns In many cancers, FAK becomes overactive or over-produced, helping tumour cells survive, move and spread. That has made it a target for cancer-fighting drugs such as narmafotinib. Among the key findings, the paper reported reduced tumour fibrosis and enhanced anti-tumour activity when narmafotinib was combined with chemotherapy. Other results included reduced cancer dissemination and metastatic spread in a pancreatic cancer model and the down-regulation – or diminished activity - of multiple genes linked to chemotherapy resistance. In this case, the drug appears to turn down genes that usually help cancer cells resist chemotherapy. The effect is to weaken the cancer cells’ defences, leaving chemotherapy better able to do its job and potentially lowering the number of cancer cells that remain alive after treatment. Amplia Therapeutics chief executive officer and managing director Dr Chris Burns said: “These studies strengthen the scientific rationale for the clinical development of narmafotinib and provide further insight into the multifaceted mechanisms through which narmafotinib can act in the treatment of this devastating disease.”



The update follows a busy clinical run for the Melbourne-based biotech. In May, Amplia launched the first stage of a Phase 2b registration-enabling pancreatic cancer study that will test daily dosing of narmafotinib with the chemotherapy drugs gemcitabine and Abraxane in newly diagnosed advanced pancreatic cancer patients. A registration-enabling study is a pivotal clinical trial designed to produce the core evidence needed to support an application for approval to market a new drug. Its job is to show that a treatment is safe at the proposed dose, that it helps patients and that the data package is strong enough for regulators such as the US Food and Drug Administration or Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration to assess. The study is expected to enrol 12 patients across two dose cohorts at three or four Australian sites, with patient enrolment planned for the fourth quarter of this year. Amplia’s June quarterly also underlined why the company is pressing ahead. Mature ACCENT trial data presented at the American Association for Cancer Research showed favourable safety and encouraging efficacy for narmafotinib, with a 36 per cent overall response rate and a 70 per cent disease control rate, compared with 50 per cent for chemotherapy alone. The data also showed median overall survival of 11.1 months — an improvement of more than two months — and progression-free survival of 7.7 months when narmafotinib was used with standard chemotherapy.



The company ended the June quarter with $24 million in cash, giving it a handy buffer as it pushes narmafotinib further into pancreatic cancer and prepares to test the same drug in a second oncology target. That expansion comes through PRROSE, a phase two trial being run under an agreement with the Australia New Zealand Gynaecological Oncology Group (ANZGOG) to evaluate narmafotinib alongside standard chemotherapy in 15 to 20 patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer. For Amplia, the latest paper is not a clinical result — but it is another useful building block. And in a field where every extra piece of biological support counts, the company will no doubt be happy to bank more evidence as it heads toward the next stage of its pancreatic cancer program. World.title: Anthropic’s Claude AI hacked three real companies during testing
World.content:
Updated TechnologyAI Anthropic’s Claude AI hacked three real companies during testing David Swan Updated July 31, 2026 — 1:08pm ,first published July 31, 2026 — 9:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anthropic has revealed its Claude artificial intelligence models broke into the computer systems of three real companies during safety testing, days after rival OpenAI disclosed a similar failure. The models were told they were working inside a sealed practice environment with no connection to the internet, but a set-up error meant they were not. When Claude went hunting for a way into its practice target and found real companies instead, it treated them as part of the game and broke in. On June 13, Anthropic suspended worldwide access to its two most powerful AI models. Bloomberg It did not need anything sophisticated. Anthropic said the models got in through weak passwords and systems left open without a login. The company found three incidents after reviewing 141,006 test runs, a check it began after OpenAI said on July 21 that several of its models had broken out of a locked-down test and reached the systems of AI platform Hugging Face. The earliest Claude incident happened in April.



Related Article Cybersecurity AI broke out of its cage and hacked a company. The grid could be next In each test, the model was set the same exercise: break into another machine and retrieve a piece of hidden information. The tests were run with an outside contractor, Irregular. In the first case, the made-up company which Claude had been told to attack shared its name with a real website. Unable to reach the fake target, the model went after the real one and got hold of passwords and a database holding several hundred records of real business data. Anthropic called it the most serious of the three, and the only one where a model kept going after working out the target was real. In the second, Claude found a note inside the practice environment telling staff to download a piece of software that did not exist. So it wrote its own booby-trapped version, set up an email address and an account, and uploaded it to a public library used by programmers worldwide. It sat there for about an hour and was downloaded onto 15 real computers. One belonged to a security firm that automatically installs new software to check it for viruses, which let Claude’s code steal that firm’s passwords and reach further into its systems. The model’s own written reasoning shows it saw the danger. If this were the real internet, it noted, publishing the software would be “NOT okay, and surely not the intended solution”. It then talked itself into believing the whole thing was staged and so carried on.



Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei. Bloomberg A third model, an experimental version never released to the public, scanned about 9000 possible targets and broke into one company’s website before it realised the system was real and stopped. Related Article Exclusive

AI ChatGPT’s evil twin: How criminals and extremists are using AI to lay traps Anthropic said none of the models tried to escape or chase goals of its own, and that the protections built into the versions of Claude that the public uses would have blocked all of it. The company was contacted for further comment. It has stopped running hacking tests that can reach the internet. Ian Rogers, a former Apple executive now working on AI security at digital security company Ledger, said the incident was a preview. “This happened in one of the world’s best-resourced AI labs,” he said. “Soon, there will be millions of AI agents connected to our email, calendars, financial accounts and enterprise systems.”



The three companies were told on July 27, and two had no idea they had been hacked. Irregular said its investigation was continuing and that it appreciated Anthropic’s “collaboration and transparency”. Related Article AI Silicon Valley’s AI spending spree comes with an Australian invoice Liming Zhu, a CSIRO research director working with the Australian AI Safety Institute on the problem, said the setup error explained most of what happened but not all of it. A well-behaved system should turn cautious when the evidence stops matching its instructions, he said, and the model that kept going after working out the target was real showed poor judgement under pressure. He was warier about treating the newest model’s decision to stop as progress, calling it “an encouraging observation, not an established trend”. It had still scanned thousands of systems and broken into one before it pulled up. The bigger issue for Australian businesses, Zhu said, is that ordinary AI assistants sold for everyday work keep the same hacking abilities under the bonnet. A badly worded instruction or too much system access can bring them out.



Pre-release safety testing is the main check on what frontier models can do before they reach the public, and governments, including Australia’s, are weighing how far to rely on that self-testing. After the OpenAI breach, the Australian Signals Directorate issued a public warning saying that the case showed what powerful AI systems will soon be capable of, and the new Australian AI Safety Institute briefed federal departments. Neither body can compel an AI company to report anything, however. The federal government dropped its plan for mandatory rules covering high-risk AI, and while the European Union and California already require serious AI incidents to be disclosed, Australia does not. World.title: How AFLW’s historic Australia-Ireland clash turned two Swans into rivals
World.content:
SportAFLAFLW How AFLW’s historic Australia-Ireland clash turned two Swans into rivals Jonathan Drennan July 31, 2026 — 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney Swans teammates Paris McCarthy and Zipporah “Zippy” Fish are used to doing detailed analysis on opponents each week in the AFLW; they just never expected to be doing it on each other. On Saturday, the friends will collide for their countries. Fish will represent Australia and McCarthy for Ireland at a sold-out North Sydney Oval for the first AFLW international match. Swans pair Paris McCarthy (left) and Zippy Fish will square off in a historic clash between Ireland and Australia at North Sydney Oval on Saturday. Wolter Peeters The pair have been reflecting on the long and often challenging journey they have taken to represent their countries. Fish grew up in the remote small town of Newman in Western Australia’s Pilbara region. McCarthy’s childhood was spent in the rural town of Castleisland, in County Kerry, Ireland.



Despite growing up on opposite sides of the world, McCarthy and Fish remain deeply connected to the beautiful small towns that shaped them as elite footballers. “When I do go out on Saturday, that will be in the back of my head that, for me, yes, I’m representing Ireland, but I am also representing Castleisland, where I came from,” McCarthy said. “I feel like I was always given the opportunity to play at a high level at whatever I did; on Saturday, that’ll be there in my mind: that I’m going out and bringing that flair from Castleisland.” Fish spent years kicking a football on the oval in Newman with no expectation of being a professional athlete, but her talent proved impossible to ignore. After being drafted by the Swans, Fish and her father Troy drove from Perth to Sydney, frequently stopping in towns along the way, giving her an insight into the diversity of Australia she wants to represent on Saturday.



“I’ve met a lot of great people along the way, and they’ve all done a lot for me, so I’ll be playing for everyone I know, really,” Fish said. “I think that’s mainly one of the reasons that I play footy is to try and be an inspiration to those young girls, because I was that little girl one time. I just hope to inspire young girls and see them live out their dreams.” Zippy Fish in action for the Swans Getty Images There are 46 Irish players on AFLW lists with 30 others who have previously played in the league. Despite the well-trodden path of her compatriots in the league, McCarthy now feels she is coming to grips with AFLW, having starred in Gaelic football in Ireland. She also played a season of top league college basketball with East Tennessee in the US.



“You come to a new country to play a new sport and you go from a big fish to the smallest fish,” McCarthy said. “You do sometimes think, ‘If I went back to Ireland, would I just go back to being a big fish again?’ “But that’s part of being a professional athlete. It’s not always going to be fun and I think that’s what I like about it: every day I can get better.” Alongside figuring out how to keep Fish, the 2025 AFLW Rising Star, quiet on the field, McCarthy has spent a long time thinking about what singing the Irish national anthem (Amhrán na bhFiann) at North Sydney Oval far from home will mean to her and her teammates. “I’ve thought about the anthem every day this week; I think that’s the one thing that will put me into the game and thinking about going out and giving it everything,” McCarthy said. “I feel like the national anthem means a lot to every Irish person and I haven’t heard it in four years, too, to get the opportunity to stand alongside those girls for Ireland and listen to it will definitely be something really special and something I’ll remember for the rest of my career.”

World.title: There can only be one Taylor Swift. For the rest of us, there’s life
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsCelebrity life Opinion There can only be one Taylor Swift. For the rest of us, there’s life Our young companion had given up on fame. Who was I to argue? Anson Cameron Spectrum columnist, The Age July 31, 2026 — 1:57pm

July 31, 2026 — 1:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The rain had closed the roads, and we were stranded on the far side of the Flinders in a remote shearers’ quarters cooking outside on an open fire waiting for the wind to dry the country and set us free. Stuck with us on this far-flung station was a young woman, travelling by herself – an independent soul, edgy tattoos, doing yoga in the morning before lone walks to ephemeral waterfalls. She had a purposefully serene bearing that reminded me of someone who has recently faced down troubles and is minute-by-minute ignoring the pain, deciding to play life like it’s someone else’s problem. Nothing would excite her too much now ... she was too distant to be hurt. It was like she’d chosen to be old. We got talking, and it turned out she had been a musician, and had gained some traction in that world – she was Googleable, I found videos and songs online. But it had ended now, she said. At 17 she’d given herself 10 years to make it and that 10 years was up. It hadn’t worked, so she was putting the dream behind her. “No teenager knows what a decade is,” I said. “You made a bet with an unknown currency.” Photo: Robin Cowcher I thought of telling her no dream was over until you called it over, but I couldn’t do it. She was right – her dream of living as a musician was likely behind her now. For most people, their belief in their own exceptionality is as comforting as a god on their shoulder – but at some stage, tasting piquant daily truths, the fantasy sickens, loses pace, dies ... and they have to live on after its death.



Which makes me wonder about the value of the dream, and of dreaming, of believing you’ll be Taylor Swift, Bad Bunny, Banksy, Picasso, Hunter Thompson, Cate Blanchett, Anais Nin ... of becoming a musician, an artist, an actor, an influencer. Fame has always been a big sell at school, and an easy one to the young, with them wanting the adumbration they see of it. At 15, no one hears the siren song of accountancy or bureaucracy. They eagerly opt to be the next Springsteen, and there is no shortage of adults telling them it’s doable, not far-fetched at all. But your stories are rejected, your tunes called derivative, you fluff the audition, your art doesn’t sell. It’s a risky thing, the dream, if you’ve invested heavily. Is it wrong for the adult world, the kindly chaperones and trained educators, to enliven the dream, it being so unlikely, so distracting and, eventually, so injurious? Or is the dream a necessary belief for many young people, a crucial bridge spanning that decade from the nihilist teens until the acceptance of the mortgage and the pram? Related Article Opinion I no longer tell people I’m from Victoria. They can get their laughs elsewhere I think a certain type of kid needs the dream. Some kids are Springsteen for just as long as they need to be, until their imaginations tire and their egos temper to fit the likelihoods, and it no longer hurts not to be Springsteen. What else was going to get those kids through the preposterous disappointments of youth but the dream? The idea of being a repeat of your parents is way harder to stomach at 17 than at 27, when you’ve made a grudging peace with the everyday. Maybe kids need the dream as a vaccination against despair, until the realisation that this is it, and that your parents weren’t so urgh after all – they were just people who held their heads up and got on with living life by the day, carrying water, chopping wood, after their dreams had died.



There’s life after the dream, I wanted to tell this achingly ex muso. Without the responsibility of being the next Taylor Swift, you’re freed to take pleasure in a picnic, a baby’s foolery, a new bike, love, swimming, making bread, cutting deals ... any of the run-of-the-mill labours and micro-splendours that school around us to make a worthwhile world. We last saw her wandering in a red stone gorge. She’d taken “shrooms” and was entranced by the tumbling water and kaleidoscopic trees, all given licence for high jinks by psilocybin. They say that drug is a powerful tool for self-discovery. I know getting lost is. She’d been lost already that day, she told us, and we thought she probably would be again. She seemed determinedly adrift in the ruins of an imagined life. Next week, once the roads had dried, she’d be back in her city signing on to a happy enough afterlife, I hoped.

World.title: The five-star Melbourne luxury hotel that sits dusty and abandoned
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life The five-star Melbourne luxury hotel that sits dusty and abandoned Cara Waters Updated July 31, 2026 — 1:51pm ,first published 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The luxury Shangri-La hotel overlooking Carlton Gardens is set to be shelved with the developer applying to turn what was going to be a five-star hotel into apartments. What should be 500 rooms in the gleaming tower remain dusty concrete shells without fittings or fixtures even though it was first supposed to open in 2024, with the opening then pushed out to 2026. A proposed Shangri-La hotel overlooking the Carlton Gardens is set to be scrapped. Ruby Alexander There has been no progress in four years at the 61-level hotel with the entrance blocked by temporary fencing and piles of dead leaves beside the shuttered doors. The Shangri-La is one half of a $600 million twin-tower structure at 308 Exhibition Street that was completed by builder Multiplex in August 2023.



No progress has been made at the 61-level hotel for four years. Ruby Alexander Its neighbour, a 59-level residential tower called Sapphire by the Gardens, is connected to the empty Shangri-La tower by an arching bridge on level 46. Billionaire Adrian Portelli owns the $39 million penthouse in Sapphire by the Gardens into which he famously craned his McLaren Sena GTR sports car. However, Portelli is unlikely to have to share his view with Shangri-La guests after the hotel’s developer, Setia (Melbourne) Development Company, a subsidiary of Malaysian conglomerate Setia SP, filed an application with the government seeking a planning permit to convert the hotel shell into 393 residential apartments. Shangri-La Melbourne was supposed to open in 2024 but the rooms are still empty shells. Arsineh Houspian



Related Article City life ‘Lambo guy’ Adrian Portelli’s light party keeps the city awake A spokesperson for the Department of Transport and Planning said the proposal would be considered in accordance with the relevant planning scheme. “Any proposal will be considered on its merits – as this application is currently under assessment it would be inappropriate to comment further,” he said. Setia (Melbourne)’s financial report filed last week recorded a $14.4 million loss for the financial year. “Construction for the hotel tower has not started and the company continues to assess strategies in relation to the completion of the development,” the report states.



Green Street News, which writes on commercial real estate, has reported that disagreement over construction costs scuppered the hotel deal, with Shangri-La wanting Setia to deliver the fitout for the cost that was quoted pre-COVID. The twin gleaming glass towers cover half a city block at the northern end of Melbourne’s CBD opposite the gardens that house the historic Royal Exhibition Building, the site of Australia’s first parliament. Billionaire Adrian Portelli inside his penthouse apartment in Sapphire by the Gardens with Zeher Khalil of Site Inspections. YouTube/Site Inspections Setia sold the management rights for the hotel complex to the global luxury brand Shangri-La in 2017, and in 2022 the incomplete hotel was unsuccessfully offered for sale for $500 million for the empty building – effectively $1 million for each room key. The plans for the hotel include a grand ballroom with a 2500-person capacity, function rooms and event spaces, a health club, spa and wellness centre, as well as restaurants and bars.



The Age has previously reported the cost of the hotel fitout before the COVID-19 pandemic had been budgeted at about $60 million, but inflation and cost increases for materials and labour have since inflated that estimate to $80 million. That puts a $580 million price tag on the fully furnished and fitted-out hotel. The plans for Adrian Portelli’s $39 million Melbourne penthouse at Sapphire by the Gardens. Wentao Zhang lives in the adjoining Sapphire by the Gardens tower and said in his three years as a resident, there had been no progress on the fit-out of the Shangri-La. “It’s completely empty inside and neglected, some of the windows are broken,” he said. “I’ve heard they’ve run into financial difficulties.”



Zhang said residents of Sapphire by the Gardens have no access to the sky-bridge floor on level 46 which is supposed to connect the apartments to the hotel. Related Article Commercial real estate The Melbourne luxury hotel that needs just one thing Cancelling Shangri-La’s Melbourne hotel means that the luxury brand will only have two sites in Australia: the Shangri-La Sydney and the Shangri-La the Marina in Cairns. André Jacques, regional director of marketing at Langham Hospitality Group and director of the Victorian Tourism Industry Council, said it would be disappointing if Shangri-La’s Melbourne hotel was abandoned and turned into apartments. “It would be a shame, considering how many apartments there are already in Melbourne,” he said. “From an international hotel brand standpoint, and a luxury hotel brand, it’s very positive to have another brand like Shangri-La in the market.”



Jacques said 6500 new hotel rooms had opened in Melbourne in the last six years, but occupancy rates were strong and there was still demand for luxury hotels. Setia SP, Setia (Melbourne) and Shangri-La declined to comment on whether plans for the hotel have been permanently shelved. World.title: ‘There are people still waiting to be rescued’: Foreigner among victims as Japan quake toll rises
World.content:
WorldAsiaEarthquakes ‘There are people still waiting to be rescued’: Foreigner among victims as Japan quake toll rises Mari Yamaguchi Updated July 31, 2026 — 1:38pm ,first published July 30, 2026 — 3:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kumamoto: Soldiers and emergency workers combed through a badly damaged shopping mall and collapsed houses looking for trapped survivors on Wednesday after a powerful earthquake that killed at least 34 people, including a foreigner, in south-western Japan. The 7.1-magnitude earthquake that hit a day earlier in the Kumamoto area on the southern main island of Kyushu also left at least 86 people injured, five of them seriously, the prefectural government said. The tally has been steadily growing, fanning fears it may continue to rise. Loading Some of the most serious damage was at the Aeon Mall shopping centre in the town of Kashima, which was bustling with thousands of people when the quake happened. The company said some 3000 customers were evacuated to a parking lot before a gas explosion happened in another part of the mall, where some people were still working. Fumika Ono was shopping at a mall with her older sister when the ground shook so fiercely she lost her balance and ducked. Children began screaming and goods scattered on the floor.



The 19-year-old was among the crowd of shoppers who managed to escape safely. Related Article Updated

Earthquakes Race to find survivors of deadly Japan quake as death toll rises The sweltering weather heightened worries about the survivors as rescuers braved the heat. It remained unclear how many people might still be missing. The mall’s second floor collapsed, trapping people. Witnesses said the explosion shook the area as much as the quake. Three people remained missing, while four deaths were confirmed at the mall site, according to Aeon President Akio Yoshida.



“We take it seriously that an explosion happened and precious lives were lost,” Yoshida told a news conference in Kumamoto, where he bowed deeply along with two other executives. Japanese media footage of the mall showed that part of the ceiling had caved in, and metal pieces and other debris were scattered about as helmeted and masked rescue workers searched the area. The rescue operation inside Aeon mall. Japan's Fire and Disaster Management Agency via AP The explosion followed the 7.1-magnitude earthquake. Getty Images Kiyoshi Matsunaga, 74, who lives in the mall’s neighbourhood and was at a supermarket just a few blocks away, said Tuesday’s quake reminded him of a deadly quake 10 years ago that hit Kumamoto and killed 50 people.



He stopped in his tracks when the shaking began while he was pushing his cart toward a cash register. Things scattered from the shelves. He could not move, he recalled. “I was frightened,” he said. Japan is one of the most quake-prone nations in the world. In the Nuyamazu district, a pair of temple gates at a 16th-century Buddhist temple collapsed. They had just been repaired five years ago.



Yuki Kiyozumi, deputy chief priest at the temple, recalled how she had to crawl on the floor because the shaking was so violent. She had just returned home from a meeting and was about to feed her cat. “I don’t even know if or how we can rebuild them again,” she said, while cleaning up damaged ornaments and furniture. A man helps clean the damaged gate of Jofukuji Buddhist temple in Kumamoto. AP Photo/Hiro Komae The fallen torii gate near a shrine in Yatsushiro. Yu Nakajima/Kyodo News via AP In nearby Yatsushiro, a chimney collapse at a Nippon Paper Industries factory killed five people while seven others were rescued from the debris, according to the Kumamoto prefectural government disaster team.



Four people were still believed to be trapped there, it said. A smokestack at Nippon Paper Industries’ Yatsushiro Mill collapsed in the earthquake. undefined/Kyodo News via AP In the first reported death of a foreign national, a Vietnamese technical intern was killed after a crane fell on him at a factory where he worked, according to the Vietnamese government. He had arrived in Japan in January. Seven other Vietnamese technical interns at the factory evacuated safely. Separately, a Vietnamese woman married to one of the workers was injured when a wall collapsed and was being treated at a hospital. Nearly 34,900 homes were still without electricity and some 15,000 homes without running water, Kumamoto officials said. More than 8800 people left their homes to stay in over 400 shelters, where power sources were being added to provide air conditioning.



Aerial police footage showed some homes in residential areas were completely flattened, including a few that crumbled into a nearby river. Japan’s Self Defence Forces joined rescue workers in the search and rescue operations. Hundreds of professionals were helping with the effort, including firefighters from Taiwan. Related Article Explainer

Earthquakes Scientists know where the big earthquakes will hit. They just don’t know when “There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it’s a race against time,” Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said. “We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can.” Takaichi said the government was preparing to deliver food and other necessities to hard-hit areas. She also offered her condolences to the victims and sympathy to their relatives, while urging those affected by the quake to take care of themselves under the hot weather.



Bullet train services remained suspended. Although operations at Aso Kumamoto Airport resumed Wednesday, some airlines cancelled flights as a precautionary measure. AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Local transmission of H5N1 declared as alarm sounds for local birds, sea lions
World.content:
PoliticsFederalBird flu Local transmission of H5N1 declared as alarm sounds for local birds, sea lions Mike Foley Updated July 31, 2026 — 1:30pm ,first published July 29, 2026 — 12:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dreaded local transmission of the deadly H5N1 bird flu has been declared in South Australia, sounding the alarm for avian species around the country and sparking fears for a colony of endangered sea lions, which are also susceptible to the virus. The South Australian government said on Wednesday that 11 new cases of the virus had been detected among greater crested terns, a local species that does not leave the country. CSIRO national laboratory testing underway is expected to confirm the SA results. It is likely that migratory seabirds from the Antarctic brought the virus to Australia and it then spread among terns. Australian sea lions are endangered, and the Kangaroo Island colony of 1000 is one of the country’s largest. David Whitley Seven detections were made on South Australia’s south-east coast, and four on Kangaroo Island.



SA Primary Industries Minister Clare Scriven said results showed it was “very, very likely” the birds were infected with H5N1 virus. Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the virus was believed to be spreading in terns and that with the onset of local transmission, it would spread in local populations. “We do expect with this local transmission there will be further transmission in Australian wildlife,” Collins said. Australia’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Beth Cookson, said little could be done to stem the virus moving around the country. “In the natural environment there are limited feasible actions to contain the spread,” Cookson said.



Bird flu viruses have circulated around the globe for decades. H5N1 is a particularly deadly variant and has killed hundreds of millions of birds around the world. It is believed that an outbreak in Australia could spark an environmental disaster, risking extinction of dozens of species including marine mammals such as dolphins and seals that also suffer from infection. Related Article Bird flu Deadly bird flu puts 100 species of Australia’s ‘isolated’ wildlife at risk of mass deaths Scriven said popular beach tours to the colony of about 1000 sea lions at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island had been halted. The virus has not been detected among the marine mammals, but tours were halted to stop any potential disturbances that could harm the colony. There are also about 100,000 long-nosed fur seals on or around Kangaroo Island. These animals can also contract the virus. “Everyone knows how susceptible the [sea lion] population is, and they are an endangered species,” Scriven said.



H5N1 arrived in South America in 2022 and killed more than 30,000 South American sea lions, 17,000 southern elephant seal pups and unknown numbers of porpoises, dolphins and otters, as well as at least 650,000 native birds. More than 13,000 seal pups were killed by the virus on Australia’s sub-Antarctic Heard Island territory, which was more than three-quarters of new births on the island. Conservation groups are calling for the immediate deployment of a $200 million fund to boost wildlife resilience. They argue that while the virus cannot be stopped from spreading among wildlife, investment in habitat restoration and programs to cull feral predators can help native animals survive the outbreak. “With only 12,000 individuals left, the Australian sea lion simply cannot absorb the kind of losses we have seen bird flu inflict on marine mammals overseas,” said Australian Marine Conservation Society campaign director Alexia Wellbelove. “Every colony, every pup, every individual matters when a population is this small. We cannot afford to wait.”



Invasive Species Council senior advocate James Johnston said emergency wildlife funds were critical. “We can’t stop bird flu reaching every corner of Australia, but we can give our wildlife a much better chance of surviving it,” he said. Related Article Biodiversity ‘Finish line in sight’ for world-leading cat eradication on Kangaroo Island The Albanese government committed $113 million to preparations to deal with an H5N1 incursion, with an emphasis on planning to identify an outbreak swiftly and a response to limit its spread. This includes funding to prepare biosecurity officers to respond to an outbreak in farmed poultry, which may involve quarantining farms or districts and restricting transport between locations.



Tens of millions of dollars have also been committed to environmental measures such as building pup shelters on Kangaroo Island to help reduce infant mortality in sea lions, removing weeds from islands to improve habitat for seabirds, and funding pre-existing captive breeding programs for endangered species such as the Tasmanian devil, orange-bellied parrot and regent honeyeater. The funds would also pay for teams to remove carcasses of infected animals swiftly to prevent further spread and limit contact between wild and farmed birds. Australia’s unique wildlife, which has evolved in isolation for millions of years, could be particularly vulnerable to H5N1. But little is known about native species’ vulnerability. There have been no detections of the virus in farmed poultry. An outbreak would cause a significant impact on chicken meat and egg production. H5N1 in the United States has caused more than 170 million birds to be culled since 2022, while egg prices had tripled by 2025. H5N1 is not considered a significant risk to human health. However, pet birds and cats usually become extremely ill and die when infected.



Dogs are more resistant to the virus and rarely die or become severely ill. The same is believed to be true for rabbits and guinea pigs as well as cows, sheep, pigs and horses. People are encouraged to look out for possible infections in birds and marine mammals. Signs include sudden death or difficulty breathing, standing, walking or flying. Sick animals should not be touched, but their location should be noted, with photos and videos, before calling the bird flu hotline on 1800 675 888. CLARIFICATION A previous version said the new strain of bird flu threatened otters, which are only found in Australian zoos. The closest native animal is the otter-like rakali.

World.title: Fresh data backs Amplia push against pancreatic, ovarian cancer
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Fresh data backs Amplia push against pancreatic, ovarian cancer Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright July 31, 2026 — 1:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Amplia Therapeutics has received encouraging lab results which highlighted the use of its lead drug narmafotinib, saying it can attack several of the nastier features that make the cancer so hard to treat. The research, led by Professor Paul Timpson and colleagues at Sydney’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research, was the results of extensive laboratory work on narmafotinib in pancreatic cancer models and was posted online on the biology preprint server bioRxiv. Amplia Therapeutics’ says fresh preclinical research data has strengthened the case for its drug candidate narmafotinib against pancreatic cancer cells, pictured. Amplia says the work adds further evidence that narmafotinib, a focal adhesion kinase (FAK) inhibitor, may improve outcomes by targeting tumour fibrosis, chemotherapy resistance and metastatic spread - three big hurdles in a disease that remains one of cancer medicine’s toughest assignments. FAK is a protein inside cells that acts like a control switch for movement, survival and attachment. It sits where cells anchor to their surrounding environment and helps tell them whether to grow, move or shut themselves down.



‘The research conducted by Professor Timpson’s team over recent years is now being shared with the broader scientific community.’ Amplia Therapeutics chief executive office and managing director Dr Chris Burns In many cancers, FAK becomes overactive or over-produced, helping tumour cells survive, move and spread. That has made it a target for cancer-fighting drugs such as narmafotinib. Among the key findings, the paper reported reduced tumour fibrosis and enhanced anti-tumour activity when narmafotinib was combined with chemotherapy. Other results included reduced cancer dissemination and metastatic spread in a pancreatic cancer model and the down-regulation – or diminished activity - of multiple genes linked to chemotherapy resistance. In this case, the drug appears to turn down genes that usually help cancer cells resist chemotherapy. The effect is to weaken the cancer cells’ defences, leaving chemotherapy better able to do its job and potentially lowering the number of cancer cells that remain alive after treatment. Amplia Therapeutics chief executive officer and managing director Dr Chris Burns said: “These studies strengthen the scientific rationale for the clinical development of narmafotinib and provide further insight into the multifaceted mechanisms through which narmafotinib can act in the treatment of this devastating disease.”



The update follows a busy clinical run for the Melbourne-based biotech. In May, Amplia launched the first stage of a Phase 2b registration-enabling pancreatic cancer study that will test daily dosing of narmafotinib with the chemotherapy drugs gemcitabine and Abraxane in newly diagnosed advanced pancreatic cancer patients. A registration-enabling study is a pivotal clinical trial designed to produce the core evidence needed to support an application for approval to market a new drug. Its job is to show that a treatment is safe at the proposed dose, that it helps patients and that the data package is strong enough for regulators such as the US Food and Drug Administration or Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration to assess. The study is expected to enrol 12 patients across two dose cohorts at three or four Australian sites, with patient enrolment planned for the fourth quarter of this year. Amplia’s June quarterly also underlined why the company is pressing ahead. Mature ACCENT trial data presented at the American Association for Cancer Research showed favourable safety and encouraging efficacy for narmafotinib, with a 36 per cent overall response rate and a 70 per cent disease control rate, compared with 50 per cent for chemotherapy alone. The data also showed median overall survival of 11.1 months — an improvement of more than two months — and progression-free survival of 7.7 months when narmafotinib was used with standard chemotherapy.



The company ended the June quarter with $24 million in cash, giving it a handy buffer as it pushes narmafotinib further into pancreatic cancer and prepares to test the same drug in a second oncology target. That expansion comes through PRROSE, a phase two trial being run under an agreement with the Australia New Zealand Gynaecological Oncology Group (ANZGOG) to evaluate narmafotinib alongside standard chemotherapy in 15 to 20 patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer. For Amplia, the latest paper is not a clinical result — but it is another useful building block. And in a field where every extra piece of biological support counts, the company will no doubt be happy to bank more evidence as it heads toward the next stage of its pancreatic cancer program.
