World.title: Gang patch ban inconsistent with Bill of Rights, High Court finds
World.content:
A new court decision could send the gang patch ban back to the government for review following a High Court ruling that a Wellington man's conviction for displaying gang insignia contravenes the Bill of Rights.

But the Minister of Justice said the point of the legislation was to be "tough" on gang members and the law "will not be changing".

This week, the Wellington High Court found the prohibition of the display of gang insignia was inconsistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990.

The ruling came in relation to the conviction of a patched member of a New Zealand gang in December 2024 after he was sighted - via CCTV - on the footpath outside a Wellington restaurant.

The man was wearing a cap which displayed a family member's name and included the name of the gang in a font and colours commonly associated with the gang.

The man's details have been suppressed.

The man's lawyer, Chris Nicholls said - if the ruling went unappealed - it would trigger a referral back to Parliament to re-examine the legislation.

"There's a series of rules that then have to be followed. The matter's got to be referred back to Parliament and then recommendations can get made and Parliament can decide what it's going to do in response.

"Parliament doesn't have to do anything. However it's my understanding that this inconsistency can be referred to the United Nations. Because the Bill of Rights Act came out of New Zealand's commitment to the provisions of the International Covenant of Civil and Political Rights.

"So, not only is this Gangs Act law inconsistent with the Bill of Rights, but it's also inconsistent with previous commitments that have been given by previous Parliaments to New Zealand's international obligations to uphold political and civil rights."

The conflict between the legislation and the Bill of Rights was acknowledged by Attorney-General, Judith Collins in the lead up to the law being put into place in 2024.

Nicholls said this week's High Court ruling was the "aftermath and the reality" of the Gangs Act in operation.

"My client - who was convicted of a minor offence under the law - is able to seek this public law remedy of a declaration and effectively say 'Whilst I have this conviction - which is correctly entered under the law of the land - never-the-less the circumstances of my conviction were that this law was also inconsistent with fundamental rights that I have under freedom of expression'.

"So it's an affirmation that fundamental rights have been breached."

Nicholls said the Gangs Act targeted a small group of already marginalised people and would be unlikely to be supported by the public if similar legislation was directed toward a wider section of New Zealand society.

He said similar declarations of inconsistency made by the High Court were "rare and not made lightly".

"This is - in my view - an important safeguard and check and balance on Parliament. Where fundamental rights have been breached it forces Parliament to re-look at issues and I think that's right and that's why we took the case," Nicholls said.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith was unrepentant of the impact of the legislation on the rights of gang members.

"This is tough legislation. That is the point.

"We've said right from the start this legislation will affect and limit the rights of gang members."

He said Parliament considered the Bill of Rights when passing the legislation and had chosen to prioritise New Zealander's right " to live without fear and intimidation in their communities".

"Gang members make up less than one quarter of 1 percent of the New Zealand adult population, yet are linked to about 18 percent of serious violent crime. We make no apologies for getting tough on law and order.

World.title: 'There's a game going on here': Luxon asks for votes in response to Peters' immigrant comments
World.content:
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has condemned Winston Peters' comments about a Green MP as "racist" and "outrageous", but says he maintains confidence in him as Foreign Minister.

He is not worried about New Zealand's relationship with China, saying "career politician" Peters has had a lot of spats with the ambassador "over many many years".

Accusing the New Zealand First leader of "playing a game", Luxon has avoided sacking him as suggested by former political leaders and the opposition - instead using the opportunity to ask for votes.

Luxon told reporters Peters' comments were "very offensive and completely inappropriate", and asked directly if they were racist, he agreed.

"Lawrence Xu-nan is a full equal Kiwi - as much as a Kiwi as Winston Peters - and he deserves to be able to say whatever he wants to say in Parliament in the same way Winston Peters says what he says."

He thought Peters' comments were deliberate.

"He's a career politician. He's been there for 40-plus years. He's using language that's deliberate to get attention from the media and from others on himself. He had a pretty bad week with New Zealand First last week, and I get that, but I just think we're beyond the distractions and the sideshows."

However, he said he still had confidence in Peters as Foreign Minister.

"Yes, I mean he's been successful as a foreign minister, but the reality is we're now in full-blown campaign mode."

Luxon said Peters had a history of spats with the Chinese Ambassador, who commented on Thursday, but the relationship between the two countries was longstanding and "in really good heart".

"We're three months out from an election. Kiwis get to decide what happens next, and I just say to you, think very deeply about your vote, I want 100 percent of the seats around that Cabinet table to be National party ministers - that's why I keep saying 100 percent party vote National."

RNZ

When asked if he would sack Peters as Foreign Minister if China demanded it, he said that was "hypothetical".

Luxon was making the comments at the afternoon public meeting in Tauranga - a seat held by National since 1938, apart from a stint between 1993 and 2005 when it was held by Peters himself.

Peters had on Wednesday responded to heckling from Xu-nan during a general debate speech with a tirade where he told the Chinese-born New Zealand citizen to "go back to your own country".

"That's where they lie like a flatfish, but they don't lie like that here, all right?" Peters said. "This is called a democracy, unlike what you're used to."

The comments have drawn criticism from across Parliament, with National's campaign chair Simeon Brown calling them racist, while National and ACT's leaders Luxon and David Seymour said they were inappropriate and attention-seeking.

The opposition has gone further, saying Peters should be sacked as Foreign Minister - a position echoed by former leaders Helen Clark and Don Brash.

'We have legal immigration in this country'

Luxon had earlier responded to questions at the public meeting from one woman who put the problem bluntly.

"Excuse my language sir, but there is a s--- of a man who is destroying this country. Last term it was the Chinese, this term it's the Indians. What are you going to do with Winston Peters," one woman asked him.

"He is insulting this country globally and he is getting away with it and he is destroying race relations in this country, sir it has got to stop."

"Well said," Luxon responded, "I wouldn't expect anything less".

He said the answer was "pretty simple".

"Party vote National," he said, to applause.

"Because you may like some things that Winston Peters says, but the bottom line is he opposed the China FTA, he opposed the Indian FTA, he was part of a government that banned oil and gas causing electricity crisis in New Zealand in 2024 that meant people lost their jobs.

"And also he's the person that put Jacinda Ardern into power and wrecked our economy. So let's be a little straight up about it."

He said unlike the United States, England, Germany, France and other jurisdictions, New Zealand's immigration was focused on building infrastructure and had shifted to high-skill migrants.

"I'm just saying to you, there's a game going on here and let's be honest about it because I want you to understand a few things: It's very easy to denigrate immigrants and to drive xenophobia in this country ... he's trying to talk about a problem that we don't have.

"He may think he's Nigel Farage and Marine Le Pen and Pauline Hanson and Donald Trump, but ... we have legal immigration in this country."

He defended the Green MP Lawrence Xu-nan who Peters had criticised in Parliament, saying he had "as equal right be in that Parliament and as a first class citizen in the same way that Winston Peters may be as well".

"There is no difference. He is a Kiwi and he deserves to talk. You may disagree with what he says, but in a democracy, that's how it goes. And he deserves to say in Parliament what he wishes to represent and say in the same way that Winston Peters demands that he can say that too."

He repeated previous comments backing migrants, saying they came to New Zealand leaving everything behind and worked "really hard, they take one job, they take two jobs, three jobs to get a deposit for a house or a business ... they don't go on welfare, and they get their kids and they wake up every day and get them to school".

World.title: Ngāi Tahu Farming chosen to operate country's largest farm, Molesworth Station
World.content:
Ngāi Tahu Farming has been chosen by the Department of Conservation to operate the country's largest farm.

Molesworth Station, an iconic 180-thousand hectare high country farm that spanned Marlborough and North Canterbury, was run as a cattle farm by state-owned Pāmu Landcorp.

The area, known formally as the Rangitahi/Molesworth Recreation Reserve, covers 180,000 hectares of land owned by the Crown and administered by the Department of Conservation (DOC) .

DOC announced on Friday afternoon it would invite Ngāi Tahu Farming - a subsidiary of Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu Group - to apply for a concession to manage the land.

Four other bids, including one by former farm manager Jim Ward, were unsuccessful.

DOC deputy director-general regional operations Henry Weston said farming would remain the core commercial activity at Molesworth but it was also a nationally important drylands ecosystem with significant biodiversity, heritage, recreational and cultural values.

"This decision ultimately came down to Ngāi Tahu Farming, a wholly owned subsidiary of Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu Group, having the strongest experience of farming at scale in the high country of those who applied. They have strong financial and business foundations offering long-term security for the Crown, making them the best applicant for the opportunity to negotiate the concession," Weston said.

Molesworth Station. Ngāi Tahu / SUPPLIED

"Ngāi Tahu Farming currently farms three high country stations, spanning 36,000 hectares, as part of the 100,000 hectares of farming and forestry land it manages across the South Island.

"Final details of the farming operations will be determined through the concession process and will need to deliver on our high expectations regarding public access and weed and pest control.

"DOC ran a thorough process, weighed up a range of expert advice and materials, and made a decision in the best interest of Molesworth, one of New Zealand's truly special places."

DOC expected public access and weed and pest control would be maintained or improved and details would emerge during the concession process.

Jim Ward told RNZ he was informed of the decision during a short phone call about an hour and a half before the announcement was made publicly on Friday afternoon.

Jim Ward, former manager of Molesworth station. (File photo) PAMU / SUPPLIED

"I'm absolutely gutted. The last 12 months have been a huge body of work getting it in front of people. We are all a bit deflated at the minute to be honest," Ward said.

"My wife and I put 24 years into Molesworth plus this last year. It was looking to the future, looking to cement Molesworth as a place for mum and dad and the kids of New Zealand, to build on what we had started. It was a totally different concept - a station for the nation - making it into a charitable trust. It was quite a bold concept, but it was the right thing to do."

DOC had not told him why his bid was not successful.

"I'm still pretty numb but the decision's been made and I'll just have to go find myself something else to do," Ward said

Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu welcomed the news.

Chief executive Ben Bateman said DOC's decision reflected the iwi's proven capability in farming, conservation and commercial management.

"We are committed to making sure the terms of any concession we negotiate are good for all New Zealanders. Public access, biodiversity and ecological stewardship are central to how we would manage Rangitahi Molesworth," Bateman said.

"For us, Rangitahi is not simply a farming opportunity. It is an ancestral landscape woven into the whakapapa of Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kurī, Ngāti Māmoe and Waitaha. To be entrusted with its stewardship is a responsibility we approach with humility and determination."

Te Rūnanga o Kaikōura chairperson Hariata Kahu said it was an important milestone for her hapū, Ngāti Kurī.

"For many generations we have longed to play a more active role in protecting Rangitahi Molesworth. Growing up, we learn the pūrākau of Rangitahi and the journeys our people made through this landscape. The Awatere and Waiautoa rivers are part of those stories and even the name Rangitahi speaks to the coming together of those waters," she said.

"To know that if we are granted a concession we would have the opportunity to help care for this whenua is incredibly significant. For Ngāti Kurī, this is about ensuring future generations can experience Rangitahi, much like our ancestors did, with its landscapes and stories protected."

The iwi would now work through the details of its concession application

Federated Farmers president Colin Hurst said he welcomed the clarity DOC's decision provided.

"The Department of Conversation has run a really robust, competitive and fair process to get to this point," Hurst said.

"We congratulate Ngāi Tahu Farming on putting forward a strong business case and being selected as the preferred operator to negotiate for the lease. Molesworth is an incredibly special property for all New Zealanders, owned by all New Zealanders, so it's important whoever takes on the lease is well set up to succeed."

Ngāi Tahu Farming had the experience and financial resilience to farm a property like Molesworth Station, Hurst said.

"Ngāi Tahu Farming has a strong balance sheet that would allow them to keep farming through tough years with drought or poor commodity prices. It's also well placed to run an integrated system with existing finishing farms around North Canterbury - so the decision makes sense from that perspective.

World.title: Wellington City Council proposes wide-ranging job cuts
World.content:
Wellington City Council is proposing wide-ranging redundancies to staff.

It is understood the proposals could mean dozens of job cuts among multiple teams.

The proposals could affect about 50 people, RNZ understands, including those from the Economic and Engagement, Creative Capital, Property, Planning and Environment teams.

Staff have been called into both group and individual meetings this week, it is understood.

Public Service Association assistant secretary Tom Buckley said more job losses were "the last thing Wellington needed" on top of cuts that had hit the city hard.

"These are people with skills, with experience, and with families to support. They deserve better particularly at a time when the job market is tight.

"This also doesn't make much sense with amalgamation of councils on the cards - this is precisely the wrong time to be doing a restructure like this.

"The PSA is standing by and supporting all those impacted by the proposal and will be urging the council to think again."

Last year chief executive Matt Prosser commissioned Deloitte to analyse the council's processes, as well to achieve rates affordability and improve performance.

The report said the council had 330 more staff than it should, based on the number of full time employees per thousand households.

It said through "right shaping" the council workforce, tighter controls on spending, and contract compliance, the council could save up to $79 million over three years.

A Wellington city council spokesperson confirmed staff were being consulted on the changes.

The proposals were part of budget reductions - an effort to identify $31.7 million of savings to reduce forecast rates, the spokesperson said.

"As such, it would not be appropriate to comment on the specifics of employment consultation processes while they are underway. Our focus is on ensuring Council kaimahi are supported, heard, and their feedback reflected in any final change decisions.

World.title: The growing business of making snow from the sun
World.content:
How to make snow from the sun is among the engineering feats of innovative solar energy company Sunergise, which is seeing rapid growth.

Sunergise chief executive Paul Makumbe said the business had seen more growth in past 12 months than in the eight years before.

Among a pipeline of upcoming projects was a large solar development for Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, which was about twice the size of a recent 2 megawatt (MW) facility for a Mānawa Bay retail development, located within the Auckland Airport campus.

Sunergise also built a 1.05 MW solar plant to power about 30 percent of Auckland-based Snowplanet's power requirements, with the 70 percent balance of power supplied from New Zealand's national grid.

"How do we make snow out of snow? We figured it out with Snowplanet," Makumbe said.

The year-round indoor attraction operated 24 hours a day and produced about 80 cubic metres of fresh snow a week to maintain its 8,000 square metres of slope.

"This is one of 50 sites that we currently have under our power purchase agreement," Makumbe said, adding the facility produced more power than it can use, with the surplus flowing back to the grid.

"So the way that works is we effectively are responsible for designing the system, building the system, and operating the system, and instead of them paying their retail provider, they pay us for the power that they use from the system," he said, adding that model allowed businesses to get access to solar on a "no-capital outlay basis."

Sunergise also built solar facilities on behalf of other businesses.

"We're starting to see a lot of the utilities asking us to build these solar plants on their behalf," he said.

"We've been around for about 14 years, and we've got contracts and agreements with commercial clients across New Zealand and the Pacific."

He said the pipeline for future development was strong.

"I think we we are seeing quite strong demand from corporates looking to take you know their power demand into their own hands.

"I think people are starting to realise that having control of their energy requirements... is a competitive advantage."

He said obtaining resource consent was not typically an issue for the business as the bulk of Sunergise's installations were on the rooftops of existing facilities.

"There's a lot of kind of planning and design work that goes into it, but we don't have to interact with the resource consent process."

However, the Snowplanet development did need to got through the resource consent process.

He said the company was not thinking of growth beyond New Zealand and the Pacific.

"There's a lot of work to be done in New Zealand and the Pacific, and we don't want to get ahead of our skis, so to speak.

World.title: Man arrested amid investigation into alleged historic sexual abuse
World.content:
A man has been arrested amid a police investigation into alleged historic sexual offending.

Detective Inspector Scott Anderson said in a statement on Friday a 63-year-old man had been arrested in relation to alleged historic sexual offending.

"The man has been charged with four counts of unlawful sexual connection with a male aged 12 to 16 and three counts of indecent assault on a boy aged between 12 to 16."

He has interim name suppression.

World.title: Complex Auckland sinkhole could take up to two months to fix
World.content:
A large sinkhole that opened up in Auckland's St Mary's Bay will be complex to fix, Watercare says, because the damaged wastewater pipe is five metres underground - below large transmission pipes.

The hole emerged a week ago and is about five metres long by three metres wide and over a metre deep in parts.

It is in a part of Hackett Street that was badly damaged by flooding three years ago and had been covered by a steel plate since then.

Watercare's chief operations officer Mark Bourne said fixing it could take up to two months and about 10 metres of wastewater pipe needs to be replaced.

"Hackett Street has a large amount of underground infrastructure, which makes work like this challenging," he said.

"The street has both large transmission pipes and smaller local water and wastewater pipes at varying depths underground, which means we have to plan repair work carefully to make sure we don't affect other infrastructure."

Nick Monro

Bourne said the damaged wastewater pipe is five metres underground and located beneath large transmission pipes, which will make the repair complex and technically challenging.

"We are in the process of engaging a specialist contractor to start work on the damaged wastewater pipe. This is expected to be a significant project because of the depth of the pipe and the complexity of the site."

When the sinkhole appeared, residents from the St Mary's Bay Association raised concerns about the area's ageing water infrastructure.

It comes as Watercare plans to spend $15.2 billion on Auckland's water and wastewater infrastructure over the next 10 years, resulting in an average household's water bill rise of about $8 a month.

Tony Skelton. Nick Monro

Tony Skelton has lived in St Mary's Bay for 53 years and said the repair work started at midnight on Tuesday and has continued since.

"We have a reasonable amount of confidence that this time they're going to address the underlying issues with the emergency overflow point and give us some peace of mind that it will be fully and totally repaired."

He said there is traffic and noise disruption and a large repair site that is cordoned off.

"We're not complaining, it's get the job done as far as we're concerned. We as residents are comfortable with some disruption on the basis that we're going to get the problem resolved."

The wastewater infrastructure in the area dates from the 1910s.

Bourne said it is necessary to do the pipe repairs.

Nick Monro

"We really appreciate the community's patience while we do this complex work. We apologise for the inconvenience, and we will make every effort to get these repairs done and keep residents and key stakeholders updated on our progress," he said.

Hackett Street is home to drinking water, wastewater and stormwater infrastructure that serves both the local area and wider Auckland.

In the 2023 flooding, a small hole appeared in the road near 16 Hackett Street, later found to be caused by a failure in a deep wastewater pipe beneath other services.

"To ensure public safety, a steel plate was installed over the hole while investigations were undertaken. We discovered that there was damage to a local wastewater pipe," Bourne said.

Nick Monro

"During this period, we did regular site inspections to monitor the area to make sure it remained stable and wasn't deteriorating."

Earlier this month, an unrelated leak occurred on a nearby drinking water transmission main and that has now been repaired.

Bourne said many clay pipes across the water network are in good condition despite their age.

"The pipes' age alone does not mean they need replacing. We decide when to renew them based on evidence of their condition and performance," he said.

World.title: World Rugby says no ultimatum given to Samoa over governance fiasco
World.content:
World Rugby has denied reports that it gave Samoa an ultimatum to sort out problems over which body governs the sport in the country, or face a ban from international competition.

Prime Minister La'aulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt announced earlier this year that he was establishing a rival union to take over the role of Lakapi Samoa (the Samoa Rugby Union).

But World Rugby denies reports that it had told Samoa that failure to accept the review would result in Samoa copping a ban - it also confirmed it is involved as a mediator to resolve issues at Lakapi Samoa.

A spokesperson for World Rugby told RNZ Pacific: "We are in active and constructive dialogue with all parties and remain focused on a positive resolution."

Tuilaepa Sailele Mallielegaoi Facebook / HRPP

Yesterday, Samoa's opposition leader Tuilaepa Sa'ilele Malielegaoi said that Samoa faced suspension by World Rugby because of "a dirty political move" by the government and particularly his rival, the current prime minister, La'auli.

Tuilaepa spoke to RNZ Pacific after the government announced that it was pulling its support of Lakapi Samoa due to "unresolved internal issues and division" at the national rugby union, and amid reports that Samoa was risking being banned from World Rugby.

RNZ Pacific has contacted Lakapi Samoa and the Samoan government's press secretariat for a response to Tuilaepa's comments.

Tuilaepa stepped down as long-time chairman of the Samoa Rugby Union earlier this year after his political stand-off with La'auli threatened to stall a new funding programme for the Pacific's three top rugby unions.

La'auli had refused to sign any new agreement with the Fijian and Tongan rugby unions until Tuilaepa and his board resigned and made way for new appointments.

Lakopo Mapu of Samoa scores a try despite the challenge of Marcus Ramage of Hong Kong China during a match between Samoa and Hong Kong China on 4 July 2026 in Santiago, Chile. Marcelo Hernandez / World Rugby/World Rugby via Getty Images

Fiji fiasco

The crisis surrounding Samoa rugby has shades of the political problems which caused Fiji to be banned from the World Rugby Council in 2023 over governance concerns, after the government in 2023 effectively control of the Fiji Rugby Union (FRU).

The following year, the FRU was reinstated as a member of the governing body's council afterb a suspension of almost 15 months.

However, the FRU has become embroiled in more problems lately, after a dispute over player payments became public.

This week, the FRU board chairman John Sanday said the union had a plan B in place to ensure Flying Fijians players don't make 'ridiculous' demands of management in future.

This follows an incident during Fiji's recent Nations Championship stint in Europe, where they lost all three test matches to Wales, England and Scotland.

Fiji's flanker Lekima Tagitagivalu (C) and teammates huddle after conceding a sixth try during the Rugby Union Nations Championship match between Fiji and England at Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool on 11 July 2026. AFP / Oli Scarff

Sanday said players demanded an increase of their daily allowances from FJ$500 a day to $1,000, but the FRU only agreed to pay FJ$600 per day.

That was despite the fact that players had signed contracts pre-tour.

Sanday said the players argued that the union would make a lot of money from the three games it technically "hosted" on the northern tour.

He has now revealed the FRU will review the squad's make-up and form a standby squad ready to play for Fiji if current players don't change their attitude.

World.title: Magpies coach throws support behind Bobby Hill as star exits
World.content:
Collingwood's Bobby Hill has exited the club amid support from coach Craig McRae after the premiership hero was racially abused on social media.

The Magpies have formally split with Hill, cutting short the 26-year-old's bumper contract, which was due to expire at the end of 2030.

"I'm going to take a break from football to keep working on myself and regain my passion for the game," Hill said in a statement released by the Magpies today.

Hill was the star of Collingwood's 2023 premiership under coach Craig McRae, winning the Norm Smith Medal for a four-goal grand final showing against Brisbane.

But having taken stretches of personal leave, he hasn't played at AFL level for almost a year — making just three VFL appearances in 2026.

On Thursday, before the Pies lost to Geelong at the MCG, Hill shared on Instagram a vile direct message from a Collingwood supporter that included a racist slur among other insults.

"You have disappointed this whole club and it's (sic) 100 thousand plus fans what you have done the last 18 months," the account also posted.

"… I hope nothing but the worst for you."

Hill posted a screenshot of the message and captioned it "anyone know this tough guy?"

The Magpies have publicly supported Hill throughout his turbulent period, and McRae again expressed his care for the forward's wellbeing — and disgust at those posting abusive comments on social media.

"Bobby, our thoughts are with you," McRae said after the MCG defeat on Thursday night.

"Not just for Bobby — what's going on? It's a crazy place at times, isn't it?

"I don't do social media, so bear with me, but I did look on a website which had feedback, and the feedback is unbelievable.

"It's just a cesspool for people just to vent. I find it fascinating that's actually something that people would be interested in.

"If Bobby's listening there, I'm sorry to hear that's the case. We'll always love him. It's sad to hear that."

This morning, the Pies' football manager Charlie Gardiner confirmed the end of Hill's contract.

"The club has been working with Bobby over the past 12 months to put support structures in place to help him work through some personal matters," Gardiner said in a statement.

"Despite this, Bobby has unfortunately struggled to meet his commitments to the club consistently this year and agreed that taking a break from football is the best decision for him and his family."

Meanwhile, the Magpies are counting the cost of Thursday night's loss with veteran defender Jeremy Howe suffering a fractured arm.

It is the same arm that he broke horrifically after a nasty landing from an aerial contest, also against Geelong, in 2023.

"The likelihood is he'll probably need an operation," McRae said post-game.

Utility Harry Perryman suffered a left hamstring injury — having strained his right hamstring earlier in the season.

And Brownlow medal favourite Nick Daicos has a bruised right foot, but he played out the game.

World.title: How a classification change ended Korey's Commonwealth Games hopes
World.content:
As the track cycling competition at the 2026 Commonwealth Games gets underway, Australians expecting to see Paralympic champion Korey Boddington in action will be left disappointed.

The popular para cyclist, who won the kilometre C4-5 time trial in Paris, has joined swimmer Alexa Leary as another high-profile para athlete removed from the Glasgow Games after a reclassification of his disability.

Leary, the reigning S9 100m world record holder, was to make her Commonwealth Games debut in Scotland but was reclassified as an S10 athlete earlier this year.

Partly due to the stripped-down nature of these Games, there are no sprint freestyle events for S10 swimmers at the Tollcross pool, with the only event in that category being the 200-metre individual medley, which Leary does not compete in.

Boddington, the reigning Sir Hubert Opperman Trophy winner and 2025 Australian cyclist of the year, was also reclassified, twice in the space of a year, first becoming eligible to compete, and then ineligible.

Boddington's year as a C3 athlete

Korey Boddington is the world record holder in the kilo at C3 and C4 classifications. (Supplied: Cycling New Zealand)

Classification for para athletes has long been a contentious and complicated issue.

The process exists in para sport to enable athletes with different impairment types — not necessarily the same disabilities — the chance to compete on a relatively level playing field.

"International classification is conducted by a panel comprising medical classifiers and technical classifiers before a competition, after which they will be informed which class they are in and why," AusCycling told ABC Sport in a statement.

"Their role is to assess whether an athlete has an eligible impairment that meets the minimum impairment criteria for Para cycling, assess the extent to which the athlete is able to execute the specific tasks and activities fundamental to Para cycling, and, where required, undertake observation in competition assessment."

Within the classification framework imposed by the sport's governing body, the UCI, Boddington — who won two Paralympic medals as a C4 athlete — was, briefly, reclassified as a C3 athlete in 2025.

This indicates a higher level of impairment than under which he competed in Paris. In cycling, the scale is from 1-5, where 1 is the most severe impairment and 5 the least.

This is not uncommon.

Boddington only made his first national team appearance in the Paralympic year of 2024.

He endeared himself to the Australian public with his love of burritos, enjoying up to four of them a day: "You know how many carbs are in the wrap, and you can specifically portion out all your protein that are on them," he told AusCycling in 2025 by way of explanation.

It earned him the affectionate nickname the Flying Burrito.

Korey Boddington was a breakout star of the Paris Paralympics. (Getty Images: PA Images/Andrew Matthews)

For an athlete like Boddington, who lives with an acquired brain injury and had not spent all that long in the sport, it is understandable that his classification level was still being sorted out.

But having been reclassified, Boddington promptly won four world championship gold medals as a C3 athlete at the 2025 world championships in Rio, winning the men's sprint, 1,000-metre (kilo) time trial and elimination race before helping Australia clinch victory in the mixed C1-5 team sprint.

The 30-year-old Queenslander, the world record holder for the C4 flying 200m sprint time trial, also broke world records in the C3 flying 200m sprint and the C3 kilo at the Oceania Championships in Cambridge, New Zealand in February this year.

He won four gold medals in total at those championships: the kilo, sprint, individual pursuit and mixed C1-5 team sprint, as well as winning silver medals in the elimination and scratch races.

All signs were pointing towards Boddington competing in the C1-3 3,000m individual pursuit and 1,000m time trial events at the Games in Glasgow.

However, upon his return from New Zealand, Boddington was reclassified a C4 athlete and competed in that category at the TrackNats in Brisbane in late March.

Boddington still won gold in the sprint, elimination, scratch, kilo and C1-C5 team sprint at the Anna Meares Velodrome.

However, there are only four men's para cycling events set to be contested on the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome in Glasgow; none of which C4 athletes are eligible for — the sprint and 1,000m time trial in the tandem B category, and the 3,000m individual pursuit and 1,000m time trial events in the C1-3 classification.

Classification can be 'tough'

Korey Boddington won gold in the men's C4 1,000m time trial at the 2024 Paralympic Games in Paris. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Being rubbed out of a major competition like the Commonwealth Games, the only multi-sport event where able-bodied and para athletes compete on the same program, through no fault of their own, is a bitter pill for the athletes to swallow.

And classification can be a very sensitive and personal process.

A Four Corners investigation in 2023 found that some Paralympic athletes were deliberately exaggerating their impairments in a bid to win medals and that the system itself was ripe for manipulation.

Australians embroiled in Paralympics scandal Former athletes and officials tell Four Corners the system of Paralympic classification is flawed and easily manipulated.

AusCycling said it took care to ensure that its athletes are educated about classification throughout their time in the sport.

That takes the form of education about the classification system itself, guidance from classification experts, discussion of possible classification outcomes, and planning for different scenarios.

"The focus is on ensuring athletes understand the UCI Classification Rules, including eligible impairments, sport class profiles and assessment methods, while continuing to focus on their development and performance goals," the statement read.

The statement also noted that "not all classification outcomes can be anticipated, particularly for more complex impairment profiles".

Classification for para athletes can take place over the course of an athlete's career to ensure they are in their correct category for competition.

They may also have to be tested if the criteria for their classification change or if the governing body changes its tests. In cycling, that falls under the UCI's jurisdiction.

When a classification panel allocates a sport class to an athlete, it also assigns a status to that status: confirmed, review at the next available opportunity, review with a fixed review date or expired.

Needless to say, most athletes have to go through the process multiple times during their career.

Double world champion Tara Neyland detailed the process of classification. (Supplied: AusCycling)

Two-time world champion on the road and three-time track world champion Tara Neyland, who is also competing in the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome at these Games, said in a detailed Instagram video in May that classification days can be incredibly tough.

Neyland lives with facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, a genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness, which means her level of impairment is likely to change over time.

"Being a progressive degenerative condition, they need to keep reassessing as my body will keep changing," Neyland said in her Instagram video.

AusCycling noted that in instances such as Neyland's, athletes can request a medical review, but it is not imposed by AusCycling out of competition if it is against the athlete's wishes.

Regardless, the process is clearly incredibly emotionally draining for the athletes involved.

"Classification day is a tough one," Neyland said.

"Essentially you're being assessed, being graded, for your level of impairment of your condition, disability, injury, whatever it may be, however you define it.

"It can bring up a lot of emotions.

"It's a necessary part of para sport so that we can be as fairly graded as possible, but it's still quite challenging.

"For me, until coming into para sport, I've tried to view myself as someone who's incredibly capable, and then to flip the mindset and have to prove your level of impairment and speak to all your challenges and struggles and areas that, for me, weaken, struggle to do the same things that an able body can do is hard."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

AusCycling said it was committed to helping athletes with any issues that arose from classification changes.

"Ultimately, classification exists to protect the integrity and fairness of Para sport," AusCycling's statement read.

"While the prospect of reclassification can be challenging, particularly given its potential impact on competitive opportunities and performance goals, AusCycling remains committed to prioritising athlete wellbeing and supporting athletes' continued performance throughout the entire process.

"Athlete wellbeing remains a key priority throughout any classification review process, whether anticipated or unexpected.

"Appropriate support is identified both on the ground and remotely to ensure athletes are well supported throughout the process."

World.title: 'It was weird': De Minaur beats Hewitt in Aussie tussle
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has cast aside sentiment to end Cruz Hewitt's breakout run and storm into the Washington Open quarter-finals.

The top seed and defending champion produced a clinical display to defeat the 17-year-old Hewitt, son of former world number one Lleyton, 6-2, 6-3 in just 61 minutes.

De Minaur shared a warm embrace with Hewitt at the net as Lleyton looked on from the stands at Stadium Court.

"It was definitely weird," de Minaur said.

"I knew I was going to play him on the tour some day, but I didn't actually expect it to be this week. It was an amazing feeling."

Cruz Hewitt has breakthrough Tour win Cruz Hewitt wins for the first time at ATP Tour level, his Washington upset of former world number 37 Marcus Giron set to rocket him up the tennis rankings.

A Wimbledon boys' finalist this month, Hewitt idolised de Minaur while growing up around the Davis Cup team captained by his father.

"Even [with] all the lead-up, seeing all the incredible pictures that we have together and how we've grown up, I'm glad I managed to get through," de Minaur said.

"But I'm sure we're going to have many battles in the years to come."

Australia's world number six charged to the net with authority and displayed great hands en route to improving his win-loss record to 29-14 this season.

Despite his defeat, Hewitt is set to soar some 252 spots in the rankings to a fresh career high of about world number 360 after qualifying in Washington and then winning his maiden ATP match.

Competing for the first time since marrying British WTA star Katie Boulter this month, de Minaur next faces American Brandon Nakashima, who ousted seventh-seed Jakub Mensik 7-6 (5), 3-6, 6-4 to reach his second consecutive Washington quarter-final.

Nakashima holds a 2-1 edge over the Australian, with de Minaur's lone win against the American also coming in last year's quarter-finals before he went on to lift the title.

AAP

World.title: England hires NZ's Fleming to coach men's Test side, Root as captain
World.content:
English cricket has turned to another New Zealander to coach the men's Test team, hiring former Kiwi star Stephen Fleming, while batting great Joe Root has been reappointed as captain.

Fleming replaced his former teammate Brendon McCullum, who was fired after losing the Ashes series in Australia 4-1 over the winter and, last month, losing at home to New Zealand 2-1.

England now has an all-New Zealand coaching set-up, with McCullum remaining in charge of the one-day and Twenty20 teams.

Fleming will not take charge until after Pakistan's three-Test tour, which begins on August 19 in Leeds. McCullum's former assistant, Marcus Trescothick, will be the interim England coach for that series.

Root was previously the permanent Test captain from 2017-22 in a national record 65 Tests. He won a record 27 of those matches but has won only one of his past 18 in charge.

The 35-year-old Root formally replaces Ben Stokes, who retired suddenly from international cricket after the New Zealand series in June. Stokes had endorsed his vice-captain, Harry Brook, as the next captain.

McCullum sacked as Test coach The architect of England's controversial Bazball approach to Test cricket is given his marching orders after a disappointing string of results.

Fleming said he was excited to work with Root and Brook, adding: "I know what it feels like to have the weight of leadership and international cricket take their toll."

Fleming was New Zealand's longest-serving captain across 80 Tests and he won 28 of them. He played for three English county teams and won a league title with Nottinghamshire in 2005.

"English cricket gave that to me and it is a privilege to have this chance to give something back," he said in a statement.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The England and Wales Cricket Board said it was allowing Fleming to spend time with family as he stepped down from his role at the Chennai Super Kings only this month.

Fleming led Chennai to a record five titles and 10 finals in the Indian Premier League. He also coached sister franchises in South Africa and the United States.

He will prepare England for three Tests in South Africa in December-January.

Fleming has only seven Tests in charge to ready England for the home Ashes series next year.

AP

World.title: Quick hits: Tongan dance moves bring joy, David Beckham hits the velodrome
World.content:
A para athletics race will be run again amid much drama, a Tongan weightlifter thrills the crowd with his dancing, and Nigeria wins the fashion stakes at the velodrome.

Here are the quick hits from day seven of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Para athletics race to be re-run

Eliza Ault-Connell was knocked out of the women's 1500m T54 final. (Getty Images: PA Images/Martin Rickett)

After a dramatic crash that took out two athletes, a disqualification that reordered the medal spots, and a subsequent protest, para athletics officials ordered a re-race of the women's 1,500m T54 final.

The race was thrown into chaos early on when Australian Eliza Ault-Connell went down heavily in a nasty crash, with Mauritian world champion Noemi Alphonse also knocked out of contention.

Canadian Nandini Sharma, who went on to finish second across the line, was disqualified for causing the crash.

After having that medal taken off her, Australia's Mikaela Dingley was promoted into the bronze medal position.

However, Australia and Mauritius protested the decision and, after Athletics Canada's appeal was dismissed, authorities decided to re-run the race, with some commentators saying it should have been stopped at the time of the crash.

Sharma will not be able to take to the start, with Canada saying it was "disappointed" in the decision.

"Having considered the multiple appeals that were submitted, the Jury has decided that the disqualification will stand," the statement read.

"While Athletics Canada is disappointed with this decision, we accept the process and look forward to Nandini competing again in the T53/54 400m race."

The re-race will be held on Friday 7:24pm AEST.

2. World record falls

Tara Neyland broke her own C4 4,000m Individual Pursuit world record. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Australian para cyclist Tara Neyland laid down a stunning time to top qualifying in the women's C4-C5 4,000m individual pursuit qualifying, setting a world record.

Her factored time was 4:45.796, achieved at an average speed of 49.716km/h.

Neyland later returned to the track to win gold in the final.

The 32-year-old is already a three-time world champion on the track and a two-time world champion on the road.

The women's individual pursuit distance officially moved from 3,000m to 4,000m on January 1, 2025, so competing at this distance is still relatively new.

Which perhaps accounts for England's Morgan Newbury breaking the world record in the C5 classification qualification period.

3. Tonga's dancing weightlifter

Josh Uikilifi treated spectators to his best dance moves. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

If weightlifting medals were handed out for post-lift moves, Tonga's Joshua Uikilifi would have topped the podium.

Uikilifi had the SEC Armadillo crowd eating out of the palm of his hand as he competed in the men's 110kg classification.

He treated spectators to some spectacular dance moves after each successful lift.

Uikilifi produced a total of 331kg to finish fourth behind Fiji's Taniela Rainibogi, who won gold with a Games record of 378kg.

4. Nigerian para cyclists turn heads

The Nigerians were the best dressed at the velodrome on day seven. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Australia dominated the medals on the opening day at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome, but it was Nigeria which turned heads.

The Nigerian para cyclists hit the track in eye-catching uniforms, reportedly inspired by the kit worn by the national men's football team at the 2018 FIFA World Cup.

Oyindamola Abdullahi Tijani and pilot Okeyah Bethel looked magnificent as they contested the men's tandem B 1,000m time trial.

They deservedly got the seal of approval across social media platforms.

For the record, Tijani and Bethel finished fifth in the final.

Scotland's Neil Fachie (pilot: Aaron Pope) won gold ahead of James Ball (Matthew Rotherham) of Wales.

Australia's Kane Perris (Luke Zaccaria) took bronze.

5. Ronaldo and Beckham in the velodrome

If you thought the only sightings of David Beckham and Ronaldo at a major global sporting event were going to be in North America this year, then we have news for you.

Yes, that's right, David Beckham and Ronaldo were at the Sir Chris Hoy velodrome in Glasgow, a stone's throw away from the footballing theatre of Celtic Park.

Well, David Beckham Elkatohchoongo and Ronaldo Singh Laitonjam were there, joining Rojit Singh Yanglem in India's team sprint squad.

"My father was a footballer in the national team, and he was a huge fan of David Beckham," Elkatohchoongo told AFP in 2023 at the Asian Games.

"When I was born in the hospital, they told my mum: if it's a boy, then it's David Beckham."

Laitonjam was also named after a footballer, not actually Ronaldo but Ronaldinho.

His father had, according to AFP, made a bet with his work colleagues that the Brazilian would score against England in the 2002 World Cup match they were watching.

The Barcelona legend promptly did, and minutes later Laitonjam senior received a phone call telling him that his wife was in labour.

"Just as the ball went in the goal, I must have started making an appearance," Laitonjam told The Hindu newspaper.

"I think my dad won some money that day. That's probably why I got that name. He felt I was very lucky for him."

David and Ronaldo could not add the necessary star power to the Indian team their namesakes may have demanded, though, finishing seventh and last in qualifying.

World.title: 'Never for sale': European nations vow World Cup boycott over FIFA plan
World.content:
European nations have agreed to boycott the World Cup and all other FIFA competitions in protest over president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in soccer's biggest tournament to private equity investors.

"UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions," the European soccer body said after an urgent online meeting of its 55 member nations.

On a seismic day in soccer politics, support in Asia and CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) for FIFA and Infantino was also shaken.

The next scheduled FIFA tournament is in weeks in Europe — the Women's Under-20 World Cup hosted by Poland from September 5 — and the four British federations comprise FIFA's only bidder to host the 2035 Women's World Cup. That decision is due on November 23.

"Some things are simply too important to sell," UEFA said in a statement. "The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale."

The strategy meeting was called to counter Infantino's offer of $US20 million ($28.45 million) to each of FIFA's 211 global members, which has to be accepted by mid-September.

Infantino's secret project to spin off its commercial operations in a new $US20 billion ($28.45 billion) subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), 20 per cent owned by private investors was revealed on Tuesday.

The core investor would be a New York investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

Infantino wrote to the 211 members — already the effective owners of FIFA as a non-profit association under Swiss law — that if they approved FFE, their promised $US10 million basic funding for the next four years would double to $US20 million. He projected their FIFA funding through 2038 would be $US86 million ($122 million) each, instead of about $US36 million ($51 million).

A breakdown of FIFA's bid to sell the World Cup Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to investors would grant them control over the World Cup.

"This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football," said UEFA, where Infantino was a staffer and its CEO-like general secretary when he was first elected to lead FIFA in 2016.

Infantino's high-stakes gambit now could threaten his previously secure 11-year presidency of FIFA as anger and frustration with him rise among soccer stakeholders, including three of the six continental bodies.

FIFA has set a November 18 deadline for potential candidates to declare in a presidential vote of the 211 members scheduled next March in Rabat, Morocco.

Infantino had seemed after the World Cup to have a clear path to being re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term in office until 2031, despite a furore over letting United States forward Folarin Balogun play against Belgium after a red card in his previous game.

"Game over, Gianni #InfantinOUT," the Football Supporters Europe group, which advises UEFA on fan issues such as ticket prices, posted after the boycott threat.

UEFA detailed why soccer officials fear external investors owning a stake in the global game's biggest events, including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women.

"The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever," UEFA said. "Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure."

Infantino has presented the private equity offer as a chance to "turbocharge" funding development of soccer across the world, where a majority of the 211 FIFA members rely on its funding.

Officials from about 40 UEFA members spoke at the urgent meeting, with anger expressed that FIFA is not using some of its multi-billion-dollar reserves to fund extra development programs.

"As a result of today's discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive," the European soccer body said, "unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership."

CONCACAF also released a statement saying its organisation was built on service, "transparent governance, and the long-term stewardship of football".

"History has shown FIFA and the football family what happens when the custodians of the game lose sight of these values," it said.

Deep concerns were raised about the lack of due process, the short deadline imposed, the lack of review or approval by relevant bodies, and the need for private investment to fund programs.

"For these reasons, CONCACAF and its 41 Member Associations have rejected the proposal," it said.

The associations called on their FIFA Council Members to engage FIFA to determine how existing reserves could be used to increase FIFA Forward funding for football development across the region, and urged that all matters follow proper governance processes.

CONCACAF did not threaten a boycott of FIFA competitions. However, Europe's 55 associations and CONCACAF's 41 would make nearly half of the 211 total votes available.

"FIFA's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football," the Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said in a letter to its 46 members of FIFA, warning of risks to their own competitions.

Sheikh Salman, an ally of Infantino since losing the FIFA presidential election to him in 2016, wrote: "Such an initiative will not succeed without the support of all the confederations, which is not the case now."

In a video message published Wednesday by FIFA, Infantino insisted spinning off its money-making operations was "an offer, not an obligation."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

A FIFA presentation for its members, co-written with its banking advisors from J.P. Morgan and seen by the AP, set a goal for FFE as "commercial rigour and expertise to better capitalise on broadcast rights, sponsorships and a growing tournament portfolio."

That growing portfolio would likely include adding more teams to FIFA competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup for men and women, and potentially staging them more often than every four years, including in the US.

FIFA adding teams, games and competitions would squeeze the value, status and space in the congested global fixture calendar for those that fund and are organised by the six continental soccer bodies like UEFA and the AFC.

A threatened World Cup boycott from Europe helped derail Infantino's 2021 plan to stage World Cups every two years instead of four.

AP/ABC

World.title: Australia's old friend wasn't at the Glasgow velodrome, but the old enemy was
World.content:
The crowds at the 2026 Commonwealth Games have varied in size and spirit.

Particularly at the Scottish Event Campus, not far from the city centre, casual fans will wander down and get a taste of the action if they've got time on their weekend.

It's school holiday time in Glasgow too, so plenty of families looking for a way to occupy the kids have made their way into the various arenas.

You may never get the chance to watch again, so a spot of 3x3 basketball or bowls, accompanied by some frankly excellent tunes and an overpriced carton of chips, is a decent way to spend four hours.

Aussie sprint stars through to 200m finals, gold rush at the velodrome Australia's track cycling squad claims three golds on the first day of competition at the velodrome, as Lachie Kennedy and Torrie Lewis fly into their second finals of the week.

That's especially true when the weather has been so dreary to start the Games.

But on a day when it dried out at last, thousands made a decidedly purposeful pilgrimage to the velodrome at the Glasgow International Arena, just next to the home ground of Celtic Football Club.

This was not something you happen upon. This was something you go to. This was the moment Scotland had been waiting for at the arena named for one of their favourite sons, Sir Chris Hoy.

Ironically, before every race it was a pre-recorded Sir Chris (the real thing might have caused a riot) and fellow Scottish icon Duncan Scott telling the crowd to quiet down — or "haud yer wheesht", as Scott said — for the starter's buzzer.

But even Sir Chris — the six-time Olympic, 11-time world and two-time Commonwealth cycling champion — couldn't have contained his house when it was Scotland's Neil Fache (along with pilot Aaron Pope) who won the first gold of the track cycling program for these Games in the men's tandem B 1,000m time trial.

Scots Neil Fachie MBE (left) and pilot Aaron Pope won the first gold medal of the cycling program in Glasgow. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

Australian Kane Perris won Australia's first medal in that event alongside pilot Luke Zaccaria, and earlier in the day, Tara Neyland had picked up Australia's first world record in any event at these Games when she clocked 4:49.648 in qualifying for the C4-5 4,000m individual pursuit.

She later went on to win gold, but only after the women's team pursuit squad started what the cycling team hopes will be a gold rush in Glasgow.

Trailing New Zealand at the halfway mark of the gold medal race against New Zealand, the team of Georgia Baker, Claudia Marcks, Alyssa Polites and Felicity Wilson-Haffenden put away their schedule and just started racing.

"That's my happy place. When we start racing, that's when I'm happiest. When the board goes away, and the hand signals come out, that's when I come into my own," 21-year-old gun Wilson-Haffenden said.

Women's team pursuit gold marked the start of what promises to be a big Games for Australian cycling. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"Just pedal. I was riding 50-cent coins by the end; the pedals weren't going around smooth but giving as much power as I had, grit the teeth, and get to the finish line."

England pipped their men's counterparts, and Jessica Gallagher was unable to defend her Birmingham gold in the tandem B sprint final after a tyre failure caused a nasty crash with the New Zealanders in the second race.

But, as pilot Jacqui Mengler-Mohr put it: "It's not how many times you fall, it's how many times you get back up."

Silver medallists Jessica Gallagher (right) and Jacqueline Mengler-Mohr had a nasty fall as they won tandem B sprint silver. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

And getting back up was exactly what the men's team sprinters did, going one better than the women's team and taking down their English rivals in the final.

They never looked like getting caught over the 1,000m race as Leigh Hoffman won a title as the leader of a new-look team with 23-year-old Danny Barber and 22-year-old Ryan Elliott.

The revamp came after the defection of Olympic gold medallist and sprint superstar Matthew Richardson, whose name Elliott wouldn't even utter when talking about the rivalry with Team England.

"I think it's definitely grown a lot since the swap and defection," he said.

"Between the GB guys maybe a bit less so but definitely between the defector himself."

Australian defector Richardson out of Games after fall Matt Richardson, a three-time Olympic medallist in Paris for Australia before he sensationally defected to the land of his birth, has been ruled out of the Commonwealth Games.

He wasn't the only departure after the team's gold medal at the Paris Olympics, with Matthew Glaetzer retiring and Tom Cornish pivoting to endurance events, making way for Elliott and Barber.

"There's a big change in the roster after Paris, and everyone's question then is: how well can our system back up? What's their depth?" he said.

"Us as the younger guys coming through wanted to prove we have depth in Australia and we're here because we're hungry."

Hoffman said he enjoyed riding with teammates who were 100 per cent in it for Australia.

Ryan Elliott (left), Danny Barber and Leigh Hoffman won team sprint gold in their new formation. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"It would've been great if he stayed with Australia but his heart was obviously never always in it, so good riddance," he said.

Richardson is no longer coming to Glasgow after an ugly fall during a keirin race in Japan just days ago, and Hoffman is disappointed he and Barber won't get a crack at him in the individual event.

"I would have loved for him to come here and race and see how I and Danny stack up against him," Hoffman said.

"I'm upset he's not here, but that is what it is. … I've got plenty of other fish to worry about."

England, Wales, Scotland, Australia and New Zealand are some of the world's strongest track cycling nations, with Malaysia's Azizul Awang and Nicholas Paul from Trinidad and Tobago threats for Hoffman and Barber.

But the good news is Hoffman isn't going anywhere.

"We checked his passport and his lineage," Elliott said.

"So he's good."

World.title: Ex-MAFS star Ridge Barredo sticking to weightlifting despite ugly injury
World.content:
Ridge Barredo's description of the knee injury that ended his Commonwealth Games weightlifting campaign is enough to turn most of us off even watching the sport for good.

"I heard it pop on the third attempt, I tried to give it my all and I heard it pop [out] and pop back in," he said of his failed third snatch attempt in the men's 110kg class.

"Just to feel it was a little bit scary. Initial pain was an eight or nine out of 10."

Barredo said it was the first time he had ever experienced an injury like that, sustained as he tried to throw 162 kilograms over his head.

Loading Instagram content

By the time he spoke to media, having been helped off the Armadillo stage, he said he was just "a little bit uncomfortable" and described the pain as down to a six or seven out of 10.

This was his third Commonwealth Games and the 30-year-old vowed to be back at Amdavad in four years.

"It's not the end. I'm still relatively young, still hungry for it, still want to be the best in Australia," he said.

"I'm not done yet, no way. Not a chance. I'll be back for sure. Four times, watch, mark my words."

And he said this difficult and painful journey is still preferable to a return to the scene that made his descriptor on Google not "athlete" or "weightlifter", but "internet personality".

That's thanks to his turn on reality TV show Married At First Sight three years ago.

One of only a handful of successful couples from the program, Barredo and wife Jade are still together.

Loading Instagram content

Jade and daughter Victoria were in the crowd watching as he suffered his injury.

And while the program worked out for him, Barredo says his TV days are over.

"My TV career is definitely done, I've found my partner. I'm off reality TV. Wouldn't recommend it," he said.

"If you want to have some fun in a toxic environment, go for it, but personally I wouldn't be going back."

He's not the only Games athlete shunning the reality TV scene (for now) with Scottish swimmer Katie Shanahan revealing she had to make a choice to continue swimming or go on Love Island last year.

'If you've got a lane, you've got a chance' An unexpected source kicks off another record-breaking night for Australian swimming as we get implicit and explicit reminders that we shouldn't take this for granted.

Shanahan opted not to enter the villa, ultimately winning silver in the women's 200m backstroke on the first night of the Glasgow swimming program.

"I'm the biggest Love Island fan ever. I've watched every season," Shanahan told BBC Scotland.

"Last year the producers asked me and [English swimmer] Abbie Wood if we would be interested in doing it.

"I couldn't go on, though, because [I was] focusing on the swimming, but who knows in the future?

"I was a bit tempted but the swimming had to come first."

Tech.title: Tim Cook hints at iCloud Plus tier for AI power users
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple may allow users to pay to increase their AI usage limits. During an earnings call on Thursday, Apple CEO Tim Cook said that he believes people will want to use Apple Intelligence and the upcoming Siri AI “a lot,” adding that “we will have some kind of upgrade possibilities on iCloud Plus where people can buy up the stack.”

This fall, Apple will broadly launch its long-delayed Siri AI with iOS 27, which can do things like answer questions about what’s on your screen and take action across your apps. It also includes a new standalone Siri AI app that offers a ChatGPT-like interface.

In June, Apple said that its AI features, including image generation, have “daily usage limits because they rely on powerful server models.” It added that “increased access” is available across most of its iCloud Plus plans, but it seems that Apple may want to add tiers for people who plan on using its AI features heavily.

Apple reported earning $30.74 billion in revenue from its services business over the past few months, which includes subscriptions like iCloud Plus, Apple TV, and Apple One.

Tech.title: Xbox CEO lays out priorities in memo after major ‘reset’
Tech.content:
After a massive Xbox “reset” that laid off thousands of employees and spun off four studios, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma wants to get Xbox back to growth. In a memo obtained by The Verge, Sharma told staff by the end of fiscal year 2027 (which runs through next June), “we will return XBOX to player and revenue growth.” Xbox will also “improve profits back in line with industry averages,” Sharma said. “Every function and studio will own part of that outcome.”

Since taking over Xbox in February, Sharma has made sweeping changes to attempt to turn things around. Previously, she has cited challenges like a low accountability margin, increasing component costs for hardware, an “over extended” slate of studios, and platform infrastructure that’s “not built for the battle ahead.” In addition to the major structural changes, Xbox made Gears of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution Xbox console exclusives and is planning to do more. Sharma has also set an ambitious and nearly impossible goal to make Xbox “one of the few companies that entertains more than a billion people each day.”

In Thursday’s memo, Sharma laid out four Xbox priorities for fiscal year 2027:

CORE: Strengthen our platform, led by console CONTENT: Grow great games into global franchises CREATION: Make Minecraft the world’s creator platform CONNECTION: Extend the worlds that fans love

Xbox will measure progress toward its goals in three “stages,” Sharma said. The first is to return to growth by the end of fiscal year 2027. The second is to turn its bets into growth; “In FY28 and FY29, our Four C’s and roadmap must move into businesses producing meaningful player value and revenue acceleration.” The third is to “scale what works,” and by fiscal year 2030, “our ambition is to be halfway to our long-term daily-player goal with sustained double-digit growth in players and engagement and industry leading margins.”

Sharma shared some vague numbers about Xbox’s current playerbase. “XBOX is one of the largest stadiums in the world, bringing together more than 100 million people every day, more than 500 million each month, and nearly one billion each year,” she wrote. She also noted that console “generates the majority of XBOX revenue and remains the foundation of our fandom” and that it is still Xbox’s “flagship experience.” Xbox’s OS, Game Pass, Windows, and streaming “become our platform for new players and developers.”

The company is also shifting its studio system from a decentralized model to one that’s “more focused around our strongest franchises and biggest new ideas,” Sharma said — something that’s already become evident with changes like the big new Fallout push. Xbox will build “long-term plans” for its biggest franchises “across film, television, consumer products, sponsorship, live experiences, and form new partnerships globally, including China.” Three Xbox franchises “already generate more than $1 billion annually,” though Sharma doesn’t specify which those are.

To grow its share in casual games, Xbox plans to lean on Candy Crush-maker King as well as Microsoft Causal Games, Sharma said. And Xbox is planning to invest in Minecraft “more than ever before.”

Tech.title: Apple’s iPhone and Mac sales keep growing despite RAM shortages
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple’s iPhone and Mac sales are on the rise even as a global memory shortage squeezes device makers. In its third-quarter earnings report released on Thursday, Apple revealed that iPhone sales jumped 22 percent to $54.25 billion and Mac sales increased 29 percent to $10.35 billion, driving the company’s overall revenue to $109.4 billion.

The company expects supply chain constraints to worsen in the coming months. During an earnings call, Apple chief financial officer Kevan Parekh said Apple expects “supply constraints to increase significantly” in the next quarter, adding the shortage will impact the iPhone, Mac, and iPad. Meanwhile, Apple CEO Tim Cook warned that the company predicts it will “pay even higher memory costs” in the coming months.

It’s the company’s last earnings report with Cook at the helm. Cook is set to step down on September 1st, with John Ternus, Apple’s vice president of hardware engineering, taking his place.

Apple raised prices across its Macs, iPads, and other devices in June as it contends with a RAM shortage expected to last until 2027 and beyond. The move also included a price hike for the company’s new MacBook Neo, which now costs $699 instead of $599. Since its debut in March, the Neo disrupted the affordable laptop market with its lightweight form factor and speedy performance.

Apple hasn’t raised the prices of its iPhones yet, but analysts predict that the iPhone 18 could cost up to $200 more when the lineup launches this fall. Apple is planning to widely release its more personalized Siri AI alongside the iPhone 18, allowing its assistant to answer questions about what’s on your screen, search across apps, and perform tasks, like adding events to your calendar.

This week, Apple also announced a new Upgrade program that will let you lease an iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, or Mac for a set monthly price.

Additionally, Apple reported $30.74 billion in services revenue, which incorporates subscriptions like Apple One and Apple TV. Parekh added during the earnings call that the company now has more than 1.5 billion subscribers across its services. Apple also reported $7.88 billion in revenue for wearables and a lower-than-expected $6.2 billion in iPad revenue.

Tech.title: The loss of Situational Awareness
Tech.content:
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.

I am not by any means an expert at finance but I think I do now have some advice for people who are: Do not name your hedge fund anything that will be hilarious if it blows up. Don’t use a name like “Long-Term Capital Management” or “Amaranth Advisors” (named for the floral symbol for immortality). Certainly do not call yourself “Situational Awareness,” which might as well just be “Hubris, Inc.”

Anyway, Situational Awareness, the hedge fund started by a 24-year-old former OpenAI employee that focuses on artificial intelligence bets, has sold most or all, depending on who’s reporting, of its entire public stock portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel after several bad weeks for AI stocks, and that’s the situation we are all now aware of. You may recall earlier this week I noted the market had gotten particularly nervous about AI risk; as it turns out, we have discovered one firm that was swimming without a bathing suit.

How bad is it? Well, according to CNBC, the fund was worth $45 billion at the start of July. It is now worth $10 billion, after the sale of assets to Griffin. The previous record holder on all-time trading losses was Archegos Capital Management, which lost $8 billion in 10 days in 2021, according to The Wall Street Journal. If these numbers hold, Situational Awareness’ AI bets lost three times as much.

Every detail of this disaster is funnier than the last. Situational Awareness had a staff of eight, of whom four were investment professionals. “The fund’s largest holdings at the end of the first quarter included Nebius Group, Sandisk, Micron and CoreWeave, according to filings,” CNBC wrote. “All four of those stocks are down more than 35 percent this month.” I expect we will hear more in the coming days, especially from the Wall Street professionals who were on the other side of these jokers’ trades.

“Basically, this investment firm will be kind of like a brain trust on AI.”

How did we get here? Situational Awareness LP was named for a series of facile essays about machine intelligence published by the improbably named Leopold Aschenbrenner, the 24-year-old mastermind of the hedge fund. “We are building machines that can think and reason,” he writes, betraying that he has no idea what thinking could possibly mean. “By 2025/26, these machines will outpace many college graduates. By the end of the decade, they will be smarter than you or I; we will have superintelligence, in the true sense of the word. Along the way, national security forces not seen in half a century will be unleashed, and before long, The Project will be on. If we’re lucky, we’ll be in an all-out race with the CCP; if we’re unlucky, an all-out war.”

There is a part of me that wants to go line by line to dunk on every claim here, beginning with the very first sentence, “You can see the future first in San Francisco,” but I am going to stifle the impulse. The essays are the theoretical underpinnings of the hedge fund. The upshot is that artificial general intelligence is real (lol) and will arrive in 2027 (lmao). So the entire point of the hedge fund was to dump as much money as possible into AI stocks and then get very, very rich.

“Basically, this investment firm will be kind of like a brain trust on AI,” Aschenbrenner told Dwarkesh Patel in a four-hour podcast interview, the preferred intellectual medium of the Silicon Valley elite. “We’re going to have way more situational awareness than any of the people who manage money in New York. We’re definitely going to do great on investing, but it’s the same sort of situational awareness that is going to be important for understanding what’s happening, being a voice of reason publicly, and being able to be in a position to advise.”

Why would these purportedly serious people buy in on a 24-year-old’s very first hedge fund?

Situational Awareness’ backers included Patrick and John Collison, who cofounded Stripe, and two Meta AI leaders, Daniel Gross and Nat Friedman. The fund’s director of research was Carl Shulman, who’d worked at Peter Thiel’s Clarium Capital. Eventually, Jane Street — the Wall Street firm budding young Effective Altruists, including Sam Bankman-Fried, join — bought in too. “Jane Street’s investment in Situational Awareness is particularly notable because the firm rarely allocates capital to outside money managers,” The Wall Street Journal wrote in June.

Why would these purportedly serious people buy in on a 24-year-old’s very first hedge fund? My best guess is that Aschenbrenner’s investors were relying on the social bona fides he had cultivated. Social proof is the laziest and most disastrous way to vet people — ask any Theranos investor, or for that matter, anyone who had Bernie Madoff managing their money — but I suppose it’s good enough for Silicon Valley.

At age 17, Aschenbrenner was called “an economics prodigy” by Tyler Cowen, a libertarian economist famous in certain Silicon Valley circles. Cowen’s Emergent Ventures even gave him a grant, according to Fortune. Aschenbrenner published essays in Works in Progress, a publication funded by Stripe. During his time at Columbia University, Aschenbrenner cofounded the college’s Effective Altruism chapter. After graduating in 2021 as Columbia University’s valedictorian at age 19, Aschenbrenner went on to work at the FTX Future Fund, the philanthropic arm of cryptocurrency exchange FTX, which collapsed after Sam Bankman-Fried’s fraud was revealed. Among his coworkers at the fund were William MacAskill, the philosopher-king of the Effective Altruism movement, and Avital Balwit, who would later become the chief of staff at Anthropic.
